policies.title: Fundamental Rights, HCBS Settings Requirements, Rights Restrictions and Individual Choice
policies.applies_to: All staff, care providers, consultants, volunteers and the standing committee of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To make sure individuals' fundamental rights are ensured, that the home meets the federal HCBS settings requirements, that any restriction is justified, time-limited and reviewed, and that services promote individual choice.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] ensures each individual's fundamental rights in accordance with Health-General Article §7-1002, Annotated Code of Maryland. This policy meets COMAR 10.22.02.10A(2) and DH Form DD.APP.1.1 p.1, item A(2) — Individuals' fundamental rights are ensured. It also meets COMAR 10.22.02.10A(3) and DH Form DD.APP.1.1 p.1, item A(3) — Services provided in a manner that promotes individual choice and the exercise of individual rights. The home is provider-owned or controlled, and therefore meets 42 CFR 441.301(c)(4): each person has a lease or equivalent residency agreement, privacy, a lockable bedroom door, roommate choice, and access to food and visitors. A modification of any of these conditions is allowed only under 42 CFR 441.301(c)(4)(vi), based on a specific assessed need documented in the person-centered plan. Rights restrictions not related to challenging behavior are reviewed by the standing committee, which sets time frames (COMAR 10.22.02.14E). [AGENCY NAME] signs and keeps current the Community Settings Rule attestation on the DDA Addendum for Licensed Services and Sites (MDH Form DD.ADD.1.0) for the home.

definitions.definition: The rights of individuals receiving services under Health-General Article §7-1002, including dignity, privacy, freedom from abuse and neglect, and participation in decisions about one's life.
Any limitation of a fundamental right or a settings-rule condition (e.g., locked food storage, limited visitors, door locks, restricted access to money or property).
A requirement of 42 CFR 441.301(c)(4) for provider-controlled residences: lease or equivalent agreement, privacy, lockable bedroom doors, roommate choice, and access to food and visitors.
The committee under COMAR 10.22.02.14E that reviews rights restrictions, with equal numbers of licensee staff and non-employees.
A person who advocates for the individual, such as a family member, guardian or friend.

procedures: At or before move-in, the Program Director reviews the individual's rights in plain language with the individual and the proponent, using the person's preferred communication method, and gives a written copy. The review is documented in the record.

Each individual receives a residency agreement that serves as the lease or equivalent legally enforceable agreement, as described in PCS-01. The agreement is signed before move-in or at move-in, and a copy is given to the individual.

Each individual's bedroom has a door that locks, and the individual (and staff as needed for emergencies) has a key. The Program Director verifies and documents this during the pre-occupancy checklist and at each quarterly environmental check (HE-01).

Each individual has a private bedroom unless a different arrangement was approved by DDA and chosen by the person. Where a person shares a room, the Program Director documents the person's choice of roommate and revisits it whenever the person asks.

Individuals may have visitors at the times they choose, subject only to modifications documented under 42 CFR 441.301(c)(4)(vi). Staff do not require advance notice, approval or sign-in conditions that are not in the person-centered plan.
Individuals have access to food and drink at all times, including a place to store and prepare food, unless a modification is documented in the plan with an assessed need (see HE-02).
Staff knock and wait for permission before entering a bedroom or bathroom unless there is an emergency. Personal care is provided privately.

Staff offer choices daily, including meals, clothing, schedule, activities, community outings, how money is spent, and who provides support when possible. Staff record choices made and any choice that could not be honored and why.
Staff support communication so that each person can express choices, using the supports in the IP and PA-05.
Staff never impose a rule, restriction or house practice that limits a right. A restriction that staff think is needed is submitted in writing to the Program Director, who works with the IP team.

A proposed restriction not related to challenging behavior must document: the specific assessed need, positive interventions and supports tried, less intrusive methods tried, the description of the condition, data collection and review plan, a time limit, assurance that the restriction causes no harm, and the individual’s or proponent’s informed consent (PA-11). The restriction must be in the person-centered plan before implementation (42 CFR 441.301(c)(4)(vi)).

The standing committee reviews each rights restriction not related to challenging behavior and sets time frames for review (COMAR 10.22.02.14E). The committee’s decision, time frame and any conditions are recorded in the minutes. Members involved in the individual's case do not decide on it.
Restrictions related to challenging behavior are handled under PA-08 and PA-09, not this policy.

The Program Director tracks each restriction on a Rights Restriction Log, with start date, review date and end date, and removes the restriction as soon as the need ends or the time frame expires unless the committee renews it.

The Program Director reviews the Community Settings Rule attestation on the site addendum annually and whenever the home changes, and does not sign it unless the home meets each condition. Corrections are made before signing.

Staff are trained on rights and choice at orientation, within 3 months of hire (COMAR 10.22.02.11D), and annually (SP-03). Any suspected rights violation is reported to the Program Director immediately and handled under PA-04, PA-06 or BP-01 as applicable.

responsibilities.duty: Adopts this policy, signs the Community Settings Rule attestation, and ensures that the home meets each condition.
Reviews rights with individuals, keeps the Rights Restriction Log, verifies lockable doors and access to food and visitors, and brings proposed restrictions to the IP team and committee.
Reviews rights restrictions not related to challenging behavior, sets time frames, and keeps minutes. Members refrain from decisions on cases they were involved in.
Honor rights and choices, never impose unapproved restrictions, and report concerns.
Exercise rights and choices, and consent to or decline proposed restrictions.

documentation: Signed rights review for each individual
Residency agreement or lease
Pre-occupancy and quarterly environmental checks showing lockable doors and access to food and visitors
Person-centered plan documentation for any settings-rule modification
Rights Restriction Log
Standing committee minutes and decisions on restrictions
Daily choice documentation
Signed Community Settings Rule attestation on the DDA site addendum

policies.title: Privacy, Confidentiality and HIPAA
policies.applies_to: All staff, care providers, consultants, volunteers and standing committee members of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To protect the confidentiality and privacy of every individual's personal and health information in paper and electronic form.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] maintains confidentiality for each individual as required by Health-General Article §7-1010, Annotated Code of Maryland. This policy meets COMAR 10.22.02.10A(4) and DH Form DD.APP.1.1 p.1, item A(4) — Confidentiality for each individual as per Health-General Article §7-1010. [AGENCY NAME] also follows the HIPAA Privacy and Security Rules (45 CFR Parts 160 and 164) for protected health information. Records are kept at the site where the person is served (COMAR 10.22.02.13A). Information is released only with a valid written authorization or when the law requires or permits it. Electronic records comply with HIPAA privacy and security rules and are backed up and stored off-site (COMAR 10.22.02.13E). Standing committee members must keep confidentiality under Health-General §7-1010 (COMAR 10.22.02.14E).

definitions.definition: Any information that identifies an individual or relates to the person's services, health, behavior, finances, family or history, in any form.
Individually identifiable health information protected under 45 CFR Parts 160 and 164.
A written, signed, dated release by the individual or legal decision-maker that states what information may be shared, with whom, for what purpose, and for how long.
Sharing only the information needed for the purpose.

procedures: At admission, the Program Director explains confidentiality and privacy practices to the individual and proponent in plain language, gives a written notice of privacy practices, and records the acknowledgment.

Each staff member, consultant, volunteer and standing committee member signs a confidentiality agreement before access to any information and annually after that. Signed agreements are filed in personnel or committee records.

Records are stored at the site in locked cabinets, or in a locked room, accessible only to authorized staff. Records are never left unattended or visible to visitors, other individuals, or the public.

Electronic records require unique user names and passwords. No password is shared, and each user's access is limited to what the job requires. The Program Director removes access on the same day a staff member leaves or changes roles.

Computers, tablets and phones that hold PHI use screen locks and encryption where available. PHI is not stored on personal devices, in personal email, or on social media. Texting PHI is prohibited unless through a secure system approved by [AGENCY NAME].
Electronic records are backed up regularly and stored off-site in a secure manner (COMAR 10.22.02.13E; see EP-05). The Program Director confirms and logs backup checks at least monthly.
Staff discuss individuals' information only with those who need it to provide services, and never in common areas, in the community, or within hearing of other individuals or visitors.

Information is released only with a valid, current written authorization, or when permitted or required by law, for example to DDA, OHCQ, Adult Protective Services, law enforcement, or emergency medical personnel in an emergency. Each release is recorded in the individual's record on a disclosure log with the date, recipient, content and purpose, and who approved it.

In a medical emergency, staff send the individual's medical information with the person to emergency personnel so it is readily accessible (COMAR 10.22.02.13C; see HW-02). This is recorded on the disclosure log.
Individuals and their authorized representatives may request to see their records. The Program Director responds in the time required by law and documents the request and response.

Photographs, videos and other images of individuals are taken or shared only with written consent. Individuals’ names and images are not used in publicity or fundraising without written authorization.

Standing committee members receive only the information necessary to the review and return or securely destroy materials after meetings. Minutes use identifiers that protect confidentiality (COMAR 10.22.02.14E).

Staff report any suspected or actual breach (lost record, misdirected fax or email, unauthorized access, stolen device) to the Program Director immediately. The Program Director investigates within 1 working day, mitigates harm, notifies the affected individual and proponent, notifies others as required by law, and records the breach and corrective action. [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] reviews each breach.
Staff who breach confidentiality face corrective action up to and including termination, and a violation that is also an incident is reported under PA-06.
Records are retained for at least 6 years and then destroyed securely, shredded or electronically wiped, with a destruction log (see REC-01).
Confidentiality is covered in orientation and refreshed annually (see SP-03). The Program Director audits record security at least quarterly and records the results.

responsibilities.duty: Adopts this policy, designates a privacy official, reviews each breach, and ensures backups and security controls are in place.
Controls record access, secures records at the site, manages the disclosure log, investigates breaches and performs quarterly audits.
Sign confidentiality agreements, access only what they need, protect information, and report breaches immediately.
May authorize or decline releases and request access to records.

documentation: Notice of privacy practices acknowledgment
Signed confidentiality agreements (staff, volunteers, consultants, committee members)
Signed authorizations for release
Disclosure log
Access lists and user account records
Backup verification log
Breach reports and corrective actions
Quarterly record security audits
Record destruction log

policies.title: Grievances and Complaints
policies.applies_to: All staff, individuals, proponents and the standing committee of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To give individuals and their proponents a clear, safe and effective way to raise grievances and complaints, to ensure prompt resolution, and to protect them from retaliation.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] implements a grievance process with safeguards that protect against retaliatory actions for the filing of any grievance. This policy meets COMAR 10.22.02.10A(5) and DH Form DD.APP.1.1 p.1, item A(5) — Implementation of a grievance process (the regulation adds: with safeguards which protect against retaliatory actions for the filing of any grievance). [AGENCY NAME] gives each individual and proponent enough information about the grievance process to use it (COMAR 10.22.02.10D; see DG-01). Individuals and proponents may also complain directly to the MDH Office of Health Care Quality, Developmental Disabilities Team, at 410-402-8100 or 877-402-8220, at any time and without first using the agency process. OHCQ may investigate complaints through announced or unannounced visits (COMAR 10.22.02.04D). Abuse, neglect, exploitation and other reportable incidents are not handled only as grievances; they are reported and investigated under PA-06 and BP-01.

definitions.definition: Any complaint or expression of dissatisfaction by an individual or proponent about services, staff, rights, the home, or any decision by [AGENCY NAME], whether oral or written.
Any adverse action, threat, harassment, loss of service or privilege, or change in treatment because someone filed or supported a grievance.
The person designated by [AGENCY NAME] to receive and track grievances: [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] or designee.

procedures: At admission and annually, the Program Director gives each individual and proponent a written grievance notice in plain language and accessible format. It explains how to file, who to tell, the response time frames, protection from retaliation, and the OHCQ complaint line (410-402-8100 / 877-402-8220). The Program Director reviews it aloud and records that this was done (see DG-01).
The notice is posted in a common area at the home where individuals can see it, and updated whenever a name or phone number changes. Contact information for the Grievance Coordinator is [PHONE].

A grievance may be made orally, in writing, by sign or assistive communication, or through a proponent, and with or without a form. Any staff member who hears a grievance accepts it, does not discourage it, and gives it to the Program Director by the end of the shift.
Staff help anyone who needs assistance to file a grievance, including writing it down, interpreting or using a communication device, or contacting a proponent or advocate of their choice.

The Grievance Coordinator logs the grievance on the day received with the date, who filed it, what it is about, and who received it. Within 2 working days the Coordinator acknowledges it to the person who filed it.

If the grievance alleges abuse, neglect, exploitation, injury, a rights violation or other reportable incident, the person receiving it also reports it immediately under PA-06 and BP-01, and the Coordinator confirms that the report was made.
If the grievance is about the Program Director or Coordinator, it goes directly to [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] or the Governing Body, who appoints someone not involved to handle it.
The Coordinator makes sure that no one involved in the complaint investigates or decides it alone. The Coordinator interviews those involved, reviews records and tries to resolve the matter promptly.

As an agency standard, the Coordinator gives the person who filed a written or otherwise accessible response within 10 working days of receipt. The response states what was found, the action taken or the reason for none, and how to appeal. If more time is needed, the Coordinator tells the person why and gives a new date.

If the person is dissatisfied, he or she may appeal to [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] or the Governing Body, who reviews the matter and responds in writing. The person is also reminded that they can contact OHCQ and, as appropriate, DDA or their DDA coordinator of community services.

Anti-retaliation safeguards: staff are told in writing that retaliation is prohibited. The Program Director monitors the person's services, schedule and treatment for 90 days after filing, and records follow-up contacts with the person.
Any employee who retaliates or threatens retaliation is subject to discipline up to termination. The employee is removed from duties involving the person during the review where necessary.

The Coordinator records the final outcome, the date, the person’s satisfaction and any corrective action in the grievance log. Grievances are filed apart from the individual's record where appropriate to protect confidentiality (PA-03).

The Coordinator gives the standing committee and QA process a de-identified summary of grievances, outcomes and trends at least quarterly (GOV-03). Corrective actions for patterns are tracked until complete.

When OHCQ opens a complaint investigation, [AGENCY NAME] cooperates fully and provides records. Within 10 working days of receiving findings, or at the exit conference, [AGENCY NAME] submits a plan of correction (COMAR 10.22.02.04E), as described in REC-02.

responsibilities.duty: Adopts the process, hears appeals, handles grievances about the Program Director, and enforces the anti-retaliation rule.
Logs, acknowledges, investigates and responds to grievances, monitors for retaliation, and reports trends.
Distributes and posts the notice, reviews it with each person, and ensures that staff accept and forward grievances.
Accept grievances, help people file them, never retaliate, and forward them the same shift.
Reviews grievance trends and policy as part of rights protection.

documentation: Signed acknowledgment of the grievance notice for each individual and proponent
Posted grievance notice
Grievance log
Written responses and appeal decisions
Retaliation monitoring notes
Quarterly grievance trend summaries
Any related incident reports

policies.title: Nondiscrimination and Communication Access
policies.applies_to: All staff, care providers, consultants and volunteers of [AGENCY NAME], and all applicants, individuals and proponents
policies.purpose: To make sure services and employment are provided without discrimination and that individuals and proponents can communicate and participate fully.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] provides services without discrimination. This policy meets COMAR 10.22.02.10A(6) and DH Form DD.APP.1.1 p.1, item A(6) — Services are provided without discrimination. [AGENCY NAME] does not discriminate on the basis of race, color, national origin, language, religion, sex, gender identity, sexual orientation, age, disability, or any other characteristic protected by law, in admission, services or employment, consistent with the Americans with Disabilities Act and Title VI of the Civil Rights Act. As required by COMAR 10.22.02.11E, [AGENCY NAME] maintains a written job description for each position and a written policy to prevent employment discrimination. [AGENCY NAME] provides interpreters, accessible formats and communication supports at no cost to individuals and proponents.

definitions.definition: Treating a person differently or less favorably, or denying equal access to services or employment, because of a protected characteristic.

A change in policy, practice, environment or communication that lets a person with a disability or limited English proficiency have equal access, unless it would be an undue hardship or a fundamental alteration.
Interpreters, translated or large-print or plain-language materials, assistive technology, augmentative communication and other supports that enable effective communication.

procedures: The governing body adopts this policy. The Program Director posts a nondiscrimination notice at the home and on any website, naming the person to contact with concerns: [ADMINISTRATOR NAME], [PHONE].

Referral and admission decisions follow PCS-01 and are based on ability to meet the person's identified needs and the home's licensed capacity and compatibility. Decisions are never made on a protected characteristic. The reason for any denial is recorded in the referral file.

At referral and at admission, the Program Director asks each individual and proponent about preferred language, communication method, hearing, vision, literacy and any accommodations needed. The answers are recorded in the record and in the Support Summary (PA-01).

The Program Director arranges free qualified interpreters, including sign language, for individuals and proponents who need them for meetings, planning, health appointments and rights reviews. Family members and other individuals are not used as interpreters except at the person's own request, which is documented.

Vital documents (residency agreement, rights notice, grievance notice, consent forms, emergency plan summary) are made available in the person's preferred language and accessible format, such as plain language, large print, braille, audio or pictures, on request and without delay.
Staff learn and use each person's communication methods and devices, keep devices charged and available, and document any communication barrier or changes.

The Program Director reviews physical accessibility. The home’s wheelchair accessibility status, including entrances, bathrooms and bedrooms, is accurately stated on the DDA site addendum, and any accommodation requested by a current or prospective resident is evaluated individually (see HE-01).

Accommodation requests are recorded on an Accommodation Log with the date, request, decision, date implemented, and follow-up. Denials of a request are made only by [ADMINISTRATOR NAME], in writing with reasons, and the person is told how to file a grievance (PA-04).

Employment: [AGENCY NAME] recruits, hires, trains, schedules, pays, disciplines and terminates without discrimination. Each position has a written job description that lists essential duties and qualifications, reviewed at least annually (COMAR 10.22.02.11E).

Employees may request reasonable accommodations. The Program Director or [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] discusses the request, documents it and decides promptly. Medical information about employees is kept separate from personnel files (see SP-04).
Staff are trained on nondiscrimination, cultural humility and communication access at orientation and annually (SP-03).

Anyone may report discrimination to the Program Director or [ADMINISTRATOR NAME], or file a grievance under PA-04. Retaliation is prohibited. Reports are investigated within 10 working days and the outcome is recorded.
Discrimination involving a threat to health or safety, or abuse or neglect, is also reported under PA-06 and BP-01.
The standing committee and QA process receive a summary of accommodation requests, discrimination complaints and communication-access gaps at least annually (GOV-03).

responsibilities.duty: Adopts the policy, approves job descriptions and the employment nondiscrimination policy, and decides on denied accommodations.
Assesses communication needs, arranges interpreters and formats, maintains the Accommodation Log and posts notices.
Use each person's communication method, treat everyone equally and respectfully, and report discrimination.
Tell the agency what accommodations and communication supports are needed.

documentation: Posted nondiscrimination notice
Communication needs assessment in the record and Support Summary
Interpreter and accessible-format records
Accommodation Log
Written job descriptions for all positions
Written employment nondiscrimination policy
Referral denial reasons
Discrimination reports and outcomes
Annual accommodation summary for QA

policies.title: Reportable Incidents and Investigations
policies.applies_to: All staff, care providers, consultants, volunteers and the standing committee of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To make sure that all incidents are identified, reported, investigated and reviewed according to the DDA Policy on Reportable Incidents and Investigations (PORII), and that findings are used to protect individuals.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] reports and investigates all incidents in accordance with DDA's Policy on Reportable Incidents and Investigations (PORII). This policy meets COMAR 10.22.02.10A(7) and DH Form DD.APP.1.1 p.1, item A(7) — All incidents are reported and investigated in accordance with DDA's Policy on Reportable Incidents and Investigations (PORI, revised 10/1/2007). The agency follows the version of the PORII currently in effect, including any revision after 10/1/2007, and the incident levels, report deadlines, forms and investigation requirements stated in it. Procedures and forms are reviewed against the current DDA PORII at least annually and whenever DDA issues a revision. The standing committee reviews the incident protocol and all incidents (COMAR 10.22.02.14E). OHCQ monitors compliance and investigates incidents and complaints (COMAR 10.22.02.03 and .04).

definitions.definition: Any event listed or described as reportable in the current DDA PORII, including injuries, abuse, neglect, exploitation, deaths, missing persons, medication errors, restraint use, serious illness, police involvement and property or other events.
DDA's Policy on Reportable Incidents and Investigations, as currently in effect.
The person designated by [AGENCY NAME] to ensure incident reporting and investigation are completed on time: [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] or designee.
An OHCQ investigation of immediate jeopardy, which OHCQ starts within 2 working days (COMAR 10.22.02.03).
[AGENCY NAME]'s written response to survey findings (COMAR 10.22.02.04E).

procedures: First priority: whoever discovers an incident makes sure the individual is safe and gets needed medical care (call 911 in an emergency), separates the person from any alleged abuser, and preserves the scene and evidence (see HW-02 and BP-01).

The staff member who witnessed or found out about the incident notifies the shift lead and the Program Director or on-call administrator immediately, by phone, and does not wait until the end of the shift.

The Program Director or on-call administrator determines the PORII incident level and reports to DDA, OHCQ and other agencies (Adult Protective Services, Child Protective Services or law enforcement as applicable) by the deadline and by the method that the current PORII specifies for that level. The report is made by the deadline even if some information is not yet known, and is supplemented later.

The Program Director notifies the individual's guardian, family or proponent, and the DDA coordinator of community services, as required by PORII and consistent with the individual's wishes and confidentiality (PA-03), and records the time, person notified and who made the notice.

The staff member involved completes the incident report on the current DDA form before leaving the shift, stating facts only: who, what, when, where, how discovered, injuries, actions taken and notifications. Reports are not altered after submission. Additions are made as dated addenda.
The Incident Coordinator confirms every required report was submitted on time and keeps the confirmation in the incident file.

The Incident Coordinator assigns a trained investigator who is not involved in the incident and has no conflict of interest (PA-12). Where PORII or the facts require, DDA, OHCQ or law enforcement investigates, and [AGENCY NAME] cooperates fully and does not interfere.

The investigator begins promptly, secures evidence, interviews the individual (with support), witnesses and staff, reviews records and schedules, and completes a written report within the time limits that PORII sets for the incident level. The investigation addresses cause, whether any policy, rights or IP requirements were violated, and contributing factors.

Staff alleged to be involved in abuse, neglect or exploitation are removed from contact with individuals during the investigation, with no loss of pay unless the law or policy allows, and are told not to discuss the matter with witnesses. Retaliation against anyone who reports is prohibited (PA-04).
The Program Director puts immediate protective and corrective steps in place, such as changes in supervision, staff retraining, repairs or health follow-up, and documents the date each is done.

The Incident Coordinator sends the completed investigation report and any required follow-up to DDA and OHCQ as required by PORII, and gives the individual and proponent the outcome as the law allows.

The standing committee reviews the incident protocol and all incidents, including investigation findings and corrective actions, at its meetings. A member involved in an incident, or in its investigation, may not take part in the decision on that incident (COMAR 10.22.02.14E). Minutes are kept and are confidential.

The QA process tracks incident counts, types, times, locations and staff involved, analyzes trends at least quarterly, and responds promptly when health or safety is at risk (COMAR 10.22.02.14B; GOV-03).

When OHCQ visits or investigates, the Program Director gives access to the individuals, staff and records. For Priority 1 (immediate jeopardy) investigations, OHCQ begins within 2 working days (COMAR 10.22.02.03), so the Program Director keeps incident files ready at all times.

[AGENCY NAME] submits a plan of correction at the exit conference or within 10 working days of receiving findings, or sooner if OHCQ requires it (COMAR 10.22.02.04E). Only the OHCQ Director may grant an extension, up to 30 days. If a POC is unacceptable, [AGENCY NAME] submits a revised POC within 10 working days (COMAR 10.22.02.04F).

Staff are trained on incident recognition and reporting at orientation and annually (SP-03). The Program Director checks the incident forms, levels, deadlines and contacts against the current DDA PORII at least annually and updates this policy and staff training after each revision.

responsibilities.duty: Ensures resources for investigations, reviews serious incidents, and approves the plan of correction.
Determines level and tracks deadlines, assigns uninvolved investigators, files reports and keeps incident files.
Ensures immediate safety, makes required notifications, and implements corrective actions.
Respond to the emergency, report immediately, document factually, and cooperate with investigations.
Reviews the incident protocol and every incident while excluding involved members from decisions, and maintains confidentiality.

documentation: Completed incident reports on the current DDA form
Proof of timely reports to DDA, OHCQ and other agencies
Notification log for guardians, families and the DDA coordinator of community services
Investigation reports, evidence and corrective-action records
Standing committee minutes
Incident trend analyses
OHCQ findings, plan(s) of correction and OHCQ acceptance
Annual PORII comparison record

policies.title: Medication Administration (MATP) and Compliance with Nursing Delegation (COMAR 10.27.11)
policies.applies_to: All direct support staff, Medication Technicians, the delegating Registered Nurse, the Program Director and any consultant or volunteer present in the group home
policies.purpose: To make sure every medication and treatment given to a person living in the home is given safely, by a person who is trained and authorized to give it, and in the way DDA's medication curriculum and Maryland nursing delegation rules require.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] administers medications only in accordance with DDA's medication curriculum, the Medication Administration Training Program (MATP). This policy meets COMAR 10.22.02.10 A(8) (DH Form DD.APP.1.1 p.1) — Medications administered in accordance with MATP, and COMAR 10.22.02.12D. [AGENCY NAME] also complies with COMAR 10.27.11 (Nursing delegation). This policy meets COMAR 10.22.02.10 A(9) (DH Form DD.APP.1.1 p.1) — Compliance with COMAR 10.27.11. Unlicensed staff may give medications or treatments only when they are certified by the Board of Nursing as Medication Technicians and are working under the delegation of a Registered Nurse (RN). Oral solid medications are supplied in unit-dose packaging unless the person's Individual Plan (IP) says otherwise. Medication for a person who will be away from the home is packaged separately. [AGENCY NAME] asks the pharmacy to generate Medication Administration Records (MARs), Treatment Administration Records (TARs) and physician order forms. Staff follow the detailed procedures in NU-01 through NU-07. No one gives a medication or treatment unless trained, certified where required, and delegated or otherwise authorized to do so.

definitions.definition: The Medication Administration Training Program, DDA's medication curriculum that unlicensed staff must follow when administering medication.
An unlicensed staff member certified by the Maryland Board of Nursing to administer medications under the delegation of an RN.
An RN's assignment of a nursing task to a trained unlicensed person, under COMAR 10.27.11, with the RN remaining accountable for assessing, teaching and supervising.
The Medication Administration Record and Treatment Administration Record on which each dose or treatment is documented at the time it is given, refused or missed.
Medication that the pharmacy packages as individual doses, for example blister cards or single-dose pouches.

procedures: Before a staff member may give any medication or treatment, the Program Director checks and records that the person is at least 18, holds current First Aid and CPR certification with an in-person skills check, and holds current Board of Nursing Medication Technician certification. Documentation goes in the personnel file (SP-04).

The Program Director confirms that the delegating RN has assessed the person, the task and the staff member, and has issued written delegation under COMAR 10.27.11 before the staff member performs any delegated task. The delegation is filed in the individual's record (NU-07).

Staff who give medications follow DDA's MATP curriculum for every dose, including the required checks of the person, the medication, the dose, the time and the route, and hand washing before and after (PA-15).
The Program Director or RN obtains orders and medications from the prescriber and pharmacy according to NU-01. Staff accept only medication with a current prescriber order and a pharmacy label.
At each pharmacy order the Program Director asks the pharmacy for unit-dose packaging of oral solids, unless the IP states a different method. Any exception is written in the IP.

At each pharmacy order the Program Director asks the pharmacy to supply pharmacy-generated MARs, TARs and physician order forms, and checks the MAR against the written order on receipt. Differences are resolved with the prescriber or pharmacy before any dose is given.

When a person will be away from the home (visit, day program, hospital, overnight stay), the Medication Technician prepares that medication in separate packaging, labeled for that person and trip, and documents on the MAR what was sent and who received it. Medications returned are counted and reconciled on return.
Staff give medications and store them as described in NU-02, and handle controlled drugs, including counts, under NU-03.
Staff document each dose on the MAR immediately after giving it. Refusals, held doses and omissions are recorded with the reason. Staff never document a dose in advance.

Any medication error is handled under NU-04: the person is checked for harm, the prescriber, RN or poison control is contacted as needed, the Program Director is told, and any required incident report is filed (PA-06).

The RN reviews MARs and TARs, observes medication administration and re-evaluates delegation at the intervals the RN sets in the delegation plan, and at least whenever the person's condition or medications change (NU-07).

Staff do not give a medication or treatment they have not been trained and delegated to give. They call the RN or the on-call supervisor instead. If a certified Medication Technician is not on shift, the Program Director arranges coverage immediately (SP-01).
Whether a person may self-administer medication is determined only through the assessment process in NU-05 and recorded in the IP. Staff do not assume a person can self-medicate.

The Program Director checks expiration of each Medication Technician certification and each RN delegation monthly and removes any staff member from medication duty on the day the certification or delegation lapses.
The QA standing committee reviews medication error data at least quarterly (GOV-03).

responsibilities.duty: Assigns only certified and delegated staff to medication duty, verifies credentials monthly, ensures packaging and pharmacy-generated forms are requested, and reviews errors.
Assesses, delegates, teaches, supervises and re-evaluates under COMAR 10.27.11, and reviews MARs and TARs.
Administers medications per MATP and delegation, documents every dose, and reports errors, refusals and changes in condition at once.
Do not give medications or delegated treatments. Support the person's routine and notify the Medication Technician or RN of concerns.
Reviews medication error trends and corrective actions.

documentation: Board of Nursing Medication Technician certification, First Aid/CPR and skills-check records in each personnel file
RN delegation orders and re-evaluations in the individual record
Pharmacy-generated MARs, TARs and physician order forms
Medication packaging and absent-individual medication log
Medication error and incident reports
Monthly credential verification log

policies.title: Positive Behavior Support, Behavior Plans and Medications Used to Modify Behavior
policies.applies_to: All staff, the Program Director, clinicians who develop behavior plans, prescribers, the standing committee and the governing body
policies.purpose: To make sure anyone whose behavior requires intervention is supported with positive, person-centered approaches first and receives the safeguards Maryland regulations require, and that any restriction is planned, approved, tracked and reviewed.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] provides every individual whose behaviors require intervention with the safeguards required by COMAR 10.22.10. This policy meets COMAR 10.22.02.10 A(10) (DH Form DD.APP.1.1 p.1) — Any individual whose behaviors require intervention receive the safeguards required by regulation. Behavior plans are written and approved as COMAR 10.22.10.05 requires. Medications used to modify behavior follow COMAR 10.22.10.07, and monitoring follows COMAR 10.22.10.11. [AGENCY NAME] verifies the current text of these rules at each annual policy review (CS-01) and updates this policy to match. Proactive, person-centered supports come first, and staff document that less restrictive options were tried. The standing committee approves every behavior plan that uses restrictive techniques (COMAR 10.22.02.14E(1)(d)). Every restrictive technique used under a plan is tracked in the QA system as COMAR 10.22.02.14B requires: who, which technique, date and time, whether it was an emergency use or planned, and its effectiveness. Restraint and seclusion are covered separately in PA-09.

definitions.definition: Person-centered strategies that teach skills, change the environment and reinforce desired behavior to reduce challenging behavior, without relying on restrictions.
A written plan, part of or attached to the Individual Plan, that describes the behavior, its likely function, positive supports, any approved restrictive techniques and how progress is measured.
Any intervention that limits a person's movement, access or rights as part of managing behavior, including those described in PA-09.
A medication prescribed primarily to influence behavior rather than to treat a diagnosed medical or psychiatric condition, subject to COMAR 10.22.10.07.
The committee established under COMAR 10.22.02.14E with equal numbers of agency staff and non-employees (individuals, proponents or community members).

procedures: When staff see behavior that may put the person or others at risk or interferes with daily life, they record it in the daily documentation (PA-01) and tell the Program Director the same day.

The Program Director convenes the person's team, including the person, their proponent or legal decision-maker and a qualified clinician, within a time set by the team to review the behavior, possible causes (pain, illness, medication effects, communication needs, environment, trauma) and the supports needed.

The team first uses positive, proactive approaches: skill teaching, communication supports, environmental changes, choice-making and reinforcement. Each approach tried, its dates and its results are documented to show that less restrictive options were attempted before any restriction is considered.
If a behavior plan is needed, a qualified clinician writes it following COMAR 10.22.10.05, in plain language, with the person and proponent involved, and attaches it to the Individual Plan (PCS-02).
Informed consent for the plan, and for any medication used to modify behavior, is obtained from the person or legal decision-maker as described in PA-11 before implementation.

A behavior plan that includes any restrictive technique is not implemented until the standing committee has reviewed and approved it. Committee members involved in the person's case do not vote on it.

Medications used to modify behavior are prescribed and reviewed in line with COMAR 10.22.10.07. The RN and prescriber review the ongoing need, dose, side effects and effect on behavior, and the review is documented (NU-06, NU-07).

Before implementing the plan, the Program Director makes sure every staff member who works with the person has been trained on it, including prevention strategies and any technique they may use. Training is documented (SP-03).
Staff implement the plan exactly as written. They document each behavior incident, each strategy used and the outcome in daily documentation.

Each use of a restrictive technique is entered in the restrictive technique log the same shift: who, which technique, date and time, emergency or planned, and effectiveness. Unplanned use is reported as an incident (PA-06).

The Program Director and clinician monitor the plan under COMAR 10.22.10.11. They review data at least monthly, and more often if behavior or restriction use increases, and revise the plan when it is not working.

The QA standing committee reviews restrictive technique data at least quarterly for trends by person, staff, shift and technique. It makes recommendations and the Program Director implements them (GOV-03).
Rights restrictions that are not related to challenging behavior follow PA-02 and are reviewed by the standing committee with a time frame.
Behavior plans and restriction logs are kept confidential (PA-03) and filed in the individual record (REC-01).

responsibilities.duty: Ensures positive supports are in place, plans are approved before use, staff are trained, and logs are completed and reviewed.
Assesses, writes and revises behavior plans and monitors their effect.
Use positive supports, implement the plan only as written and document behavior and any technique used.
Approves plans that use restrictive techniques and reviews restriction data and incidents.
Review medications used to modify behavior and side effects.
Reviews QA reports on behavior supports and restrictive technique use.

documentation: Functional assessment and behavior plan with consent
Record of less restrictive approaches tried
Standing committee approval minutes (confidential)
Restrictive technique log (who, technique, date/time, emergency or planned, effectiveness)
Staff training records on each plan
Medication-for-behavior review notes
Quarterly QA trend report

policies.title: Restrictive Interventions, Restraint and Seclusion
policies.applies_to: All staff, the Program Director, the standing committee and the governing body
policies.purpose: To limit restrictive interventions to the narrow circumstances Maryland regulations allow, to protect the safety and dignity of the person, and to make sure every use is approved, logged, reported and reviewed.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] uses restrictive techniques only as COMAR 10.22.10.06 allows, and under the specific restraint rules for physical restraint (COMAR 10.22.10.08), mechanical restraint (COMAR 10.22.10.09) and chemical restraint (COMAR 10.22.10.10). [AGENCY NAME] verifies the current text of these rules at each annual policy review (CS-01) and updates this policy to match. This policy meets COMAR 10.22.02.10 A(10) (DH Form DD.APP.1.1 p.1) — Any individual whose behaviors require intervention receive the safeguards required by regulation. A restrictive technique may be used in a behavior plan only after the standing committee has approved the plan (COMAR 10.22.02.14E(1)(d)). Every use is logged and reviewed in QA (COMAR 10.22.02.14B). Any use outside an approved plan is an emergency use and is reported as an incident under DDA's reportable incident procedures (the PORII; see PA-06). Staff may use only techniques they have been trained in. Restraint and seclusion are never used for staff convenience, as punishment, or as a substitute for adequate staffing or positive supports.

definitions.definition: A technique that restricts a person's freedom of movement or access to their own space or belongings in response to behavior, including restraint and seclusion.
Holding or limiting a person's body movement by staff, governed by COMAR 10.22.10.08.
Use of a device to restrict movement, governed by COMAR 10.22.10.09.
Use of a medication to control behavior and not to treat a condition, governed by COMAR 10.22.10.10.
Involuntary confinement of a person alone in a space they cannot leave.
Any use of a restrictive technique that is not specifically authorized in an approved behavior plan.
DDA's Policy on Reportable Incidents and Investigations, which sets reporting requirements for incidents.

procedures: Staff use de-escalation, redirection, space, choice and the person's own calming strategies first. The Program Director ensures these are written in each person's plan and known to all staff on shift (PA-08).
A restrictive technique is used in a planned way only if it is written in a behavior plan that the standing committee has approved and that has the person's or legal decision-maker's consent (PA-11).

Staff may use a technique only if they have been trained in it and the training is current in their personnel file (SP-03). Untrained staff do not take part in a restraint and instead call for help, call 911 if there is imminent danger, and keep others safe.

The Program Director verifies before each shift schedule is finalized that a staff member trained in each technique in a plan is available for every shift on which that technique might be needed (SP-01).

Staff end any restraint as soon as the danger has passed. Staff monitor the person's breathing, circulation, comfort and distress throughout and stop immediately if there is any sign of injury or medical distress, then call 911 and follow HW-02.
Staff do not use any technique that is prohibited by the rules cited in this policy, and do not use restraint or seclusion as punishment, for convenience, or in place of staffing.
Immediately after any use, staff check the person for injury, give first aid or arrange medical care, and offer comfort and the chance to talk about what happened.

The staff member completes the restrictive technique log before the end of the shift: who, which technique, date and time, whether it was emergency or planned, duration and effectiveness. The Program Director reviews the entry within one business day.

Any use outside an approved plan is treated as an emergency use. The staff member notifies the Program Director immediately, and the agency files the incident report within the PORII deadlines and as described in PA-06.

After any emergency use the Program Director convenes the team to review the event, determine whether a behavior plan is needed or should be revised, and refer the plan to the standing committee for approval before further planned use (PA-08).

The standing committee reviews every incident involving a restrictive technique and the QA restrictive technique data at least quarterly. Members involved in an event do not take part in deciding it (GOV-03).
The Program Director analyzes trends by person, staff, shift, time of day and technique, and implements corrective actions such as retraining, plan revision, environmental change or staffing change.
Restraint and seclusion records are confidential (PA-03) and are kept in the individual record (REC-01).

responsibilities.duty: Ensures only approved, trained use, reviews logs within one business day, files incident reports and leads post-event reviews.
Use positive supports first, use only techniques they are trained in, monitor the person's safety and complete the log.
Approves plans with restrictive techniques before use and reviews all incidents and data.
Evaluates injuries or health effects after any restraint and reviews any chemical intervention.
Receives QA reports and ensures corrective action is taken.

documentation: Standing committee approval of behavior plans with restrictive techniques
Restrictive technique log
Incident reports for emergency uses (PA-06)
Post-event review notes
Staff technique training records
Quarterly QA trend report

policies.title: Payment for Property Damage
policies.applies_to: The Program Director, the standing committee, the governing body, the person's team and fiscal staff
policies.purpose: To protect people's money by requiring that a person is asked to pay for property damage they caused only when every condition in COMAR 10.22.02.10A(11) is documented.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] does not require any individual to pay for property damage unless the Individual Plan (IP) shows all five conditions in COMAR 10.22.02.10A(11). Staff never deduct money from a person's funds for damage without an approval that meets all five conditions. The agency's responsibility for ordinary wear, accidents and damage that is not shown to be the person's destructive behavior stays with the agency. This policy meets: A(11)(a) (DH Form DD.APP.1.1 p.1) — the IP shows a history of destructive behaviors documented in the behavior plan (BP). A(11)(b) — the IP shows a BP that addresses the destructive behavior. A(11)(c) — the IP shows evidence that the individual has the ability to pay for damages. A(11)(d) — the IP shows the licensee's standing committee has reviewed and approved the damage payment. A(11)(e) — the IP shows the licensee has reported the approval to the Regional Director. If any one condition is missing, no payment is required.

definitions.definition: Damage to the home, its furnishings or another person's belongings caused by an individual's actions.
A pattern of behavior that damages property and that has been documented in the person's behavior plan.
Documented evidence, such as personal funds or income, that the person can pay without losing money needed for basic needs and personal choices.
The director of the DDA regional office that serves the person.

procedures: When damage occurs, staff make everyone safe, document the facts (who, what, when, where, estimated cost) in daily documentation and tell the Program Director the same day. Staff do not discuss payment with the person or deduct any money.

The Program Director decides whether the damage was an accident, wear, a result of unsafe conditions or inadequate supports, or an act of the person. Only the last type may continue to the review in this policy.

The Program Director checks the IP and BP for the first condition, A(11)(a): documentation in the behavior plan of a history of destructive behavior. If the history is not documented in the BP, the review stops and no payment is requested.

The Program Director checks for the second condition, A(11)(b): a BP that addresses the destructive behavior with positive supports (PA-08). If there is no BP that addresses it, the review stops. The team meets to decide whether a BP is needed.

The Program Director and fiscal staff check for the third condition, A(11)(c): evidence the person has the ability to pay. They document the person's income and funds, and confirm that payment would not leave the person without money for needs, personal spending and savings (PA-14).

The Program Director discusses the damage and the proposed payment with the person, using plain language and supports for communication, and with the proponent or legal decision-maker (PA-11). The person's views are written down.

If conditions A(11)(a)-(c) are met, the Program Director refers the proposed payment to the standing committee. The referral includes the damage report, BP, financial information and the person's views, all kept confidential (PA-03).

The standing committee reviews the referral and records its decision, for condition A(11)(d). Members involved in the matter do not vote. The committee may approve, deny, or approve a smaller amount or a payment schedule.

If the committee approves, the Program Director reports the approval to the Regional Director in writing within five business days and keeps a copy of the report, for condition A(11)(e). No payment is collected before the report has been made.
The Program Director adds the five items of evidence (BP history, BP, ability to pay, committee approval, Regional Director report) to the IP before any payment is taken.
Fiscal staff record any payment in the person's personal funds ledger with a receipt, following PA-14. They never take payment from the person's funds without the written approval in the IP.
If the person or proponent disagrees, they are told of their right to file a grievance under PA-04 and DG-01, and no retaliation takes place.
The standing committee reviews all property damage payments at least annually, and the Program Director reports totals to the governing body (GOV-03).

responsibilities.duty: Investigates the damage, checks all five conditions, refers to the committee, reports to the Regional Director and ensures documentation is in the IP.
Reviews and decides on each proposed payment and records its decision.
Documents ability to pay, records any payment in the personal funds ledger and prevents unauthorized deductions.
Report damage factually and do not request or deduct payment.
Reviews annual summary of property damage payments.

documentation: Property damage report
IP and BP showing documented history and plan
Ability-to-pay documentation
Standing committee review and decision
Written report to the Regional Director
Personal funds ledger entry with receipt
Grievance record if any (PA-04)

policies.title: Informed Consent, Surrogate Decision-Making and Decision-Making Support
policies.applies_to: All staff, the Program Director, the RN, the person's team and the governing body
policies.purpose: To make sure each person makes their own decisions with the support they need, and that when someone else must decide, the right person does so under Maryland law.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] complies with Health-General §5-605 (surrogate decision-making). This policy meets COMAR 10.22.02.10 A(12) (DH Form DD.APP.1.1 p.1) — Compliance with H-G Article §5-605, Annotated Code of Maryland: Surrogate Decision Making. Every adult is presumed able to make decisions. Staff use supported decision-making and plain-language information before seeking any consent. [AGENCY NAME] identifies the legal decision-maker or proponent for each person and keeps documentation of this in the record. Staff and board members are never used as surrogates (see PA-12). Staff do not consent for a person, sign for treatment or make health care decisions unless they have been verified as the person's legally authorized decision-maker.

definitions.definition: A decision to accept or refuse a service, treatment or restriction, made after receiving understandable information about its purpose, benefits, risks and alternatives.
Helping a person understand choices and make their own decision using plain language, pictures, extra time, trusted people or other supports.
A person authorized under Maryland law, including Health-General §5-605, or by court order or advance directive, to make decisions for someone who cannot make a specific decision.
A person who advocates for the individual, such as a family member, friend or guardian, and who is involved in the person's planning.

procedures: At admission, the Program Director asks the person and any referral source who the person's legal decision-maker or proponent is, and obtains copies of any guardianship order, power of attorney, advance directive or other authority (PCS-01).

The Program Director records in the individual record whether the person makes their own decisions, uses supports to decide, or has a legal decision-maker, and for which kinds of decisions (health, finances, residence, plan).

Before any consent is requested (medical treatment, medication, behavior plan, rights restriction, release of information, photographs), the staff member or RN explains the matter in plain language, in the person's preferred communication method, and allows time for questions (PA-05).
Staff offer decision-making supports: pictures or demonstrations, visits or trial experiences, a trusted person present, and repeated conversations at the person's pace. Supports used are documented.

If a person can make the decision with support, the person's own decision is recorded and respected, including a decision the team disagrees with, unless safety rules require otherwise and the process in PA-02 is followed.

If there is doubt about whether the person can make a particular decision, the Program Director refers the question to the person's physician or other qualified professional for an assessment. Staff do not decide capacity themselves.

When a person cannot make a health care decision, the RN or Program Director identifies the surrogate through Health-General §5-605, a guardian or an advance directive, and confirms the surrogate's authority against documents before relying on it.
The surrogate is given the same plain-language information the person would receive, and the person is still included in the discussion and their preferences and views are recorded.

Consent or refusal is documented in the record with date, who gave it, the authority relied upon and the information provided. Consent for a behavior plan or a restriction is obtained before it starts (PA-08, PA-02).

Staff and board members are not used as surrogates, and are not asked to sign consents for people in the home. If no surrogate is available, the Program Director contacts the DDA regional office and the person's support coordinator for guidance (PA-12).
In a medical emergency, staff call 911 and follow HW-02 without waiting for consent. The Program Director notifies the decision-maker as soon as possible after.
The Program Director reviews decision-making status at each annual plan meeting and whenever there is a change in the person's abilities or legal status, and updates the record (PCS-02).
Any disagreement about consent or decision-making is handled through PA-04 and DG-01, and the person's choices are not changed in retaliation.

responsibilities.duty: Identifies and documents each person's decision-maker, verifies authority, and ensures consents are obtained before services or restrictions.
Explains health information and obtains consent or refusal for health care, working with the physician and surrogate.
Provide decision-making supports, respect choices and never sign consent on a person's behalf.
Ensures that no board member acts as a surrogate for a person served.

documentation: Guardianship orders, power of attorney, advance directives and other authority documents
Decision-making status summary in the record
Signed consents, refusals and the information provided
Capacity assessment referrals, if any
Record of decision-making supports used
Annual review of decision-making status

policies.title: Conflict of Interest
policies.applies_to: Governing body members, the Program Director and all staff, care providers, volunteers, consultants and standing committee members
policies.purpose: To make sure decisions about the people we serve and about agency resources are made in their interest and are free of financial or personal conflicts.
policies.policy: No member of [AGENCY NAME]'s governing body, no staff member, care provider or volunteer, and no standing committee member may have a financial or personal conflict of interest. This policy meets COMAR 10.22.02.10 A(13) (DH Form DD.APP.1.1 p.1) — No financial or personal conflict of interest - members of governing body, staff, care providers, volunteers, standing committee. Consistent with COMAR 10.22.02.08, employees and their immediate family may not be voting members of the governing body, and board members and employees may not own property that is leased back to [AGENCY NAME] (COMAR 10.22.02.08C(9)). Conflict of interest provisions are also part of the governing body's bylaws. Anyone with an actual or possible conflict discloses it and is recused from the related decision. Staff and board members are never used as surrogate decision-makers for people served (PA-11).

definitions.definition: A situation in which a person's financial, family or personal interest could, or could appear to, influence their judgment or duties toward the people served or the agency.
A spouse, domestic partner, parent, child, sibling, or any person living in the same household, or as otherwise defined in the bylaws.
Stepping out of discussion and decision on a matter in which one has a conflict.
Property owned by a board member or employee that is leased to the licensee, which COMAR 10.22.02.08C(9) does not allow.

procedures: The governing body includes conflict of interest provisions in its bylaws and adopts them by vote (GOV-01). The bylaws are reviewed at least annually.

Before taking a position, each board member, staff member, care provider, consultant, volunteer and standing committee member receives a copy of this policy and signs the conflict of interest disclosure form (CS-01).

Each person completes the disclosure form again every year and within 30 days of any change, listing financial interests, family relationships with staff, board members or people served, outside employment and any business dealings with [AGENCY NAME].

Before seating any voting board member, the Board Chair confirms that the person is not an employee or immediate family member of an employee. A person who becomes an employee or whose family member is hired must resign from voting status.

Before any lease, purchase or contract is considered, the Board Chair confirms that no board member or employee owns property leased back to [AGENCY NAME]. [AGENCY NAME] does not enter into a lease of that kind (COMAR 10.22.02.08C(9)).
A person who has a possible conflict discloses it in writing to the Board Chair (or, for the Board Chair, to the full board) before any discussion. The board decides whether a conflict exists.
A person with a conflict leaves the room and does not vote or influence discussion on the matter. The minutes record the disclosure, the recusal and the outcome.
Standing committee members do not decide on incidents, behavior plans or damage payments in which they were involved or in which they have a conflict (PA-08, PA-10, GOV-03).

Staff may not borrow from, sell to, accept gifts of more than nominal value from, or hold financial dealings with people served, their families or vendors in a way that benefits the staff member (PA-14, SP-05).
Staff and board members do not serve as a person's surrogate decision-maker, representative payee, guardian or agent for personal funds (PA-11, PA-14).
The Program Director chooses vendors, pharmacies, contractors and consultants on documented quality and price, and discloses any relationship to the board before award (PA-13).
Staff report a suspected conflict to the Program Director, or to the Board Chair if the concern involves the Program Director. Reports are made in good faith without retaliation.

The Board Chair keeps all disclosure forms and recusal records and reports to the governing body annually on compliance. Violations lead to corrective action up to removal from the board or termination of employment.

responsibilities.duty: Adopts bylaws, collects disclosures, decides on conflicts, enforces recusal and checks board composition and leased property.
Collects staff disclosures, applies the policy to purchasing and hiring and reports concerns to the board.

responsibilities.role: All Staff, Care Providers, Consultants, Volunteers
responsibilities.duty: Disclose conflicts, avoid prohibited dealings and report concerns.
Disclose conflicts and recuse themselves from matters they were involved in.

documentation: Signed annual conflict of interest disclosure forms
Board minutes showing disclosures and recusals
Governing body bylaws with conflict of interest provisions
Board roster showing employment and residency status
Lease and property ownership verification
Annual compliance report to the board

policies.title: Fiscal Practices (Generally Accepted Accounting Practices)
policies.applies_to: Governing body, Administrator, finance and billing staff, and any contracted bookkeeper or accountant of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] manages its money honestly, transparently and in line with generally accepted accounting practices (GAAP), so that the group home can operate continuously, stay licensed and enrolled in Medicaid, and keep individuals' money safe and separate.
policies.policy: This policy meets COMAR 10.22.02.10A(14) (DH Form DD.APP.1.1 p.1) — Fiscal affairs of the Licensee conducted in accordance with generally accepted accounting practices. [AGENCY NAME] keeps its books on an accrual basis under GAAP. The governing body is legally responsible for overseeing all programs and for compliance (COMAR 10.22.02.02A(2)-(3)), and it approves the mission, budget and policies (COMAR 10.22.02.08C). Room-and-board collections are kept in a separate account and ledger and are never mixed with Medicaid billing or operating revenue. [AGENCY NAME] keeps its Maryland corporate good standing (State Department of Assessments and Taxation, SDAT) and a current Medicaid (MA) number for each licensed site. No board member or employee, or their immediate family, may own property leased back to [AGENCY NAME] (COMAR 10.22.02.08C(9)). Individuals' personal funds are handled under PA-14.

definitions.definition: Generally accepted accounting practices: the standard accrual-based accounting rules, including documented controls, that [AGENCY NAME] uses for all fiscal records.
Status confirming that [AGENCY NAME] is a Maryland corporation (or a registered foreign corporation) and has filed all required reports with the State Department of Assessments and Taxation.
The Maryland Medicaid provider number issued for each licensed site, enrolled through Maryland Medicaid (MPRIME) under provider type 90 DDA.
The portion of housing and food costs collected from the resident under a written agreement; it is not Medicaid revenue.
The LTSSMaryland billing code for Community Living – Group Home, billed per person per day.

procedures: Before each fiscal year begins, the Administrator prepares an annual operating budget by site. It covers staffing, food, utilities, maintenance, vehicles, training, insurance and reserves. The governing body reviews and approves it, and the vote is recorded in the minutes (COMAR 10.22.02.08C).
The bookkeeper or accountant maintains a chart of accounts and records all transactions on an accrual basis under GAAP. Entries are supported by an invoice, receipt, timesheet or billing record.

The Administrator keeps separate bank accounts. These are (a) an operating account, (b) a room-and-board account, and (c) individual personal-fund accounts or sub-ledgers as described in PA-14. Money is never moved between them except as an approved, documented reimbursement.
Duties are divided. The person who approves a payment is not the person who records it or reconciles the bank statement. Checks or electronic payments above $[AMOUNT] need two authorized signers.

Billing staff bill W5600 per person per day in LTSSMaryland only for days supported by daily documentation and a verified census (see GOV-04). Billing staff alert the Administrator the same day a vacancy occurs, because the daily rate follows the number of people living in the home.

Room-and-board is collected only under the written residency agreement (see PCS-01). Each payment is receipted and posted to a resident-level ledger. It is never counted as Medicaid revenue, offset against a Medicaid claim, or used to pay an individual's personal expenses.
The bookkeeper reconciles every bank account within 15 days of receiving the statement. The Administrator reviews and initials the reconciliation, and the Board Treasurer reviews it quarterly.

The Administrator gives the governing body monthly financial statements: income and expense compared to budget, cash position and aged receivables. Variances over 10% of any budget category are explained in writing.

Payment from Medicaid can take as long as 180 days from the start of service. The Administrator keeps a cash-flow forecast and a reserve or line of credit sized to cover at least [NUMBER] days of operating costs, and reports it to the board.
The Administrator makes sure payroll, payroll taxes, workers' compensation and insurance premiums are paid on time. Wage and leave compliance is checked under SP-04.

The Administrator keeps a compliance calendar. It includes the SDAT annual filings, quarterly verification of SDAT good standing, Medicaid (MPRIME) revalidation for each MA number, and license renewal filed at least 60 days before the license expires (COMAR 10.22.02.02B). The calendar is reviewed monthly.

Each board member and employee completes an annual conflict-of-interest and related-party disclosure (see PA-12). The Board Chair verifies that no board member, employee or immediate family member owns property leased back to [AGENCY NAME] (COMAR 10.22.02.08C(9)) and that no employee or employee's immediate family member serves as a voting board member (COMAR 10.22.02.08).

An independent certified public accountant performs an annual audit or review. The board receives the report directly, and the Administrator documents a corrective action plan for each finding within 30 days.

Any employee who suspects theft, misuse of funds or a billing error reports it immediately to the Administrator, or to the Board Chair if the Administrator is involved. If an individual's money or property is involved, the concern is also handled as possible exploitation under BP-01 and PA-06.
Financial records are kept for [NUMBER] years, backed up off site (see EP-05), and made available to the DDA, OHCQ and Medicaid auditors on request.
The governing body reviews this policy at least annually and records the review in the minutes (see CS-01).

responsibilities.duty: Approves the budget, receives monthly financial reports and the annual audit, and oversees fiscal compliance.
Reviews bank reconciliations quarterly and monitors cash reserves.
Prepares the budget, enforces controls, maintains the compliance calendar and responds to audit findings.
Records transactions under GAAP, reconciles accounts and prepares financial statements.
Bill W5600 only for documented service days, keep the room-and-board ledger separate, and report vacancies immediately.
