Chart of accounts, general ledger and supporting invoices/receipts
Monthly bank reconciliations with reviewer initials
Monthly financial statements and variance explanations
Annual audit/review report and corrective action plan
Room-and-board ledger and receipts
Compliance calendar showing SDAT, MA number and license renewal dates
Annual conflict-of-interest and related-party disclosures

policies.title: Personal Funds and Property Management
policies.applies_to: All staff, the Administrator, and any person who handles an individual's money or belongings at [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To protect the money and belongings of every person living in the group home, to make sure their funds are used for their own needs and preferences, and to keep their funds completely separate from the agency's funds.
policies.policy: This policy provides adequate protection for the finances and property of individuals and meets each part of COMAR 10.22.02.10A(15) (DH Form DD.APP.1.1 p.1). A(15)(a): a system ensures funds are used appropriately for the individual's needs and preferences. A(15)(b): personal funds are kept separate from Licensee funds and are transferred promptly when the individual leaves. A(15)(c): the individual has timely access to funds. A(15)(d): an accounting of the individual's funds is provided on request. A(15)(e): interest is credited to the individual if the account bears interest. Room and board is collected from the resident under a written agreement and is not an individual's personal fund. [AGENCY NAME] does not borrow from, lend to, or gain any benefit from an individual's funds or property. Staff do not serve as an individual's representative payee, power of attorney or beneficiary. Any exception requires written approval of the Administrator, review by the governing body, and the individual's informed consent (see PA-11 and PA-12).

definitions.definition: Money belonging to an individual from any source (for example benefits, wages, gifts or allowances), including cash on hand and bank accounts, whoever holds it.
Items belonging to an individual, such as clothing, electronics, jewelry, furniture, devices and documents.
Mixing an individual's money with agency money or with another person's money. This is prohibited.
A written statement of all deposits, withdrawals, purchases and the current balance for an individual's funds.
A person or organization named by the benefits agency to manage an individual's benefits for them.

procedures: At admission, and whenever the person's circumstances change, the Administrator or designee asks the individual (and proponent, if any) who manages their money and what support they want. This is recorded in the Individual Plan (see PCS-02). The individual keeps control of their money to the greatest extent they choose and are able.

Before agency staff handle any funds, the individual or legal representative gives written consent that states what the agency will do. The Administrator checks that the arrangement respects the individual's rights (see PA-02).

For each individual who wants agency support, staff open a separate ledger. The ledger records the source and amount of every deposit, every withdrawal, the purpose, the date and the balance. Each entry is signed by the staff member, and a second staff member or the Administrator countersigns any transaction over $[AMOUNT].

Funds held by [AGENCY NAME] are kept in an account in the individual's own name or in a separate individual-designated account. They are never deposited into agency operating or room-and-board accounts. No individual's funds are pooled with another's (A(15)(b)).

Cash held in the home is kept in a locked box under the control of the shift lead. At each shift change, two staff count the cash, compare it to the ledger and sign the count sheet. Any discrepancy is reported to the Administrator at once.

Staff help the individual spend money on what the individual wants and needs, such as clothing, outings, hobbies, personal care and savings goals. Staff do not use an individual's funds for agency expenses, staff expenses, or items other residents share, unless the individual chooses to contribute. Receipts are obtained for every purchase and attached to the ledger (A(15)(a)).

Staff give the individual access to their money when they ask. Cash held in the home is available the same day. Money held in a bank account is made available within one business day, with staff support to go to the bank or use an ATM or card if the individual wishes (A(15)(c)). The individual is never required to justify, wait for approval of, or earn access to their own money. Any limit on access is a rights restriction handled under PA-02.

On request, the Administrator gives the individual, and the legal representative or proponent if authorized, a written accounting of the funds within five business days. Staff also review the ledger with the individual at least quarterly in the way that is most understandable to them (A(15)(d)).

If an account bears interest, the bookkeeper credits all interest to the individual and records it in the ledger. The agency does not charge fees to the individual's account except those the bank charges (A(15)(e)).

Room and board is collected only under the written residency agreement (see PCS-01). It is receipted, recorded in the room-and-board ledger, and kept apart from the individual's personal funds ledger, so the individual keeps funds for personal use.

At admission, staff make a dated inventory of the individual's belongings with the individual, listing items of significant value. Staff update it at least every six months and whenever significant items are bought, received or discarded. The individual signs it, or staff note the individual's choice not to.

Staff protect personal property from loss, theft and damage. The individual's belongings stay in their private bedroom or a locked space of their choosing. Staff do not borrow, sell, give away or use an individual's property without the individual's permission.

The bookkeeper reconciles each individual's ledger to the bank statement monthly. The Administrator reviews the reconciliations and signs them. The Administrator also spot-checks one or more cash counts each month.

When an individual leaves the home for any reason, the Administrator completes a final accounting and returns all funds and property within [NUMBER] business days. The funds go to the individual, or to the legal representative or new provider as designated in writing. Everything returned is receipted and signed (A(15)(b); see PCS-04). If the individual dies, funds and property go to the lawful representative or estate (see HW-03).

Staff report any suspected theft, misuse or missing funds or property at once to the Administrator. They also report it under BP-01 and PA-06 as possible exploitation. The agency reimburses the individual promptly while an investigation is under way when the loss is confirmed to be agency fault.
The Administrator reviews this policy at least annually and trains all staff who handle funds on it before they do so (see SP-03).

responsibilities.duty: Establishes the system, approves any exception, reviews monthly reconciliations, and provides final accountings and accountings on request.

responsibilities.role: Direct Support Professionals and Shift Leads
responsibilities.duty: Keep ledgers and receipts, do the shift cash count, support timely access to funds, and report discrepancies at once.
Keeps separate accounts and credits interest. Reconciles each individual's account monthly.
Direct how the individual's money is used, and may request an accounting or access at any time.

documentation: Individual funds ledger with receipts and countersignatures
Signed consent for agency support with funds
Shift cash count sheets
Monthly bank and ledger reconciliations
Written accountings provided on request
Dated personal property inventory
Final accounting and receipt at departure
Incident reports for any loss or suspected misuse

policies.title: Infection Prevention, Standard Precautions and Safety Precautions
policies.applies_to: All staff, care providers, consultants and volunteers of [AGENCY NAME], and all individuals and visitors in the group home
policies.purpose: To prevent the spread of infection and protect individuals, staff and visitors from exposure to blood-borne pathogens and communicable disease by following State and federal safety precautions, infection control and standard precautions.
policies.policy: This policy meets COMAR 10.22.02.10A(16) (DH Form DD.APP.1.1 p.1) — State/Federal safety precautions, infection control and standard precautions implemented. [AGENCY NAME] applies standard precautions to all individuals at all times. It follows the OSHA Bloodborne Pathogens standard, 29 CFR 1910.1030, with a written exposure control plan. All staff and care providers are trained in blood-borne pathogens before independent duties (COMAR 10.22.02.11C(3)) and in communicable diseases within three months of hire (COMAR 10.22.02.11D). The agency provides personal protective equipment (PPE) and supplies at no cost to staff, and arranges post-exposure evaluation and follow-up.

definitions.definition: Infection-control practices applied to everyone, regardless of diagnosis: hand hygiene, PPE, safe handling of sharps, respiratory etiquette, and cleaning and disinfection.
Microorganisms in human blood or other potentially infectious materials that can cause disease, such as hepatitis B, hepatitis C and HIV.
Personal protective equipment such as gloves, gowns, masks, and eye protection.
A specific contact of eye, mouth, other mucous membrane, non-intact skin or a needle-stick with blood or other potentially infectious material during work.
The written plan required by 29 CFR 1910.1030 that identifies who may be exposed and how exposure is prevented and managed.

procedures: The Administrator writes and keeps an exposure control plan for each home. It lists tasks with possible exposure (for example first aid, incontinence care, wound care, glucose checks, handling soiled laundry and cleaning body fluids). The plan is reviewed at least annually and whenever tasks or equipment change, and is available to all staff.

Before independent duties, every new employee, care provider and volunteer completes blood-borne pathogens training under 29 CFR 1910.1030. The training is repeated at least annually. The trainer and date are recorded in the personnel record (COMAR 10.22.02.11C(3); see SP-03).
Within three months of hire, each employee completes DDA-approved training on communicable diseases (COMAR 10.22.02.11D). The Administrator tracks due dates and does not let a lapse go unaddressed.

The agency offers the hepatitis B vaccination series at no cost to staff with occupational exposure risk, as 29 CFR 1910.1030 requires. Staff who decline sign a declination form and may change their mind later.

Staff perform hand hygiene with soap and water (or alcohol-based rub when hands are not visibly soiled) before and after contact with an individual, before preparing food or giving medication, after using the toilet or handling soiled items, and after removing gloves.

Staff wear gloves for any contact with blood, body fluids, broken skin or soiled items, and wear a gown, mask or eye protection when splashes are likely. Staff remove PPE carefully, discard it in a lined container and wash hands afterward. The Administrator ensures PPE is stocked and easily available in each home, including in vehicles.

Each home keeps an exposure-response kit and spill-cleanup supplies. After a spill of blood or body fluids, staff wear gloves, absorb the fluid, clean with detergent and disinfect with an EPA-registered disinfectant (or a freshly made bleach solution) used per the label, then discard the waste in a lined container.

Staff use sharps (lancets, needles) only as trained and as delegated (see PA-07, NU-07). Used sharps go immediately into a puncture-resistant, labeled container, never recapped by hand. Containers are replaced when about three-quarters full and disposed of by a licensed medical-waste method.

Staff handle laundry with soiled linens as little as possible, wear gloves, and wash at the hottest setting the fabric permits. Dishes and kitchen surfaces are cleaned and sanitized daily. Staff follow safe food handling (see HE-02).

The home is cleaned on a written schedule. High-touch surfaces (door handles, light switches, bathrooms, remotes, shared equipment) are disinfected daily and whenever visibly soiled. Shared equipment such as thermometers and blood-pressure cuffs are cleaned between users.

Staff who have fever, vomiting, diarrhea, an undiagnosed rash or other signs of contagious illness do not work with individuals until they are well, and report to the Administrator or on-call supervisor. The Administrator arranges replacement coverage under SP-01.

If an individual shows signs of an infectious illness, staff follow the physician's or RN's direction, keep the person comfortable, use appropriate precautions, and report the change of condition under HW-02 and NU-06. Staff do not isolate an individual in a way that restricts rights without following PA-02 and PA-09. Cleaning, hand hygiene, and sharing of equipment are adjusted to the illness.

The RN or the Administrator checks that immunizations (influenza, COVID-19 and others) and screenings (for example tuberculosis) are offered to individuals, consistent with each person's choice, consent and physician's orders (see PA-11, HW-01).

After an exposure incident, the employee washes the area immediately (soap and water for skin, water or saline for eyes and mucous membranes) and reports to the Administrator or on-call supervisor right away. The agency sends the employee for confidential medical evaluation and follow-up at no cost, as 29 CFR 1910.1030 requires, and documents the circumstances. When the source individual's information is needed, the agency follows PA-03 and legal requirements.

The Administrator keeps a sharps injury log. The Administrator reviews each exposure incident to see if equipment or procedures should change, and records the result. Where required, the agency reports to the proper authorities; a reportable incident is handled under PA-06.
The Administrator reports any outbreak of a reportable communicable disease to the local health department and notifies the RN, DDA/OHCQ as required (see REC-02), and the individual's proponent.
The Administrator reviews this policy and the exposure control plan at least annually and records the review (see CS-01).

responsibilities.duty: Maintains the exposure control plan, supplies, training schedule and exposure follow-up, and reports outbreaks.
Advises on infection control, immunizations and health care of individuals, and reviews health-related incidents (see NU-07).
Apply standard precautions at all times, use PPE and sharps containers correctly, stay home when ill, and report exposures immediately.
Verifies PPE and cleaning supplies are stocked each shift and assures cleaning is done and documented.

documentation: Written exposure control plan and annual review
Training records for blood-borne pathogens (before independent duties and annual) and communicable diseases (within 3 months)
Hepatitis B vaccination offer, acceptance or signed declination
Cleaning and disinfection schedule logs
Exposure incident report and confidential medical follow-up record
Sharps injury log
Outbreak notifications

policies.title: Individuals Not Performing Paid Staff Duties; Household Duties
policies.applies_to: All staff, supervisors and the Administrator of [AGENCY NAME], and all individuals living in the group home
policies.purpose: To ensure that people living in the home are never used to do the work that [AGENCY NAME] pays staff to do, and that any chores they take part in are the ordinary household tasks they choose to share, are documented in their plan, or are part of a paid training program.
policies.policy: This policy meets COMAR 10.22.02.10A(18) (DH Form DD.APP.1.1 p.1) — Individuals do not perform duties of paid staff — and COMAR 10.22.02.10A(19) — Individual only performs household duties as shared by the household, as an activity documented in the IP, or remunerated as part of a training program. Individuals are residents of their home, not workers for the agency. Cleaning, cooking, laundry, yard work, medication tasks, supervision of other individuals, transportation, and documentation are staff duties. An individual may take part in household tasks only when the task is (1) shared by everyone in the household, (2) an activity documented in the Individual Plan (IP) that the individual chose, or (3) paid work as part of a training program. Participation is always the individual's choice and may be declined without penalty. Staff do not assign chores to individuals on behalf of the agency, such as cleaning common areas to cover for staff or the agency.

definitions.definition: Tasks [AGENCY NAME] pays or contracts staff to perform, including cleaning for the agency, meal preparation for the household as the staff job, laundry for others, supervising or caring for other individuals, answering phones, and agency maintenance and paperwork.

Ordinary tasks that members of any household share, such as cleaning one's own room, doing one's own laundry, helping to set the table or cook a meal, and caring for personal belongings or a pet one owns.
A structured program in which the individual receives remuneration and instruction toward employment skills, with the plan documenting its goals (see PCS-03).
The person-centered plan that states the person's goals, supports and chosen activities (see PCS-02).

procedures: The Administrator writes and posts a duty list for each home that separates staff duties from household tasks. Staff are trained on it at orientation and again annually (see SP-03).
The Administrator assigns every paid staff duty by name on the staffing schedule and shift duty sheet. No staff duty is assigned to, or left for, an individual (A(18)).

At the planning meeting for the IP, staff ask each individual which household tasks they want to do, how often, and what help they want. Choices are recorded in the IP, including tasks the individual refuses (see PCS-02; A(19)).

Household tasks the whole household shares, such as keeping one's own room tidy or helping with a shared meal, are agreed to at a household meeting. Staff record the agreement in meeting notes and ask for each person's consent. Tasks are rotated or chosen fairly, and nobody is singled out.

A task is considered shared household work only if staff do not use it to replace their own job. Staff do the core cleaning, cooking, shopping, laundry for the home, and upkeep, and individuals contribute only as they choose and as they could in any household.

An individual may decline a household task at any time, with no loss of privileges, services, meals, outings, money or relationship with staff. Staff may not use pressure, rewards or threats to obtain participation. Any limit on a person's rights goes through PA-02.

An individual who wants to be paid for work needs a documented training program or an employment arrangement under PCS-03 that follows applicable wage laws. The IP states the program, the pay, and the supports. The Administrator confirms the arrangement is not agency work.

No individual helps care for another individual, gives medication, supervises other residents, answers the door or phone as an agency task, or is left responsible for the home. If an individual offers help on a particular day, staff may accept it as a courtesy only when it is truly voluntary and not part of an agency expectation.

Staff do not allow staff-assigned chores, such as cleaning common areas on behalf of the agency, as consequences for behavior, as a way to earn privileges, or as a condition of staying in the home (see PA-08, PA-09).
Staff record participation in household tasks and any task agreed to in the IP in the daily documentation, including whether it was the individual's choice (see PA-01).

The Administrator or designee reviews 10% of daily notes and the shift duty sheets monthly, and interviews individuals during home visits, to verify that no individual is performing paid staff duties. Findings go to the quality assurance committee (see GOV-03).

Any person who sees an individual doing a paid staff duty reports it to the Administrator immediately. The Administrator stops the practice, makes up the staff coverage, speaks with the individual, and corrects the cause. Where an individual was pressured or exploited, the matter is handled under BP-01 and PA-06.
The Administrator reviews this policy at least annually and records the review (see CS-01).

responsibilities.duty: Maintains the duty list, assigns staff duties, monitors compliance and corrects violations.
Perform all staff duties, offer choices about household tasks, honor refusals, and document participation.
Decide which household tasks the individual wants to do and may withdraw at any time.
Records chosen household activities and any paid training program in the IP.

documentation: Posted staff-versus-household duty list for each home
Staffing schedule and shift duty sheets
IP entries on chosen household tasks and any paid training program
Household meeting notes
Daily documentation of participation and choice
Monthly compliance review notes and corrective actions

policies.category: B(1) through B(7) – Emergency plan for ALUs/GHs
policies.title: Emergency Plan: Evacuation, Transportation, 72-Hour Shelter-in-Place, Identification and Role of Family
policies.applies_to: All staff, individuals, families and legal representatives of each [AGENCY NAME] group home; the Administrator; and the on-call supervisor
policies.purpose: To make sure that each individual and staff member is protected before, during and after any emergency, including fire, severe weather, power or utility failure, flood, medical emergency in the home, hazardous conditions or a public health emergency, and that each person can be evacuated or sheltered safely for up to 72 hours.
policies.policy: This policy meets COMAR 10.22.02.10A(17) (DH Form DD.APP.1.1 p.1) — Disaster/emergency plans in place with adequate drills — together with COMAR 10.22.02.10B(1) (DH Form DD.APP.1.1 p.2). [AGENCY NAME] keeps a written emergency plan for every home covering all types of emergencies, with procedures to follow before, during and after each. The plan includes B(1)(a): evacuation, transportation or 72-hour shelter-in-place of individuals and staff; B(1)(d): identification with current health, contact and other important information, immediately accessible in an evacuation, for every individual and staff member; and B(1)(e): the role of the resident, family member or legal representative in an evacuation. The remaining elements of B(1) are covered in EP-02 (drills and after-action reports), EP-03 (alternate sites and communications), EP-04 (staff recall and continuity of operations) and EP-05 (backup of records and sharing the plan). Each home also keeps a written fire evacuation plan (COMAR 10.22.02.12B), and drills under EP-02 show the plan works (A(17)).

definitions.definition: Moving everyone out of the home to a safe place because staying is unsafe.
Remaining safely in the home for at least 72 hours without outside help, utilities or resupply, with food, water, medication and supplies.
A portable packet or wearable ID for each individual and staff member containing current health, medication, contact and other important information.
The family member, guardian, or other person who advocates for or makes decisions with or for the individual.
The three phases that the plan addresses for each type of emergency: preparation, response, and recovery.

procedures: The Administrator, with the RN and the governing body, prepares a written emergency plan for each home. The plan covers fire, severe weather, power or utility failure, flooding, hazardous materials or gas leak, medical emergency, loss of water or heat, public health emergencies, and any other hazards found in a hazard assessment of the home's location. For each, the plan lists before, during and after procedures.

The plan includes a written fire evacuation plan for the home with floor plan, two exits from each level and bedroom, meeting point, and the supports each individual needs to exit (COMAR 10.22.02.12B). The plan is posted at each exit and in the staff area.

For each individual, staff write an individual evacuation profile based on the individual's IP. It states mobility, sensory, communication and behavioral needs, equipment, how many staff are needed, and the planned route. Profiles are updated within 5 days of any change of condition, and at least every six months.

Before an emergency, staff keep exits, hallways, ramps and door hardware clear and working. Staff test smoke detectors and check fire extinguishers monthly, and the Administrator keeps them working and updated (COMAR 10.22.02.12B). Staff check the shelter supplies monthly.

The 72-hour shelter-in-place kit is kept in each home. It holds drinking water (one gallon per person per day for at least three days), non-perishable food that fits each person's modified diet (see HE-02), a 72-hour supply of each person's medication and treatments (see NU-01), first aid and PPE supplies, flashlights, batteries, a battery or hand-crank radio, phone chargers or power banks, hygiene items, incontinence supplies, blankets, backup equipment and chargers for adaptive devices, and copies of the plan. The Administrator arranges a generator or equivalent plan for individuals relying on electrically powered medical equipment.

During an emergency, the shift lead acts as incident commander until relieved. The shift lead decides between evacuation and sheltering in place using the plan, local authorities' instructions and conditions in the home. The decision and time are recorded.

If evacuating, staff first call 911 if there is a fire or danger to life. Staff then move individuals out by the planned routes, with those needing the most help first when it is safe, close doors behind them, and go to the meeting point. A staff member takes a headcount from the current roster and does not let anyone re-enter until the fire department or authorities permit.

Transportation: The Administrator identifies primary and back-up vehicles with enough seating and wheelchair-accessible capacity for all individuals and staff, keeps them fueled at least half-full, and maintains a written agreement with at least one back-up transportation source (see HE-03). Staff bring the go-pack, medications, and essential equipment.

If sheltering in place, staff move everyone to the safest area of the home, check on every individual, activate supplies, keep medication and meals on schedule, monitor weather and utility status, and keep a log. The shift lead contacts the on-call supervisor at least every [NUMBER] hours. If conditions get worse, the plan changes to evacuation.

Identification: The Administrator makes sure every individual and every staff member on duty has identification with current health, contact and other important information that is immediately accessible in an evacuation (B(1)(d)). For individuals, the go-pack includes a photo, name, diagnoses, allergies, medications, doses and times, physician and pharmacy, communication needs and methods, equipment, seizure/choking/behavior supports, insurance and Medicaid numbers, and contacts for the proponent, legal representative and the agency. The packet is kept in a grab-and-go location by the exit, and a wearable or wallet ID is used for those who go out. Staff carry a card with their name, role, and the agency's contact numbers.

The RN updates health information in go-packs monthly, whenever a medication or diagnosis changes, and within 24 hours of any physician order change. Staff replace outdated copies immediately (see NU-06).

Role of the individual, family and legal representative (B(1)(e)): At admission and each annual IP meeting, the individual's preferences about evacuation and sheltering are recorded. The Administrator gives the individual and proponent a written summary of this plan, including where the family will be told the individual is being taken. The summary says that the individual participates in drills as able and tells staff of their needs, the family or legal representative does not enter an evacuation site or the home during an emergency until instructed, and they should contact the agency's emergency number, keep their contact information current, and may pick up the individual at the alternate site only after sign-out. Family members who wish to help in an emergency should coordinate with the agency (see EP-03 for notifications).

After the emergency, staff do a headcount and check each individual's health, treat injuries, and call the RN or physician as needed (see HW-02). The Administrator notifies the individuals' proponents and required authorities (see EP-03), documents what happened, and files any reportable incident under PA-06.

Recovery: Before individuals return, the Administrator or designee checks that the home is safe, utilities work, and the fire alarm and smoke detectors are working. The Administrator restores medications, food and routines, and gets emotional support for individuals and staff.

The Administrator reviews the emergency plan at least annually, after every drill or actual event (see EP-02), and when a person's needs, staffing, vehicles or building change. The governing body receives the annual review, and the review is documented (see CS-01).
All staff are trained on the plan at orientation before independent duties, and again each year and when it changes. Training is documented in the personnel record (see SP-03).

responsibilities.duty: Approves the plan and resources and receives the annual review and after-action reports.
Writes and maintains the plan, supplies, vehicles, ID packets and training, and notifies families and authorities.
Keeps health information in the go-packs current and advises on medical needs during an emergency.
Acts as incident commander, makes the evacuate/shelter decision, takes the headcount and documents events.
Know the plan, assist each individual per their evacuation profile and carry go-packs.
Share preferences and needs, keep contact information current, and follow the plan's family role.

documentation: Written emergency plan for each home, with before/during/after procedures
Written fire evacuation plan and floor plan posted at exits
Individual evacuation profiles
72-hour shelter-in-place supply inventory and monthly check log
Emergency ID packets and staff ID cards
Vehicle list and backup transportation agreement
Family/legal representative summary and acknowledgment
Emergency event log and incident reports
Annual plan review and staff training records

policies.category: B(1) through B(7) – Emergency plan for ALUs/GHs
policies.title: Emergency and Fire Drills and After-Action Reports
policies.applies_to: All staff and individuals of each [AGENCY NAME] group home; the Administrator; the governing body
policies.purpose: To test and improve the emergency plan by holding regular, realistic drills on every shift, coordinating an annual drill with local emergency planners, and recording what is learned in an after-action report and improvement plan.
policies.policy: This policy meets COMAR 10.22.02.10A(17) (DH Form DD.APP.1.1 p.1) — Disaster/emergency plans in place with adequate drills; COMAR 10.22.02.10B(1)(b) — holding an annual practice drill coordinated with local emergency planners for sheltering in place or evacuating; and COMAR 10.22.02.10B(1)(c) — preparing an after action report and improvement plan after drills that evaluates the plan and takes corrective actions. The regulation sets no fixed number of drills. [AGENCY NAME] therefore sets its own standard: at least one fire evacuation drill each quarter in each home, rotated so that every shift, including overnight sleeping hours, is covered at least twice a year, plus at least one annual drill coordinated with local emergency planners that tests sheltering in place or evacuation. Every drill is evaluated and followed by an after-action report and improvement plan. Smoke detectors and fire extinguishers are working and updated (COMAR 10.22.02.12B).

definitions.definition: A practice evacuation of the home using the written fire evacuation plan, timed and observed.
The yearly practice of sheltering in place or evacuating, planned with local emergency planners (for example the county emergency management agency or local fire department).
A written review of a drill or real event that records what happened, what worked, what did not, and why.
A list of corrective actions with an owner and due date, that comes from the after-action report.
The county or city emergency management office and the local fire/EMS officials responsible for planning for emergencies.

procedures: By January 31 each year, the Administrator prepares a drill calendar for each home. It schedules at least one fire evacuation drill each quarter, rotating among day, evening, and overnight shifts and weekdays and weekends, so that every shift is covered at least twice a year. The governing body gets a copy.

By March 31 each year, the Administrator contacts the local emergency management office or fire department to coordinate the annual drill (B(1)(b)). The Administrator records the contact (name, date and advice received) and decides with the planners whether the drill will test sheltering in place or evacuation, alternating from year to year, and when it will take place.

Before each drill, the Administrator or designee chooses the scenario and a drill observer who does not take part in the response. The observer brings a timer and the drill checklist. Drills are unannounced to the staff on duty unless the local planners require notice, and are announced to individuals according to their needs so that the drill is not harmful to them.

During every drill, staff respond as in a real event: sound the alarm, assist each individual using the individual evacuation profile, take the go-pack, make a headcount at the meeting point, and report the time to a full evacuation. In a shelter-in-place drill, staff move everyone to the designated area, check supplies, and run the communication tree (see EP-03).

Individuals take part as they are able and choose. Staff provide any supports the individual's profile calls for. If someone refuses or is too distressed to take part, staff respect that, record it, and plan a more suitable way for the person to practice (for example a walk-through).

At least once a year the drill is held when individuals are asleep, to test staff response, wake-up methods and the awake overnight staff's ability to assist everyone (see SP-01). Once a year the plan is also tested for a case where the main exit is blocked.

Right after each drill, the observer and staff hold a short debrief while the details are fresh. They discuss what went well, what delayed anyone, which individuals needed more help, and whether equipment such as alarms, door hardware, flashlights, ramps and vehicles worked.

Within 7 days of each drill, the observer completes the drill record. It states the date, time, shift, type, weather, staff and individuals present, evacuation time, any problems, and signatures of the observer and shift lead.

Within 14 days of the annual coordinated drill, and of any real emergency, the Administrator completes an after-action report and improvement plan (B(1)(c)). The report evaluates the plan against what happened. It lists strengths, gaps and root causes, and sets corrective actions with a responsible person and due date. For routine quarterly drills, the Administrator documents findings and corrective actions on the drill record.

Corrective actions that are urgent (for example a blocked exit, a failed alarm, or a person who cannot be evacuated safely) are fixed immediately or controlled with an interim measure, and the Administrator tells the governing body at once.

The Administrator revises the emergency plan (EP-01), evacuation profiles, supplies, training or equipment based on the improvement plan, and retrains staff on the changes within 30 days. The Administrator then tracks each corrective action to completion and signs when closed.
If the drill showed that the same problem happened in two drills in a row, the Administrator escalates it to the quality assurance committee (see GOV-03) for review of the cause.

Staff test every smoke detector and check every fire extinguisher at least monthly. A qualified vendor services extinguishers and replaces them as needed. Smoke detectors are replaced on schedule and batteries changed as required. Any defect is fixed the same day, or an interim fire watch is in place until it is fixed (COMAR 10.22.02.12B).

The Administrator shares the annual after-action report with the governing body at its next meeting, shares the results and plan changes with the individuals and proponents on request, and, with the local emergency planners, uses their feedback in the next year's plan (see EP-05).
The Administrator keeps all drill records, after-action reports and improvement plans for at least [NUMBER] years, available to OHCQ surveyors at any time (see REC-02).

responsibilities.duty: Reviews the annual after-action report and makes sure the improvement plan has the resources it needs.
Schedules drills, coordinates with local emergency planners, writes the after-action reports and improvement plans, and tracks corrective actions.
Times and observes the drill, completes the drill record and leads the debrief.

responsibilities.role: Shift Lead and Direct Support Professionals
responsibilities.duty: Carry out the plan during the drill, assist individuals, and give honest feedback.
Take part as they are able and choose, and tell staff what helps or worries them.

documentation: Annual drill calendar for each home
Record of contacts with local emergency planners
Drill records (date, shift, time, evacuation time, participants, problems, signatures)
After-action reports and improvement plans, with corrective action tracking and closure dates
Monthly smoke detector and fire extinguisher checks and vendor service tags
Staff retraining records after plan changes
Governing body minutes showing review of after-action reports

policies.category: B(1) through B(7) – Emergency plan for ALUs/GHs
policies.title: Alternate Sites, Redundant Communication and Notifications
policies.applies_to: All direct support staff, the Program Director, the on-call administrator and any relief or contracted staff at each [AGENCY NAME] group home
policies.purpose: To make sure that if a home must be evacuated or sheltered away from its usual location, each person's medical needs and accommodations travel with them. It also ensures all parties can be reached by more than one means, and that families, staff and the Developmental Disabilities Administration (DDA) are notified promptly.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] maintains, as part of its written emergency plan under COMAR 10.22.02.10B, a plan for alternate sites, redundant communication and notifications. This policy meets COMAR 10.22.02.10B(1)(f) (arranging for medical needs and other accommodations for individuals and staff at alternative facilities or shelters), COMAR 10.22.02.10B(1)(g) (a communication protocol among all appropriate parties that includes redundant communication means), and item B(2) of DH Form DD.APP.1.1 p.2 / COMAR 10.22.02.10B(2) (notifications to families, staff and DDA). At least one alternate site is identified for each home before any individual moves in. No individual is moved to an alternate site unless it can meet that person's medical, mobility, dietary, medication, communication and behavioral support needs as written in the Individual Plan. At least two independent communication methods are in place and tested for every home. Notification of any incident, including an emergency that is also a reportable incident, follows the PORII process in PA-06. This policy does not replace PA-06. Plans, contact lists and test records are kept available for review by OHCQ during licensure, complaint or unannounced visits under COMAR 10.22.02.04.

definitions.definition: A pre-identified location (another [AGENCY NAME] home, a community shelter, a family residence or another agreed facility) where individuals and staff can go when the home cannot be used.
Two or more independent ways to reach people, so that failure of one does not stop communication (for example landline, cell phone, text/email, two-way radio or in-person runner).
A family member, guardian, advocate or other person who supports the individual and is named in the Individual Plan or contact record.
The DDA incident reporting process used to notify DDA of reportable incidents, as described in PA-06.
A portable bag or container for each home holding the items listed in this policy for use at an alternate site.

procedures: Before the first individual moves in, the Program Director identifies at least two alternate sites for each home: one close by and one farther away in a different direction. The Program Director confirms in writing with each site owner or operator that [AGENCY NAME] may use it, and records its address, contact person and phone number.

The Program Director checks each alternate site for accessibility (ramps, bathrooms, doorways), space, power, food storage, medication storage, sleeping arrangements and privacy, using the Alternate Site Checklist. The result is recorded and filed with the emergency plan.

For each individual, the Program Director (with the Registered Nurse (RN) for health items) prepares an Emergency Information Sheet. It lists diagnoses, allergies, current medications and doses, prescribers, preferred hospital, equipment (oxygen, lifts, communication devices, adaptive equipment), diet and texture modifications, seizure and choking protocols, behavior supports, communication needs and emergency contacts. Sheets are updated whenever the Individual Plan or a medication order changes, and at least every six months.

The Program Director maintains a go-kit for each home containing the Emergency Information Sheets, a current medication supply and MAR/TAR copies for at least 72 hours, spare eyeglasses and hearing aids, comfort items, incontinence and hygiene supplies, a first-aid kit, flashlights, a charged battery pack, and a hard copy of the contact list. The home manager checks the go-kit monthly and after each use, and records the check.

When an evacuation or move to an alternate site is ordered or judged necessary, the senior staff on duty calls 911 if there is immediate danger. Otherwise they notify the on-call administrator, who confirms the site and arranges transport per EP-01.

Before leaving, staff take the go-kit and sign-out roster, and count and name every individual. Staff re-count at arrival and at the start of each shift at the alternate site. The roster is kept current.

At the alternate site, the senior staff on duty arranges each person's medical needs and accommodations before general activities: medications are given on schedule per PA-07 and NU-02, modified diets and fluids are provided per HE-02, mobility and positioning equipment are set up, and the quiet space and communication supports each person needs are provided. Any need the site cannot meet is reported to the on-call administrator immediately so the person can be moved or the need supplied.

The home manager arranges the same for staff at the alternate site: breaks, meals, rest, access to restrooms and a way to report their own needs. Staff are not required to remain beyond safe limits; coverage follows EP-04.

The Program Director maintains a Communication Protocol with at least two independent methods for each of the following links: staff to on-call administrator, on-call administrator to Program Director, home to families/proponents, home to the RN, home to the DDA regional office, and home to emergency services. Methods must include one that works without electricity and one that works without a landline or internet (for example, a charged cell phone and a text-capable device or two-way radio).

Each home keeps a printed and an electronic contact list for individuals' proponents, staff, the RN, the on-call administrator, pharmacy, physicians, the alternate sites, local emergency management and the DDA regional office: CMRO 410-234-8200, ESRO 410-572-5920, SMRO 301-362-5100, WMRO 301-791-4670. The home's assigned regional office is marked on the list as [DDA REGIONAL OFFICE]. The contact list is verified quarterly and updated within 2 business days of any change.

As soon as it is safe, and within the timeframe set in the Communication Protocol, the on-call administrator or designee notifies (a) each individual's family/proponent of the emergency, the person's condition and location, and where to reach staff; (b) staff who are off duty, using EP-04 recall procedures; and (c) the DDA regional office of the emergency, the move to an alternate site and the individuals affected. Notifications are made by phone first, with a follow-up text or email if the call is not answered.
If the emergency is also a reportable incident, the on-call administrator ensures it is reported through PORII as required by PA-06 and does not wait for the emergency to end to begin the report.

The Program Director tests the communication methods at least twice a year, and at least once during the annual emergency drill under EP-02, by contacting each party through the primary and the back-up means. Failures are recorded and corrected within 14 days.
After an emergency or drill, the Program Director reviews how the alternate site, the go-kit and communication methods worked. Problems feed the after-action report and improvement plan under EP-02.

When OHCQ conducts a licensure, complaint or unannounced visit under COMAR 10.22.02.04, the home manager produces the alternate site agreements, checklists, contact lists, communication test records and Emergency Information Sheets on request.

responsibilities.duty: Identifies and approves alternate sites, maintains the Communication Protocol, contact lists and go-kits, runs communication tests and corrects failures.
Directs the move, authorizes alternate sites, makes or delegates notifications to families, staff and DDA, and ensures PORII reporting.
Reviews and updates the health content of Emergency Information Sheets and advises on medical needs at alternate sites.
Checks go-kits monthly, keeps rosters and contact lists current and trains staff on the plan.
Take the go-kit and roster, keep individuals together and safe, provide needed medical supports and follow the communication protocol.

documentation: Alternate site agreements and Alternate Site Checklists
Emergency Information Sheets for each individual, with update dates
Go-kit inventory and monthly check logs
Communication Protocol and contact lists with verification dates
Notification logs (who was contacted, time, method, outcome)
Communication test records and corrective actions
PORII confirmation where the emergency is a reportable incident
After-action report entries

policies.category: B(1) through B(7) – Emergency plan for ALUs/GHs
policies.title: Emergency Staff Coverage, Recall and Continuity of Operations
policies.applies_to: The Program Director, home managers, on-call administrators, all direct support staff and any relief or contract staff at each [AGENCY NAME] group home
policies.purpose: To make sure each home has enough trained, qualified staff during an emergency (shelter-in-place, evacuation or extended disruption), that staff can be reached and recalled quickly, and that supports and services continue without interruption.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] maintains a written staff coverage and continuity plan for every home. This policy meets DH Form DD.APP.1.1 p.2 / COMAR 10.22.02.10B(3) (staff coverage, organization and assignment of responsibilities) and its parts: B(3)(a) (planning staff coverage needs for ongoing shelter in place or evacuations), B(3)(b) (identifying staff members available to report for work or remain during extended periods), and B(3)(c) (staff notification and recall contingency plans and procedures). It also meets DH Form DD.APP.1.1 p.2 / COMAR 10.22.02.10B(4) (continuity of operations). Under COMAR 10.22.08.04A, staffing levels and patterns are those determined in each individual's Individual Plan, and under COMAR 10.22.02.11A the agency's staffing plan must meet health and safety needs. Emergency conditions do not lower those requirements. Maryland sets no fixed numeric ratio, so the emergency staffing level for each home is set by the Program Director from the individuals' assessed needs and written in the plan. Coverage is 24 hours a day, 7 days a week, with a named back-up for every post. Anyone brought in during an emergency must meet the hiring and training requirements of COMAR 10.22.02.11 before working independently, and training is provided or arranged under COMAR 10.22.08.04B.

definitions.definition: The ability to keep delivering required supports (health care, medications, meals, supervision, communication, personal care) and to keep core business functions running during and after an emergency.
Remaining in the home for the duration of an emergency, as described in EP-01.
A call to off-duty staff to report to work or remain at work during an emergency.
A staffing position that must be filled at all times to meet individuals' health and safety needs as written in their Individual Plans.
The minimum number and skill mix of staff, set by the Program Director for each home, needed to meet all residents' needs during an emergency.

procedures: For each home, the Program Director reviews each individual's Individual Plan, level of support, overnight needs, medical and behavioral needs, and mobility needs, and records the normal staffing pattern and the Emergency Staffing Level in the Emergency Staffing Plan. The plan is reviewed at least annually and whenever a resident moves in, leaves or has a change of condition.

The Emergency Staffing Plan covers two scenarios: (a) shelter in place for at least 72 hours, and (b) evacuation to an alternate site under EP-03. For each it lists the essential posts, staff needed on each shift, required skills (e.g., medication administration, seizure response, lifting/transfers, First Aid/CPR, behavior support) and who can supply them. This meets B(3)(a).

The Program Director assigns written emergency roles for every home: incident lead on site, medication administrator, headcount/roster keeper, communications lead, transportation lead and go-kit lead. Each role has a named primary and back-up and is included in staff orientation under SP-03.

Each staff member completes an Emergency Availability Form at hire and every six months. It states whether the person can report to work or remain during an extended emergency, travel limits, caregiving or transport constraints and preferred contact methods. Participation is voluntary where an individual has a caregiving or medical limitation, and no one is penalized for stating a limit in advance. The Program Director compiles an Available Staff Roster for each home, ranked by distance, qualification and willingness. This meets B(3)(b).

The Program Director maintains a back-up pool of qualified relief staff and, where used, agency or contract staff, who have already completed required background checks per SP-02 and orientation and training per SP-03. Staff not yet cleared and trained under COMAR 10.22.02.11 are never left to work independently, even in an emergency; they may only assist alongside a qualified staff member.

A Staff Recall Procedure is kept for each home. It sets out the call order (staff already on duty, off-duty staff nearest the home, back-up pool, then administrators), two contact methods per person, the script to be used, a limit on duration of continuous work (with breaks and rest periods) and who may authorize overtime. This meets B(3)(c).

When an emergency begins, the senior staff on duty tells the on-call administrator immediately. The on-call administrator decides whether recall is needed, activates the recall procedure within 30 minutes of the decision, and records each call (time, person, response).

Staff who are asked to report must confirm by phone or text and give an estimated arrival time. If a staff member cannot be reached after two attempts by different methods, the caller moves to the next person on the roster and flags the first for follow-up.

Staff on duty when an emergency begins do not leave until relieved by a qualified staff member and handed off by shift report. The on-call administrator keeps the minimum Emergency Staffing Level at all times, including awake overnight staff as required by SP-01.

The home manager or incident lead plans relief shifts so that no staff member works beyond a safe limit. Where needed, rest areas, meals and access to medication or personal needs are provided for staff who remain on site.

A Continuity of Operations Plan is kept for the agency and each home. It identifies critical functions (direct support, medication administration, health monitoring, communication with families, payroll, billing, records access and transportation), the person responsible for each, and the back-up person or method. It also lists the actions needed to keep each function going if the usual office, staff, power, internet or vehicles are not available. This meets B(4).

Payroll, billing and documentation continue under the continuity plan. The Program Director and fiscal staff arrange for staff to be paid and for services delivered to be documented during and after the emergency, in line with GOV-04. Records access during an emergency follows EP-05.

The Program Director tests recall at least twice a year, once during the annual drill under EP-02, by contacting a sample of staff and timing responses. Results are written in the after-action report. Gaps found (for example, too few qualified back-ups) are corrected within 30 days.

After the emergency, the Program Director holds a debriefing within 14 days, returns staffing to the regular pattern in the Individual Plans, reviews overtime, rest and staff wellbeing, and updates the Emergency Staffing Plan and Available Staff Roster.

responsibilities.duty: Sets emergency staffing levels, maintains rosters and the recall and continuity plans, assigns roles, tests recall and corrects gaps.
Decides when to activate recall, ensures essential posts are filled and authorizes overtime and back-up staff.
Keeps staff availability forms current, schedules relief and rest, and briefs staff on assigned emergency roles.
Complete availability forms, answer recall calls where able, stay until properly relieved and follow assigned emergency roles.
Keeps payroll, billing and records functions running under the continuity plan.

documentation: Emergency Staffing Plan for each home with annual review date
Staff Emergency Availability Forms and Available Staff Roster
Staff Recall Procedure and recall call logs
Role assignment sheets
Continuity of Operations Plan
Recall test results and after-action report entries
Training records showing orientation, background checks and required training for back-up and relief staff

policies.category: B(1) through B(7) – Emergency plan for ALUs/GHs
policies.title: Back-up of Records, Sharing the Plan with Emergency Management, and Family Summary
policies.applies_to: The Program Director, administrative and IT staff, home managers, the RN and any person who handles agency records or the emergency plan
policies.purpose: To protect individuals' and staff records and facility documents so they can be reached during an emergency, to make the emergency plan available to emergency management organizations, and to give families a summary of the plan when they ask.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] backs up records and data and stores them electronically off-site so that they can be reached in emergency conditions, shares its emergency plan with emergency management organizations, and provides families with an executive summary on request. This policy meets DH Form DD.APP.1.1 p.2 / COMAR 10.22.02.10B(5) (procedures for back-up records) and its parts B(5)(a) (backup and electronic off-site storage of appropriate records and data of individuals and staff and facility documents for access under emergency conditions) and B(5)(b) (ensuring access to an electronic copy of the emergency plans when requested by local, State or federal emergency management organizations). It also meets B(6) (provisions to share plans with local emergency management organizations) and B(7) (executive summary of procedure provided to a family member upon request). Records are kept at the site where the individual is served as required by COMAR 10.22.02.13A. Under COMAR 10.22.02.13C, an individual's medical information must be readily accessible to emergency personnel. Under COMAR 10.22.02.13E, electronic records must comply with HIPAA privacy and security rules (45 CFR 164) and be backed up and stored off-site. Back-up and sharing activities must not reduce the protection of confidential information, so only the minimum necessary information is shared and see PA-03. Records are retained at least 6 years under REC-01.

definitions.definition: A copy of electronic records and data stored at a secure location or secure cloud service that is physically and logically separate from the home and the main office.
The local, State or federal agency responsible for emergency planning and response (for example, the county office of emergency management).

A short plain-language description of the emergency plan for families that explains what the home will do and how families will be contacted, without confidential details about other individuals or security-sensitive information.
A written agreement with any outside vendor that stores or handles protected health information on the agency's behalf, as required by HIPAA.

procedures: The Program Director and the IT/administrative lead prepare a Records Inventory that lists the records to be backed up: individuals' records (identifying information, emergency contacts, next of kin, physician, diagnoses, allergies, medication lists, current Individual Plan and documentation of its implementation, Emergency Information Sheets), staff records (contact information, training and certification records, schedules) and facility documents (licenses, provider agreements, leases, insurance, floor plans, alternate site agreements, vendor contacts and the emergency plan itself). This meets B(5)(a).

The IT/administrative lead sets up automatic electronic back-up of all electronic records and data at least daily. Back-ups are stored off-site at a secure location or secure cloud service that is not in the same building or on the same power or network as the home or main office.

Back-up and storage must meet the HIPAA Security Rule (45 CFR 164): encryption of data in storage and in transit, unique user IDs, access limited by job role, audit logs, and a written business associate agreement with any outside vendor. The IT/administrative lead keeps the signed agreements on file.

Where records are kept on paper at the home (COMAR 10.22.02.13A), the home manager keeps a current copy of each person's Emergency Information Sheet in a place staff can reach quickly, and ensures it can go with the person to a hospital or alternate site. Paper records are scanned into the electronic system within 14 days of creation or update so that they are included in the back-up.

The IT/administrative lead tests the back-up by restoring a sample of records at least quarterly and records the date, what was restored, who did it and whether it worked. Failures are fixed within 7 days and re-tested.

A list of who may access the off-site back-up in an emergency (at least two people, with a named back-up) is kept in the Records Access Procedure along with log-in instructions kept in a sealed, secure place. Emergency access is logged and reviewed by the Program Director after each use.

The Program Director ensures the emergency plan, including the plan for each home, is saved as a PDF in the off-site back-up and can be sent electronically within one business day of a request. When local, State or federal emergency management or DDA/OHCQ requests a copy, the Program Director sends it by a secure method and records the date, requester and what was sent. This meets B(5)(b).

Before sending the plan outside the agency, the Program Director removes or limits confidential individual information so that only the minimum necessary information is shared, under PA-03. Individual-specific health information is shared with emergency responders only as needed to protect that person's health and safety.

Within 30 days after the plan is first adopted and after each annual update, the Program Director sends a copy of the plan to the local emergency management organization for the county where each home is located and documents the transmittal (date, recipient, method). The Program Director asks emergency management to confirm receipt and records any feedback. This meets B(6).
The Program Director invites local emergency management to take part in the annual emergency drill under EP-02 and records the invitation and the response.

The Program Director prepares an Executive Summary of the emergency plan for families, written in plain language and available in accessible formats and the family's preferred language. It covers how the agency will keep individuals safe, how families will be contacted and by what means (see EP-03), where individuals may go, and whom to call for information. It leaves out security-sensitive details and other individuals' information.

On request from a family member or proponent, the home manager provides the Executive Summary within 5 business days (sooner if possible) and records the date and recipient. The home manager also explains the summary and answers questions. This meets B(7).
At admission, the staff member who completes admission under PCS-01 tells each individual and family/proponent that the Executive Summary is available on request.
The Program Director reviews the Records Inventory, back-up system and summary at least annually and after any change in systems, vendors or the plan, and updates the version log under CS-01.

Records retention is not shortened by back-up cycles. Back-up copies of individual records are kept for the same period as the original record, which is at least 6 years even if the person leaves or dies, under REC-01 and COMAR 10.22.02.13D.

responsibilities.duty: Owns the emergency plan, sends it to emergency management on request and annually, approves the Executive Summary and reviews back-up test results.
Sets up and tests encrypted off-site back-up, keeps business associate agreements and manages emergency access.
Keeps Emergency Information Sheets accessible at the home and provides the Executive Summary to families on request.
Confirms that back-up and sharing meet HIPAA requirements and the minimum necessary standard.
Know where Emergency Information Sheets are kept and take them with individuals during evacuation or hospital transport.

documentation: Records Inventory
Back-up schedule, back-up logs and quarterly restore test records
Business associate agreements and HIPAA security documentation
Records Access Procedure and emergency access log
Log of plan requests and transmittals to local, State and federal emergency management
Executive Summary and log of family requests and delivery
Annual review and version log

policies.category: C – Staff awareness and implementation of policies
policies.title: Staff Awareness and Implementation of Policies; Policy Review and Document Control
policies.applies_to: All staff, care providers, consultants and volunteers of [AGENCY NAME], and the Program Director and governing body responsible for the policy manual
policies.purpose: To make sure everyone who works with or for [AGENCY NAME] knows the agency's policies and carries each one out as adopted, and that the manual is kept current and controlled.
policies.policy: All staff, care providers, consultants and volunteers must be aware of the agency's policies and implement each policy as adopted. This policy meets DH Form DD.APP.1.1 p.2 / COMAR 10.22.02.10C. Awareness is shown by documented orientation and a signed acknowledgment at hire and after each revision. Implementation is checked by supervision, observation and review of records. The policy manual is reviewed at least annually and whenever a regulation, DDA requirement or agency practice changes, and all versions are tracked in a version log. Training that is required by COMAR 10.22.02.11C and D is documented on the Staff Training Form (DD.APP.1.1) and kept in the personnel file. No staff member, consultant or volunteer may work independently with individuals before completing the required policy orientation and training under COMAR 10.22.02.11C. Failing to follow a policy is addressed through supervision and, if needed, discipline under SP-05.

definitions.definition: Any person or organization, paid or unpaid, that provides care or supports to an individual at [AGENCY NAME]'s direction, including relief and contract staff.
A professional engaged by [AGENCY NAME] to give advice or services, such as a nurse, behavior specialist, therapist or accountant.
A signed and dated statement that a person received, reviewed and understands the policies and will follow them.
A record of each policy revision, including the date, what changed, the reason, who approved it and the date staff were trained.
The DDA form (DD.APP.1.1) used to document the training topics required by COMAR 10.22.02.11C and D.

procedures: The Program Director keeps the complete, current Policy and Procedure Manual in a place all staff can reach at each home (paper or electronic), and keeps the master copy and version log at the main office. Superseded versions are marked and kept in an archive for at least 6 years.

On or before the first day of work, and before independent duties, each new staff member, consultant, care provider and volunteer receives a copy of or access to the policies that apply to their role. Core policies for all staff include those on rights, abuse and neglect reporting, incident reporting, confidentiality, emergency procedures, infection control and conduct.

The Program Director or a designated trainer provides a policy orientation covering each policy, how it is carried out at the home, who to call with questions, and each person's duty to report concerns. The orientation is delivered in the person's language and in a format they can understand, with questions invited and answered.

Each person signs and dates a Policy Acknowledgment form after the orientation, stating that they have received and reviewed the policies and will follow them. The signed form is filed in the personnel file (or volunteer/consultant file) within 5 business days.

Required job training and DDA-approved training under COMAR 10.22.02.11C are completed before the staff member works independently. The training under COMAR 10.22.02.11D (community integration, individual-directed planning, characteristics and needs, First Aid/CPR, fundamental rights, communicable diseases, supporting choice and communication skills) is completed within 3 months of hire. SP-03 describes the full training plan.

The trainer records each topic, date, trainer and hours on the Staff Training Form (DD.APP.1.1). The Program Director checks the form for completeness, signs it and files it in the personnel file. The training matrix is updated and reviewed monthly for due dates.

Consultants and volunteers receive an orientation matched to their role, including at least rights, confidentiality, abuse and neglect reporting, emergency procedures and policies that bear directly on their activities. Volunteers are never counted toward required staffing and do not work alone with individuals unless the Program Director has approved this in writing and the volunteer has completed the required training.

The Program Director reviews the whole manual at least once every 12 months, and sooner whenever a COMAR provision, DDA policy, waiver requirement, licensing finding or incident review shows a change is needed. The review is led by the Program Director, with input from the RN, home managers, direct support staff and, when possible, individuals and their proponents.
Each revision is dated, numbered and recorded in the version log. The Program Director has the governing body approve substantive changes and signs and dates each revised policy.

Within 14 days of each revision, all affected staff, consultants, care providers and volunteers are told of the change in a briefing or written notice and sign a new acknowledgment. Policies that are changed in response to an urgent safety concern are communicated immediately by the home manager, with the written acknowledgment following within 5 business days.

Home managers check implementation through regular supervision: they observe practice, review daily documentation, ask staff to describe how they would handle specific situations, and record findings. The Program Director samples these checks monthly.

When staff do not follow a policy, the supervisor re-trains the person within 7 days and records the retraining. Repeated or serious failures, or any that put an individual's health or safety at risk, are handled under SP-05 and may require reporting under PA-06 and BP-01.
Staff may ask for clarification of any policy and may propose changes. The Program Director responds in writing within 14 days where a written request is made.

Quarterly, the Program Director audits a sample of personnel, consultant and volunteer files to confirm each has a current acknowledgment, completed training and Staff Training Form. Missing items are corrected within 14 days and gaps are reported to the Quality Assurance Committee under GOV-03.
The Program Director keeps the manual, version log, acknowledgments and Staff Training Forms available for review at any licensure, complaint or unannounced visit.

responsibilities.duty: Adopts the policies, approves substantive revisions and oversees that the policies are carried out.
Maintains the manual and version log, conducts the annual review, ensures orientations, acknowledgments and training occur, and audits files.
Makes the manual accessible at the home, supervises implementation and retrains staff when policies are not followed.

responsibilities.role: Staff, care providers, consultants and volunteers
responsibilities.duty: Read, understand and follow the policies that apply to them, sign acknowledgments and ask questions when unsure.
Delivers orientation and training and completes the Staff Training Form accurately.

documentation: Current policy manual with master copy and version log
Archive of superseded policy versions
Signed Policy Acknowledgment forms at hire and after each revision
Orientation sign-in sheets and agendas
Staff Training Form (DD.APP.1.1) for each employee
Training matrix
Supervision and observation notes on policy implementation

policies.category: D – Grievance process information for individuals and proponents
policies.title: Grievance Process Information for Individuals and Proponents
policies.applies_to: The Program Director, home managers, the admissions coordinator and all direct support staff who interact with individuals and their proponents
policies.purpose: To make sure every individual served and their proponents have enough clear, accessible information about the grievance process to use it effectively, without fear of retaliation.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] gives each individual served, and their proponent where there is one, sufficient information about the grievance process to enable them to use it effectively. This policy meets DH Form DD.APP.1.1 p.2 / COMAR 10.22.02.10D. The information is given at admission and again at least annually and on request, in plain language, in accessible formats and in the person's own language or preferred mode of communication, consistent with the Americans with Disabilities Act and PA-05. The information includes how to file a grievance, who will help, how the grievance will be handled and how the person will be told the result, how to contact the Office of Health Care Quality (OHCQ) at 410-402-8100 or 877-402-8220, and the protection against retaliation. The grievance procedure itself, including timelines and review steps, is set out in PA-04. This policy covers how people are informed and supported to use it.

definitions.definition: A complaint or concern, spoken or written, made by or for an individual about the services, staff, home, rights or treatment, whether or not the person uses the word “grievance”.
A family member, guardian, advocate or other person chosen by or acting for the individual in dealing with the agency.

Information presented in a way the person can use, such as plain language, large print, pictures, audio, video, Braille, sign language or an interpreter, or a translation into the person's preferred language.
Any negative action or threat against a person because they raised or supported a grievance, such as changing supports, restricting privileges, discharge threats or hostile treatment.

procedures: The Program Director maintains a Grievance Information Packet that explains the grievance process in plain language. It includes how to make a complaint (verbally, in writing, by a proponent or through a staff member), the names and phone numbers of the people who can receive it, the time frames in PA-04, how a person can get help in preparing a complaint, and a statement that grievances may be made without fear of retaliation.

The packet includes the OHCQ complaint contact numbers (410-402-8100 and 877-402-8220) and the contact for the DDA regional office serving the home ([DDA REGIONAL OFFICE PHONE]), and states that a person may contact these offices at any time, whether or not they have used the agency's process first.

The packet is available in alternative formats: large print, picture-based or easy-read version, audio or video, and translations into the languages used by individuals and families served. Staff arrange for a qualified interpreter or sign language interpreter when needed, under PA-05, at no cost to the person.

At admission, the staff member completing admission under PCS-01 reviews the packet with the individual and the proponent, using whichever communication method the person uses best. The reviewer checks understanding by asking the person to explain, in their own words or by their own means, how they would raise a concern, and repeats the explanation as needed.

The individual and proponent are given a copy of the packet to keep. A staff member records the date, method, who received it and any accommodations on the Grievance Information Acknowledgment form, which is signed by the person or proponent where possible. If the person cannot sign, the staff member notes how understanding was confirmed.

A Grievance Process notice is posted in a common area of each home at a height and in a format everyone can use, with the OHCQ and agency contact numbers and the name of the person to contact. The home manager checks the notice monthly.

At least once each year, and during the person-centered planning meeting under PCS-02, the home manager or Program Director reviews the grievance process again with each individual and proponent, and gives an updated packet if anything has changed. The review is documented.
The home manager also reviews the process at house meetings at least twice a year, gives individuals the chance to raise concerns, and notes who attended and what was discussed.

At the time of admission and each annual review, the person is told who at the agency (by name or role) will help them to file a grievance, including help with writing, speaking, communication devices or going through the steps. Staff provide that help promptly when asked and never discourage or delay a complaint.

Staff explain that the person will not be punished, treated differently or have services reduced for making a complaint, and that anyone who retaliates is subject to discipline under SP-05. Staff who receive a grievance follow PA-04 and tell the Program Director the same day.

Staff who are asked about the grievance process by an individual or proponent give accurate information at once, or connect the person to the home manager the same day. Staff do not give opinions on whether a complaint is justified.

The Program Director reviews the log of grievance information given at least quarterly to confirm every individual has received the information at admission and annually. Missing items are corrected within 14 days.
The Program Director checks yearly that the packet, notice and contact numbers are current, including OHCQ and DDA contacts, and updates them within 7 days of any change.

responsibilities.duty: Maintains the Grievance Information Packet and accessible formats, verifies contact numbers and audits that information is provided at admission and annually.
Reviews the process with individuals and proponents, posts the notice, runs house meetings and arranges help to file a grievance.
Gives and explains the packet at admission and records it.
Answer questions accurately, help the person file a grievance when asked and never discourage or retaliate.
May raise a concern at any time, in any way they can communicate, and contact OHCQ or DDA directly.

documentation: Grievance Information Packet in each format and language used
Signed Grievance Information Acknowledgment forms with the date, method and accommodations
Annual review records and house meeting notes
Photograph or checklist confirming that the notice is posted
Interpreter or translation request records
Quarterly audit of information given

policies.category: Nursing – Medication P&P, Reporting/Communication and the RN Role
policies.title: Medication: Obtaining Orders and Medications
policies.applies_to: The Registered Nurse (RN), the Program Director, home managers and all staff who obtain, receive, transcribe, verify or administer medications at [AGENCY NAME] homes
policies.purpose: To make sure every medication and treatment is given only on a current, complete, written prescriber order, that medications are obtained, packaged and received safely, and that records are pharmacy-generated and accurate.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] obtains and manages medication orders and supplies as required by the Medication Technician Training Program (MTTP), which this policy follows at sections 1:4-9; 2:2-7; 2:4-2; 2:4-7; 2:3-18; and 2:3-26. This policy meets the Nursing section item “Medication P&P: Obtaining orders and medications (MTTP 1:4-9; 2:2-7; 2:4-2; 2:4-7; 2:3-18; 2:3-26)” of DH Form DD.APP.1.1 p.2. Medications are given only on a current written prescriber order. Staff follow the current MTTP and the DDA medication curriculum for transcription and order verification, as required by COMAR 10.22.02.10A and COMAR 10.22.02.12D.
