As required by COMAR 10.22.02.12D, the agency administers medication per DDA's medication curriculum, uses unit-dose packaging for oral solid medications unless the Individual Plan says otherwise, packages medication for individuals who are absent from the home separately, and asks pharmacies to generate Medication Administration Records (MARs), Treatment Administration Records (TARs) and physician order forms. Only staff who meet the training and delegation requirements in PA-07 and NU-07 may handle medication. Administration, storage, controlled drugs and errors are addressed in NU-02, NU-03 and NU-04.

definitions.definition: A health care practitioner legally authorized in Maryland to prescribe medications and treatments.
A written instruction from a prescriber that states the person's name, the medication or treatment, dose, route, frequency and reason, and the date, signed by the prescriber.
The Medication Administration Record and the Treatment Administration Record on which each dose or treatment is recorded when it is given or refused or not given.
Individually sealed doses of a medication, labeled and supplied by the pharmacy, such as blister cards or single-dose packages.
Copying an order onto the MAR/TAR. This is done only as the MTTP and the delegating RN allow, and is always checked against the original order.
The Medication Technician Training Program curriculum used by DDA providers for medication administration.

procedures: Staff give a medication or treatment only when there is a current written order signed by a prescriber. A telephone or verbal order is taken only by the RN or other staff authorized under the MTTP and PA-07, is written down immediately with the prescriber's name, date and time, read back to the prescriber and followed by a written order within the time set by the RN.

Each order must include the individual's full name, the medication or treatment name, dose, route, frequency, time of day, reason or diagnosis, any special instructions (such as with food or hold parameters), start date, and the prescriber's signature or authorized electronic signature. Staff do not give a medication from an order missing any of these items. They contact the RN or prescriber for clarification first.

Prescriber visits and follow-up: staff take the individual's current medication list, the Emergency Information Sheet and the Health Care Appointment Form to each appointment (or send them with the escort). After the visit the escort or home manager obtains the written orders and any visit summary before leaving, or requests them from the office the same day.

Staff bring new, changed or discontinued orders to the RN, or to the delegated person identified in NU-07, on the same day they are received (before the next dose). The RN reviews each order for completeness, allergies, interactions and conflicts with the Individual Plan, and decides what staff must do before the first dose.

The RN or authorized staff member requests that the pharmacy generate and send the MAR, TAR and physician order forms. Where the pharmacy cannot produce them, the RN approves a transcription method that follows the MTTP, and a second trained staff member checks it against the original order. The check is initialed and dated.

Medications are ordered from a single contracted pharmacy where possible, and the home manager keeps the pharmacy's contact details and delivery times posted. Staff order refills at least 7 days before the supply runs out, using the pharmacy's process, and record the date requested on the refill log.

Oral solid medications are obtained in unit-dose packaging unless the Individual Plan states otherwise. Where the IP allows another form, the reason and the RN's approval are recorded. Prescription labels must be pharmacy-generated and must match the order.

When a medication is delivered, two staff trained in medication administration, or one staff member and the RN, check it against the order and MAR. They verify the individual's name, medication, strength, dose, route, frequency, expiration date and quantity, and sign and date the Medication Receipt Log. Any discrepancy is not used until the RN or pharmacy resolves it.
Staff store newly received medications immediately under NU-02, and count controlled drugs on receipt under NU-03.

Before every first dose of a new or changed medication, the staff member administering it compares the MAR, the label and the order, and checks for allergies and the person's identification. Any mismatch is reported to the RN, and the dose is not given until it is resolved.

When an individual will be away from the home (home visit, day program, vacation), the staff member packages the medication for the absent period separately, labeled with the person's name, medication, dose and time, as required by COMAR 10.22.02.12D. Quantities and the hand-off are recorded on the Medication Release Form, signed by the staff member and the person or escort receiving it. Returned medication is counted and recorded.

Discontinued, expired or changed medications are removed from current stock the day the order changes and held for disposal under NU-02 and NU-03. The MAR line is marked discontinued with the date, and the RN or authorized staff member verifies this.

Prescription and over-the-counter medications and supplements, including PRN (as-needed) medications, require their own written orders. Staff do not give, share or borrow medication from another person's supply. PRN orders must state the reason, dose, frequency, maximum in 24 hours, and when to call the RN or prescriber.
If a person self-administers medication, the determination and supports in NU-05 apply and the order must still be on file.

Each month, the RN (or a person delegated by the RN) compares a sample of each home's MARs and TARs to the current orders and to medication supplies, and records findings. Errors, missing orders or transcription mistakes are corrected the same day and handled under NU-04 when they are medication errors.
Medication orders, MARs and TARs are kept in each person's record under REC-01 and COMAR 10.22.02.13, and a medication list is always available to emergency personnel.

responsibilities.duty: Reviews and approves orders, supervises transcription and verification, delegates tasks under NU-07 and audits MARs/TARs against orders monthly.
Contracts with the pharmacy, ensures the pharmacy supplies unit-dose packaging and generated MARs/TARs/order forms, and ensures staff are trained.
Ensures orders are obtained after each appointment, refills are requested on time and deliveries are checked and logged.
Give medication only on a current written order, verify the label, MAR and order, and report discrepancies to the RN before giving medication.
Provide complete signed orders, unit-dose packaging and pharmacy-generated records.

documentation: Current signed prescriber orders and telephone/verbal order records
Pharmacy-generated MARs, TARs and physician order forms
Transcription records and second-person checks, where used
Medication Receipt Log and refill log
Medication Release Forms for absences and returned medication counts
Monthly RN MAR/TAR and order audit
Records of clarifications with prescribers or pharmacy

policies.category: Nursing – Medication P&P, Reporting/Communication and the RN Role
policies.title: Medication Administration and Storage
policies.applies_to: All Medication Technicians, licensed nurses, direct support staff, the Program Director and the delegating RN at every [AGENCY NAME] group home site
policies.purpose: To make sure every person in a [AGENCY NAME] group home receives medication safely, exactly as prescribed, and that medication is stored securely, kept separate for each person and documented at the time it is given.
policies.policy: This policy meets DH Form DD.APP.1.1 p.2, Nursing section, item Nursing-2 — Medication P&P: Administration and storage (MTTP 1:1-18; 1:4-9; 2:2-7; 2:3; 2:3-26; 2:2-28; 2:4-2; 2:4-7), and the medication requirements of COMAR 10.22.02.10 (C10) and COMAR 10.22.02.12 D (C12). [AGENCY NAME] administers medication in accordance with the DDA medication administration curriculum (the Maryland Board of Nursing Medication Technician Training Program, 'MTTP'). Only a certified Medication Technician (CMT) working under the delegation and supervision of the delegating RN, or a licensed nurse, may give medication. Medication is stored locked, separately for each individual. Medication for an individual who will be away from the home is packaged separately. Each dose is documented on the Medication Administration Record (MAR) at the time it is given. Unit-dose packaging is used for oral solid medication unless the Individual Plan (IP) says otherwise, and [AGENCY NAME] asks the pharmacy to generate the MARs, Treatment Administration Records (TARs) and physician order forms. Individuals who are assessed as able to self-administer are supported under NU-05.

definitions.definition: An unlicensed staff member who holds current Medication Technician certification from the Maryland Board of Nursing and gives medication under RN delegation.
Medication Administration Record, the document on which each dose given, refused or withheld is recorded at the time of administration.
Treatment Administration Record, used to document ordered treatments such as topical care.
Medication Technician Training Program, the Board of Nursing-approved curriculum and DDA medication administration standard that staff follow.
Oral solid medication packaged by the pharmacy in individually sealed doses.
A medication ordered to be given only as needed, according to written parameters.

procedures: Before a staff member's first medication pass, and at each certification renewal, the Program Director verifies the staff member's current Medication Technician certification with the Maryland Board of Nursing and files the verification in the personnel record. Staff who are not certified or licensed do not administer medication.
The delegating RN confirms in writing which medication tasks each CMT is delegated for each individual before the CMT gives them (see NU-07).

On admission, and whenever an order changes, the CMT checks the prescriber's order, the pharmacy label and the MAR against each other. Any mismatch is reported to the delegating RN and the prescriber before the medication is given (see NU-01).

[AGENCY NAME] asks the dispensing pharmacy to supply pharmacy-generated MARs, TARs and physician order forms, and to supply oral solid medication in unit-dose packaging unless the IP says otherwise. The reason for any exception is recorded in the IP.

The CMT washes hands, gathers only one individual's medication at a time, and checks the individual's identity, the medication, the dose, the route, the time and the allergy list on the MAR before each administration. The CMT follows the steps taught in the MTTP.

The CMT explains the medication to the individual in the way the individual understands (see PA-05) and respects the individual's right to refuse. A refusal is documented on the MAR with the reason given and reported to the delegating RN on the same shift.

The CMT observes the individual taking the medication and documents the dose on the MAR immediately after it is given, with initials and signature. Documenting in advance, or after the shift, is not permitted.
For PRN medication, the CMT follows the written parameters and consults the delegating RN when the parameters are not clear. The CMT documents the reason, the time and the outcome on the MAR.
Any omitted dose, late dose, wrong-time dose or refusal is documented and reported to the delegating RN. If it is a medication error, NU-04 applies.

All medication, including over-the-counter products, is kept in a locked cabinet or locked container, separate for each individual. External-use products are kept apart from oral products. Refrigerated medication is kept in a locked box or locked refrigerator, and the temperature is checked and logged each day.
The CMT on duty keeps the medication keys on their person. Keys are handed to the next CMT at shift change and are never left in the cabinet. Controlled drugs are handled under NU-03.

When an individual will be away from the home (for a home visit, an overnight stay or a day trip), the CMT packages the needed medication separately, labels it with the person's name and the doses, and has it signed out by the person or the receiving adult. The sign-out and return are documented, and returned medication is counted and recorded.

Discontinued, expired or contaminated medication is removed from the working supply, held locked and separate, and disposed of as directed by the delegating RN and documented (see NU-03 for controlled drugs).

The delegating RN or the Program Director inspects medication storage and compares the MAR with the medication supply at least monthly, and records the findings. Storage problems are corrected at once.
For an individual who is assessed as able to self-administer, medication is stored where that person can reach it and in a way that protects other residents, as set out in NU-05.
Completed MARs and TARs are filed in the individual's record at the site and are kept at least 6 years (see REC-01).

responsibilities.duty: Administers medication only within delegated tasks, follows the MTTP steps, documents every dose when given, keeps medication locked, and reports refusals, omissions and errors immediately.
Delegates and supervises medication tasks, reviews MARs, inspects storage, and gives direction on omissions, refusals and disposal.

Verifies certifications, makes sure the pharmacy supplies unit-dose packaging and pharmacy-generated MARs, TARs and order forms, keeps locks and storage in working order, and makes sure the policy is followed at the site.

responsibilities.role: Direct support staff who are not CMTs
responsibilities.duty: Do not give medication. They support the individual's routine, report concerns to the CMT on duty, and call the delegating RN or 911 in an emergency.

documentation: Board of Nursing certification verification for each CMT
RN delegation records
Pharmacy-generated MARs, TARs and order forms
Refrigerator temperature log
Medication sign-out and return records for absences
Monthly storage inspection and MAR review record
Refusal and omission reports

policies.category: Nursing – Medication P&P, Reporting/Communication and the RN Role
policies.title: Controlled Drugs
policies.applies_to: All Medication Technicians, licensed nurses, the Program Director and the delegating RN at every [AGENCY NAME] group home site
policies.purpose: To prevent loss, diversion and misuse of controlled drugs by securing them, counting them at every shift change, investigating any discrepancy at once, and documenting their disposal.
policies.policy: This policy meets DH Form DD.APP.1.1 p.2, Nursing section, item Nursing-3 — Medication P&P: Controlled drugs (MTTP 1:4-9; 2:1-9; 2:2-5; 2:2-7), and the medication requirements of COMAR 10.22.02.10 (C10) and COMAR 10.22.02.12 D (C12). Controlled drugs are kept under double lock, separate for each individual. Two staff count them at every shift change and both sign the count record. Any discrepancy is investigated and reported immediately, and is treated as an incident under the Policy on Reportable Incidents and Investigations (PORII; see PA-06). Destruction and disposal are documented.

definitions.definition: A medication that is a controlled dangerous substance under State or federal law, and any other medication the delegating RN designates for counting.
Two separate locks between the drug and unauthorized access, such as a locked box inside a locked cabinet.
Any difference between the count on hand and the count on the record, any missing, damaged or spilled dose, or any sign of tampering.
The DDA Policy on Reportable Incidents and Investigations, followed under PA-06.

procedures: On receipt of a controlled drug from the pharmacy, the CMT on duty and a second staff member count it together, check it against the label and order, and enter it on the individual's controlled drug count record, which both sign.
The CMT stores controlled drugs under double lock, separate for each individual. Only CMTs and licensed nurses on duty have access to the keys, and the keys are never left unattended.

At every shift change, the outgoing and incoming CMTs count each controlled drug together, compare the count with the record, and both sign and date the record. The count is not completed until both signatures are on it.
If only one qualified staff member is present at shift change, the Program Director or the delegating RN designates a second person to witness the count, and the Program Director records who it was.
When a controlled drug is given, the CMT records the dose on the MAR and reduces the count record in the same moment, so the two always agree.
If a dose is dropped, refused, spilled or wasted, the CMT documents it on the count record with a second staff signature as witness and tells the delegating RN on the same shift.

If any count does not match, the CMTs stop, recount, and check the record, the MAR and the other medication for that person. If the count still does not match, they notify the Program Director and the delegating RN immediately and do not leave the home until the Program Director gives direction.

The Program Director secures the area, collects written statements from the staff involved before they leave, and reports the discrepancy as a potential incident under the PORII. If theft or diversion is suspected, the Program Director notifies the delegating RN, [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] and law enforcement as appropriate, and notifies the prescriber if the individual's care is affected.
The delegating RN reviews each discrepancy, decides on any retraining or restriction of CMT duties, and the review is sent to the Quality Assurance process (see GOV-03).

When a controlled drug is discontinued, has expired or is left over after a death or discharge, the CMT does not destroy it alone. It is held double-locked until the delegating RN directs how it is to be disposed of and who is to witness it.

The disposal is carried out by two people, at least one of whom is a CMT or licensed nurse. They record the drug, the amount, the date, the method and the place, and both sign the disposal record. For an individual who has left, a receipt for any drug released to the person or family is kept.
The delegating RN or the Program Director reviews the count records at least monthly and records the review. Count records are filed in the individual's record and kept at least 6 years (see REC-01).

responsibilities.duty: Secures controlled drugs, counts them at every shift change with a second signature, and reports any discrepancy immediately.
Makes sure double-lock storage is available, makes sure counts are done and witnessed, secures the scene and starts the incident report when a discrepancy occurs.
Reviews count records and discrepancies, directs disposal and witnessing, and decides on retraining or restriction of duties.
Makes sure incidents are reported under PA-06 and that law enforcement is notified when diversion or theft is suspected.

documentation: Controlled drug count records with two signatures at every shift change
Receipt records
Waste or spill records with witness signature
Discrepancy and incident reports under the PORII
Staff statements
Disposal records
Monthly count review record

policies.category: Nursing – Medication P&P, Reporting/Communication and the RN Role
policies.title: Medication Errors
policies.applies_to: All Medication Technicians, licensed nurses, direct support staff, the Program Director and the delegating RN at every [AGENCY NAME] group home site
policies.purpose: To protect the individual's health when a medication error occurs, to make sure it is reported at once, and to learn from every error so that it does not happen again.
policies.policy: This policy meets DH Form DD.APP.1.1 p.2, Nursing section, item Nursing-4 — Medication P&P: Errors (COMAR 10.27.11; MTTP referenced 2:3-17; 2:4-10), and COMAR 10.22.02.10 (C10). When a medication error occurs, the staff member who discovers it notifies the delegating RN and the prescriber immediately and follows their instructions. Errors are reported and reviewed under the PORII (see PA-06) and the Quality Assurance system (see GOV-03). After an error, the Medication Technician is retrained or restricted from medication duties as the delegating RN directs. Errors are handled as learning opportunities for the system and not as grounds for hiding them. Staff who report errors honestly are not retaliated against for reporting.

definitions.definition: Any deviation from the prescriber's order or from the MTTP procedure, including the wrong person, wrong medication, wrong dose, wrong route, wrong time, an omitted dose, a dose given without an order, a missing documentation entry, and any medication given or withheld in a way that is not as ordered.
An error that is caught before it reaches the individual.
The DDA Policy on Reportable Incidents and Investigations, followed under PA-06.

procedures: The staff member who discovers or makes an error first checks the individual's condition and safety. If the person is in distress, shows a serious reaction, or has stopped breathing, the staff member calls 911 first and then follows step 2.

The staff member immediately calls the delegating RN and the prescriber (or the pharmacist or poison control if the RN directs) and describes the medication, the dose, the time and the individual's condition. Staff follow the instructions given and do not attempt to correct the error on their own.
The staff member stays with the individual, observes and records any signs or symptoms and vital signs as directed by the RN, and continues to monitor for as long as the RN instructs.
The staff member notifies the Program Director as soon as the individual is safe. The Program Director notifies [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] on the same day.

The staff member documents the error factually on the MAR and on a medication error report before the end of the shift. The report states what happened, when, who was notified, the instructions received and the individual's condition. It does not blame or speculate.

The Program Director determines whether the error is a reportable incident under the PORII. If so, the Program Director submits it in the timeframe the PORII sets, and the incident is handled under PA-06.

The Program Director informs the individual and, as authorized, the legal guardian or family, and the case coordinator, of the error and of the actions taken, and documents the notification (see NU-06).

Within the timeframe the delegating RN sets, the RN reviews the error with the Medication Technician, finds the cause (for example a labeling problem, distraction, an unclear order or a staffing issue) and decides whether retraining, closer supervision or restriction of medication duties is needed.
A Medication Technician who is directed to be retrained or restricted does not give medication until the delegating RN documents that the retraining is complete and the restriction is lifted.
The Program Director corrects any system cause found, for example by changing storage, lighting or workflow, requesting clearer pharmacy labeling, or adjusting staffing.
Near misses are also reported to the delegating RN and logged so that patterns can be seen.
The delegating RN and Program Director send all errors and near misses to the Quality Assurance Standing Committee at least quarterly, with counts, causes and corrective actions (see GOV-03).

The error report, the RN review and the retraining record are filed (the retraining record in the personnel file and the error report in the quality assurance file, with a note in the individual's record) and are kept as required by REC-01.

responsibilities.role: Any staff member who discovers an error
responsibilities.duty: Protects the individual, calls the delegating RN and prescriber at once, follows instructions, and documents factually before the end of the shift.
Gives immediate direction, reviews the cause with the Medication Technician, and directs retraining or restriction of duties.
Ensures notifications and incident reporting happen, fixes system causes, and reports errors to the QA committee.
Receives same-day notice of errors and makes sure reports under the PORII are made.

documentation: Medication error report
MAR entry for the error
Notes of the RN and prescriber instructions
Incident report under the PORII where applicable
RN review and retraining or restriction record
Near miss log
Quarterly QA summary of errors

policies.category: Nursing – Medication P&P, Reporting/Communication and the RN Role
policies.title: Determining Ability to Self-Medicate
policies.applies_to: The delegating RN, Medication Technicians, the Program Director, the person-centered planning team and all individuals served at [AGENCY NAME] group homes
policies.purpose: To support each individual's right to manage their own medication to the fullest extent that is safe, by assessing ability, recording the supports needed, and storing medication so the person can reach it.
policies.policy: This policy meets DH Form DD.APP.1.1 p.2, Nursing section, item Nursing-5 — Medication P&P: Determining ability to self-medicate (MTTP Chapter 8), and the choice and independence requirements of the HCBS settings rule, 42 CFR 441.301(c)(4). The delegating RN assesses each individual's ability to take medication independently and the supports needed. The result is recorded in the Individual Plan (IP). The assessment is repeated at least annually and after any change of condition. When an individual is assessed as safe to self-administer, [AGENCY NAME] supports that choice and stores the medication so the person can reach it, while keeping it secure from other residents (COMAR 10.22.02.10 (C10) and 10.22.02.12 D (C12)). Having a disability, or needing support, does not by itself mean a person cannot self-administer.

definitions.definition: The individual takes their own medication, with or without prompts or support, and without a Medication Technician giving it.
The RN's structured assessment of whether, and with what supports, the individual can safely manage medication, following MTTP Chapter 8.
Reminders, setup aids such as a pill organizer or alarm, observation, or other help that allows the person to take part in managing medication.

procedures: Within the first 30 days after admission and before the IP is finalized, the delegating RN offers every individual a self-medication assessment and asks each person, in a way they understand, whether they want to manage some or all of their medication.

The RN completes the assessment following MTTP Chapter 8. It looks at whether the person knows what each medication is for, when and how to take it, what the common side effects are, and whom to call with a problem, and whether the person can open containers, take the correct dose and keep track of doses.

The RN considers the person's choice, history, communication needs, risks such as choking or overdose, the effect on other residents, and supports that could make independence possible. The RN involves the individual, the guardian or surrogate where one has been appointed (see PA-11), and the planning team.

The RN records the result as one of: independent; independent with supports (listing them); partially independent (listing which medications or steps); or not able at this time, with the reasons and the skills the person could work toward.
The Program Director makes sure the result is entered in the IP (see PCS-02), together with any teaching goals, so that the person can build skills over time.

If the person is assessed as able to self-administer all or some medication, the Program Director arranges storage the person can reach, for example a locked drawer or box in the person's bedroom for which the person holds the key, while keeping the medication away from other residents (see NU-02 for storage rules).

The CMT or RN checks, as the RN directs, that the person is taking medication as ordered, for example by counting doses or reviewing a self-administration log, and tells the RN of any missed or doubled doses. Checks are done respectfully and are not a way to take back control.
Medication for which the person is not assessed as independent is given by the CMT under NU-02.

The RN repeats the assessment at least annually, before the annual IP meeting, and also after any change of condition, hospitalization, new medication, change in cognition or behavior, or a medication error related to self-administration (see HW-02).

If the RN finds that the person is no longer safe to self-administer, the RN explains the reason to the person, makes a plan to restore independence where possible, and records the change in the IP. If the change limits the person's rights, PA-02 applies and the person's informed consent is sought under PA-11.
If an individual disagrees with the result, the person may ask for a review by the planning team or use the grievance process (see PA-04 and DG-01).
The assessment, the IP entry and the self-administration log are kept in the individual's record (see REC-01).

responsibilities.duty: Completes and signs the assessment, sets the supports needed, repeats it at least annually and after any change of condition, and trains staff on the supports.
Makes sure the result is in the IP, provides accessible and secure storage, and makes sure the person's choice is honored.
Gives only the medication the person is not assessed to manage, carries out the supports and checks the RN has set, and reports problems to the RN.
The individual states their wishes and takes part in the assessment. The team helps set goals for building skills.

documentation: Self-medication assessment (MTTP Chapter 8) with date and RN signature
IP entry showing the result, supports and goals
Self-administration log or count records
Annual and change-of-condition reassessments
Notes on any disagreement and its outcome

policies.category: Nursing – Medication P&P, Reporting/Communication and the RN Role
policies.title: Reporting and Communication of Health Information
policies.applies_to: All [AGENCY NAME] group home staff, including Medication Technicians, the Program Director and the delegating RN
policies.purpose: To make sure health information about each individual is reported to the right people quickly, handed over accurately between shifts, available to emergency personnel, and shared only as authorized.
policies.policy: This policy meets DH Form DD.APP.1.1 p.2, Nursing section, item Nursing-6 — Procedures re: Reporting/Communication of information (MTTP 1:2-7; 1:3-4; 1:3-7; 1:3-10 & 11; 1:4-9; 3:2-9), COMAR 10.22.02.10 (C10) and COMAR 10.22.02.13 (C13). Staff report every change in an individual's condition to the delegating RN and document it. Medical information is kept so that it is readily accessible to emergency personnel (COMAR 10.22.02.13 C). Every shift hand-off is documented. Health information is shared with prescribers, family and the case coordinator as authorized, and is protected under the HIPAA Privacy and Security Rules, 45 CFR Part 164 (see PA-03).

definitions.definition: Any new, worsening or unusual sign, symptom, behavior, injury, appetite, sleep, mood or function change, any new diagnosis, and any medication reaction.
The documented report from the outgoing staff to the incoming staff on each individual's health, medication, appointments, incidents and tasks to be done.
Sharing of protected health information with the individual's consent or authorization, or as permitted or required by law, limited to what is needed.

procedures: Any staff member who notices a change of condition reports it right away to the CMT on duty. The CMT reports it to the delegating RN by phone, and to the Program Director, without waiting for the end of the shift. In an emergency staff call 911 first (see HW-02).
The staff member documents the change on the same shift in the individual's daily record: what was seen, when it started, what was done, who was told, the instructions received and the follow-up.
The delegating RN decides whether the person needs a prescriber visit, a nursing visit or emergency care, and the Program Director makes sure it is arranged the same day or as the RN directs.

After a prescriber, hospital, clinic or specialist visit, the staff member who accompanied the person records the findings, new or changed orders and follow-up appointments on the visit form, and gives it to the delegating RN and the CMT on duty before the end of the shift.
The CMT updates the MAR and the health record for new or changed orders only after the written order has been verified (see NU-01 and NU-02).

At every shift change, outgoing and incoming staff hold a hand-off together and record it in the shift log. The log covers each person's health status, medication given or refused, controlled drug counts, appointments, incidents, behavior concerns and tasks still to be done.

The Program Director keeps each individual's current emergency information sheet (identification, diagnoses, allergies, medication list, prescriber, guardian or contact and insurance) at the site, in a place that staff can find at once. A copy goes with the individual to any hospital, ER or emergency visit so that medical information is readily accessible to emergency personnel.
The Program Director checks and updates the emergency information sheet whenever the diagnosis, allergies or medication change, and at least at each IP review.

Staff share health information with the individual's prescribers, the legal guardian or family, the case coordinator and others only as the individual or surrogate has authorized, or as the law allows, and only the minimum needed. Questions are sent to the Program Director or the Privacy Officer (see PA-03).
Staff do not discuss health information in public places or in front of people who do not need it, do not send it by unsecured text or email, and do not post it on social media.
The delegating RN reviews health communication logs during the RN's regular visits and reviews with the Program Director any report that was late or missing, and corrective steps are documented.

When a person's change of condition is a reportable incident, the Program Director also follows PA-06, and the person's family or guardian and the case coordinator are told as soon as possible. The notification and who made it are documented.

Health reports, hand-off logs and visit forms are kept in the individual's record at the site, and electronic records are backed up and stored off-site and protected under HIPAA (see REC-01 and EP-05).

responsibilities.role: Direct support staff and Medication Technicians
responsibilities.duty: Notice and report changes of condition at once, document them the same shift, complete hand-offs, and protect health information.
Receives reports, decides on the response, reviews health records and communication, and follows up on prescriber orders.
Arranges care and follow-up, keeps emergency information sheets current and accessible, and makes sure family, guardian and case coordinator are informed as authorized.
Answers questions about what may be shared and handles any suspected improper disclosure.

documentation: Daily record entries and change-of-condition notes
Shift hand-off log
Prescriber, hospital and specialist visit forms
Emergency information sheet for each person
Authorization and consent forms for release of health information
Family, guardian and case coordinator notification records
RN review notes

policies.category: Nursing – Medication P&P, Reporting/Communication and the RN Role
policies.title: The RN Role, Nursing Delegation and Health Care Coordination
policies.applies_to: The delegating RN, Medication Technicians, the Program Director, [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] and all [AGENCY NAME] group home sites
policies.purpose: To define the role of the registered nurse in the home: delegating and supervising medication tasks, auditing records, and coordinating each resident's health care.
policies.policy: This policy meets DH Form DD.APP.1.1 p.2, Nursing section, item Nursing-7 — The RN Role (COMAR 10.27.11; MTTP 6-5), COMAR 10.22.02.10 (C10), and the Community Pathways Waiver Appendix C requirements for Medication Technician certification and RN delegation (C32). [AGENCY NAME] employs or contracts with a Maryland-licensed registered nurse as the delegating RN. The delegating RN delegates and supervises tasks performed by Certified Medication Technicians (CMTs) under COMAR 10.27.11, audits Medication Administration Records (MARs), and coordinates the Health Risk Screening Tool (HRST) and health care follow-up for each resident. [AGENCY NAME] confirms the RN's licensure annually. Where Nursing Support Services hours may be authorized, [AGENCY NAME] asks DDA whether they are authorized separately for each resident (service code W5804) before billing for them.

definitions.definition: The Maryland-licensed registered nurse who decides which nursing tasks may be delegated, to whom, for which individual, and who teaches, supervises and monitors the CMT as required by COMAR 10.27.11.
The RN's transfer of a specific nursing task to a competent CMT, with the RN keeping accountability for the decision to delegate and for supervision.
Health Risk Screening Tool, the DDA-required screening tool used to rate each person's health risks and to guide nursing follow-up.
A DDA service code under which nursing hours may be authorized for an individual, subject to DDA's authorization.

procedures: Before the home opens and before any new hire is placed on the medication schedule, [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] confirms that a delegating RN is in place by written agreement or employment contract, and records the RN's name, license number and contact information.

[ADMINISTRATOR NAME] verifies the RN's Maryland license with the Board of Nursing when the RN is engaged and again every year, before the license expires, and files the verification in the personnel or contractor record. If the license lapses or is restricted, the RN stops delegating at once and [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] arranges a replacement RN the same day.

For each resident, before a CMT is given delegated tasks, the RN reviews the person's needs and orders, decides which tasks can safely be delegated under COMAR 10.27.11, confirms that the CMT's certification is current, and records the delegation in writing.

The RN teaches and checks the CMT's competence for the person-specific tasks (for example special routes, PRN decisions, seizure rescue medication, or treatments), and records the date and result of each competency check.

The RN supervises delegated tasks by regular site visits as the RN decides is appropriate for the residents' needs, by observing medication passes, and by being available by phone at all times a CMT is working. The on-call RN number is posted at each site: [PHONE].

The RN audits MARs, TARs, controlled drug count records and medication supplies at least monthly, records the findings, and gives corrective direction to the Program Director and CMTs. Repeated problems go to the Quality Assurance Standing Committee (see GOV-03).
The RN reviews every medication error with the CMT and decides on retraining or restriction of duties (see NU-04). The RN may withdraw or change a delegation at any time when it is not safe.
The RN completes or oversees the self-medication assessment for each resident (see NU-05).

The RN coordinates the HRST for each resident: making sure it is completed on the DDA schedule, reviewing the results, and making sure follow-up is carried out and recorded. The RN also makes sure the nursing and health information is built into the Individual Plan (see PCS-02 and HW-01).

The RN coordinates health care follow-up for each resident: routine and specialist appointments, immunizations and screenings, lab work, therapies, equipment, diets and any new orders. The RN works with the prescribers, the family or guardian and the case coordinator as authorized (see NU-06).
The RN reviews each change of condition reported by staff, and decides on the response (see HW-02).

Before admission and at least annually, [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] asks DDA in writing whether Nursing Support Services hours (W5804) are authorized separately for each resident, and records the answer. [AGENCY NAME] bills for nursing services only when DDA has authorized them for that resident (see GOV-04).
The Program Director gives the RN access to the records, the medication supply and the residents that the RN needs, and makes sure staff follow the RN's directions.
The RN keeps delegation records, competency checks, audit reports and visit notes. They are filed at the site and with the quality assurance records, and are kept as required by REC-01.

responsibilities.duty: Decides on and supervises delegation, checks CMT competence, audits MARs, coordinates the HRST and health care follow-up, and is available to staff by phone.
Engages the RN, confirms RN licensure annually, replaces the RN if needed, and asks DDA about W5804 authorization.
Schedules only delegated CMTs for medication passes, supports RN visits and audits, and carries out the RN's corrective directions.
Performs only delegated tasks, follows the RN's instructions, and reports concerns to the RN promptly.

documentation: RN agreement or employment record with annual license verification
Written delegation record for each CMT and each resident
CMT competency checks
Monthly MAR and medication audit reports
RN site visit notes
HRST records and follow-up
Written DDA response on W5804 authorization

policies.category: Explanation of all items checked 'No', with a compliance plan
policies.title: Compliance Plan for Required Items Not Met
policies.applies_to: Governing body, Program Director, and all staff responsible for adopting, implementing or revising policies
policies.purpose: To make sure that any required policy or policy element that [AGENCY NAME] has not yet fully met is identified, explained, assigned an owner and a due date, and brought into compliance. It also sets how those items are tracked and reported to the governing body, OHCQ and DDA.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] will not leave any required policy item unexplained. Every item checked 'No' on the DDA policy review form will have a written explanation and an attached compliance plan that names a responsible owner, the corrective action and a due date. This policy supports the written policy and procedure requirements of COMAR 10.22.02.10 (A, B, C and D). It also supports the governing body's legal responsibility for overseeing compliance under COMAR 10.22.02.02A(2)-(3) and the plan-of-correction requirements of COMAR 10.22.02.04E-F. The agency will submit the policies to OHCQ within 30 days of DDA approval. It will submit revised policies to OHCQ and DDA whenever they request them. The governing body receives status reports until every compliance plan item is closed. No policy item is considered closed until the revised policy is adopted, staff are trained, and the documentation is on file. This policy has no separate official checklist items. It is the 'explanation of all items checked No' section of the submission.

definitions.definition: A required policy, procedure or element on the DDA policy review form that the agency has not fully met at the time of submission.
A written plan for each 'No' item that states the gap, the corrective action, the owner, the due date and the evidence that will show completion.
The written response to survey findings that OHCQ requires under COMAR 10.22.02.04E, due at the exit conference or within 10 working days of receiving the findings.
The named person accountable for completing a corrective action by its due date.

procedures: Before submitting the policy manual to DDA, the Program Director reviews every policy against the DDA policy review form and marks each item Yes or No.

For every item marked 'No', the Program Director writes a plain-language explanation of why it is not met, for example 'not applicable until the first resident is admitted' or 'policy under revision'.

The Program Director opens a compliance plan entry for each 'No' item in the Compliance Plan Log. The entry records the item, the policy ID, the gap, the corrective action, the owner, the due date and the evidence of completion.
The Program Director assigns each item to one named owner (for example the RN Delegating Nurse, the Residential Manager or the Fiscal Officer). Shared ownership is not permitted.
The Program Director sets the due date for each item. Items that affect health, safety or rights are due before the first resident is admitted or immediately for current residents.
The Program Director attaches the Compliance Plan Log to the submission to DDA and keeps a copy in the licensing file.
Within 30 days after DDA approves the policies, the Program Director submits the approved policies to OHCQ and records the submission date and method.

If OHCQ or DDA asks for revised policies or more information, the Program Director assigns the revision, sets a response date that meets the date the regulator gave, and submits the revision by that date.
Owners update their log entries when each action is completed, attach the evidence (for example the adopted policy, training roster or signed acknowledgment), and notify the Program Director.
The Program Director reviews the Compliance Plan Log at least monthly until every item is closed and follows up on any overdue item within 5 business days.
The Program Director reports status to the governing body at each meeting. The report lists open items, items completed since the last report, overdue items and the reasons for delay.

When OHCQ cites deficiencies at a survey, the Program Director enters each finding in the Compliance Plan Log. The POC is submitted at the exit conference or within 10 working days of receiving the findings, or sooner if OHCQ requires it.

If OHCQ finds a POC unacceptable, the Program Director revises it and resubmits within 10 working days. If an extension is needed, the Program Director requests it from OHCQ in writing before the deadline. Only the OHCQ Director may grant an extension, of up to 30 days.
After the governing body confirms an item is closed, the Program Director records the closure date and signs the entry.
Policies revised because of a compliance plan are communicated to staff under CS-01, and staff sign that they understand the change.
The Quality Assurance process (GOV-03) reviews repeated or recurring 'No' items and POC findings as trends, and recommends system changes.

responsibilities.duty: Receives status reports, holds the Program Director accountable for due dates, and approves policy revisions.
Completes the review, maintains the Compliance Plan Log, assigns owners and due dates, submits policies and POCs, and reports to the governing body.
Complete assigned actions by the due date and provide evidence of completion.
Reviews open and recurring items as part of the QA data review.

documentation: DDA policy review form with Yes/No marked on each item
Written explanation for each 'No' item
Compliance Plan Log with owner, due date and evidence of completion
Transmittal record of policies sent to OHCQ and DDA, with dates
Governing body minutes showing status reports
POCs submitted to OHCQ and OHCQ's response
Staff acknowledgment of revised policies

policies.title: Organization, Governing Body and Program Director Responsibilities
policies.applies_to: Governing body members, Program Director, administrative staff
policies.purpose: To establish [AGENCY NAME]'s legal organization, the composition and duties of its governing body, and the responsibilities of the Program Director. It also provides for approval and regular review of the Program Service Plan.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] is incorporated in Maryland, or is a foreign corporation registered to do business in Maryland, as required by COMAR 10.22.02.02A(1). The governing body is legally responsible for overseeing all programs and for the agency's compliance with licensing requirements (COMAR 10.22.02.02A(2)-(3)). The governing body includes at least one person with a developmental disability, at least one family member of a person with a developmental disability, and at least one person with experience in developmental disabilities. At least 75% of members live in Maryland or within 100 miles of Maryland. No employee, and no immediate family member of an employee, may serve as a voting member (COMAR 10.22.02.08). The bylaws address oversight, compliance, approval of the mission, budget and policies, conflict of interest, responses to plans of correction, and approval of the Program Service Plan (PSP). No board member or employee may own property that is leased back to the agency (COMAR 10.22.02.08C(9)). The administrative head ensures the governing body reviews and updates the PSP at least every 3 years, and the agency follows the approved PSP (COMAR 10.22.02.09C-D).

definitions.definition: The board that is legally responsible for the agency, its programs and its compliance.
The administrative head of the agency's licensed services, named in the licensing application.

The DDA-approved document describing each service's rationale, scope, staffing and training, and setting and location (including the number of individuals expected to be served), required by COMAR 10.22.02.09.
A spouse, parent, child, sibling, or other person who lives in the same household as an employee.

procedures: The governing body keeps on file proof of the agency's status as a Maryland corporation, or its foreign registration in Maryland, and verifies it annually.

The governing body keeps a current roster that identifies each member's required category: person with a DD, family member of a person with a DD, or person with DD experience. Each category is filled by at least one member.
The Board Chair calculates the share of members residing in Maryland or within 100 miles at each annual meeting and whenever a member is added or leaves. The share must be at least 75%.
Before seating a voting member, the Board Chair confirms in writing that the person is not an employee or immediate family member of an employee. The member signs this attestation annually.

Each member signs the conflict of interest statement at seating and annually (see PA-12). Each member also discloses any ownership of property that could be leased to the agency. No such lease is permitted.

The governing body adopts and reviews the bylaws at least annually. The bylaws address oversight, compliance, approval of mission, budget and policies, conflict of interest, POC responses and PSP approval.
The governing body meets at least [NUMBER] times a year. Minutes record attendance, quorum, votes, conflicts declared and any member recusals.
The governing body approves the annual budget, the mission statement and all policies in this manual, and approves each revision.
The Program Director reports at each meeting on census, incidents, survey results, POC status, QA findings and staffing. The governing body documents its response.
When OHCQ issues findings, the Program Director presents the POC to the governing body for review and approval before submission, within the deadline set in COMAR 10.22.02.04E (see REC-02).
The Program Director submits any proposed change to the PSP to DDA for approval before it is implemented (COMAR 10.22.02.09B).
The Program Director schedules a governing body review of the PSP at least every 3 years and sooner if services, settings or capacity change. The review is recorded in the minutes.
The Program Director updates the PSP if the review shows changes are needed and submits it to DDA for approval before use.
The Program Director ensures that services are delivered in compliance with the approved PSP and checks this quarterly as part of the QA review (see GOV-03).

The Program Director maintains the licensing application materials, including the business plan, DD experience summary, prior licensing reports from the last 10 years and the DDA-approved QA plan (COMAR 10.22.02.02A(4)). They are updated at renewal.
The Program Director is available to DDA and OHCQ and names a designee, with that person's contact information, whenever absent. [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] can be reached at [PHONE].

responsibilities.duty: Oversees all programs and compliance, approves mission, budget, policies, POC responses and the PSP, and reviews the PSP at least every 3 years.
Maintains membership composition requirements, residency percentages, attestations and bylaws.
Manages daily operations, reports to the board, submits PSP changes to DDA, and ensures that the agency follows the approved PSP.
Keeps minutes, rosters and signed attestations.

documentation: Articles of incorporation or foreign registration and annual good standing record
Board roster showing membership categories and residency
Signed no-employee/no-family and conflict-of-interest attestations
Bylaws and annual review record
Governing body minutes
Approved PSP, DDA approval letters and 3-year review record
Application materials on file (business plan, DD experience summary, prior licensing reports, QA plan)

policies.title: Licensure, Site Approval, Licensed Capacity and Provider Agreements
policies.applies_to: Governing body, Program Director, Fiscal Officer, admissions staff
policies.purpose: To ensure [AGENCY NAME] provides community residential services only under a valid license and approved sites. It also covers staying within licensed capacity, renewing on time and keeping the Medicaid provider enrollment for each site current.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] will not provide community residential services without a license (COMAR 10.22.02.01-1). It will obtain DDA approval at least 30 days in advance to open, close or relocate a site (COMAR 10.22.02.05). It will not serve more people at a site than the license allows. Exceeding licensed capacity requires Director approval, for a maximum of 60 days plus one 60-day extension (COMAR 10.22.02.06). The agency files for license renewal at least 60 days before the license expires (COMAR 10.22.02.02B). It will not voluntarily surrender a license without submitting a closure schedule at least 90 days ahead and receiving approval from the Director (COMAR 10.22.02.02F). Each licensed site has its own 'DDA Licensed Site MA' number under the DDA Addendum for Participation in the Maryland Medical Assistance Program (PT 90 DDA). The agency keeps its Medicaid enrollment, revalidation and Maryland SDAT good standing current in MPRIME, because loss of SDAT good standing causes immediate suspension. The agency completes the DDA Addendum for Licensed Services and Sites (MDH Form DD.ADD.1.0) for each site, including the Community Settings Rule attestation.

definitions.definition: The number of people the license states may be served at a site.
A specific residence at a specific address approved and licensed by DDA for community residential services.
The Medicaid provider number assigned to each DDA licensed site.
Current status with the Maryland State Department of Assessments and Taxation, verified through MPRIME.
The statement in the DDA site addendum that the site meets the federal HCBS settings requirements.

procedures: The Program Director keeps the current license for each site posted and on file, and reviews each license's expiration date monthly.

The Program Director sets a renewal calendar. The renewal application is prepared no later than 90 days before expiration and filed no later than 60 days before expiration (COMAR 10.22.02.02B), with the governing body's approval recorded.

The renewal application includes the items required by COMAR 10.22.02.02A(4): the business plan, the DD experience summary, prior licensing reports from the last 10 years, and the DDA-approved QA plan.

The Program Director tracks the Director's decision on each application (approve, approve with conditions, deny or request more information). The Program Director meets any conditions by their due dates and records them in the Compliance Plan Log (XP-01).
Before opening, closing or relocating a site, the Program Director submits the request to DDA at least 30 days in advance and does not begin the change until DDA approves in writing.

For each new site, the Program Director completes the DDA Addendum for Licensed Services and Sites (DD.ADD.1.0). It lists the site, the capacity requested, the proposed occupancy date, whether the site is wheelchair accessible, and the Community Settings Rule attestation. The governing body reviews it before signature.
The Program Director prepares the site for the on-site pre-licensure survey and the DDA settings review (see PCS-01 and HE-01), and no resident moves in until the license for that site is issued.
The Program Director records licensed capacity for each site on the admissions tracker. Admissions staff check it before every referral is accepted (PCS-01) and never admit above it.

If an emergency makes it necessary to exceed licensed capacity, the Program Director requests Director approval first, in writing. The time limit is a maximum of 60 days plus one 60-day extension. The Program Director calendars the end date and the plan to return to licensed capacity.
The Fiscal Officer confirms that each site has its own MA number under PT 90 DDA before any claim is submitted for that site (see GOV-04).

The Fiscal Officer checks SDAT good standing quarterly, completes Medicaid revalidation through MPRIME by the revalidation due date, and reports any lapse or notice to the Program Director the same day.
If SDAT good standing is lost or a suspension notice is received, the Program Director and Board Chair act the same day to restore it, notify DDA, and document the actions taken.

If the agency decides to voluntarily surrender a license, the governing body approves the decision. The Program Director submits the closure schedule to DDA at least 90 days ahead and does not close until the Director approves it.
The Program Director ensures any closure or surrender protects residents, by transition planning and notices handled under PCS-04.
The Program Director reports license status, expiration dates, capacity exceptions and Medicaid enrollment status to the governing body at least quarterly.

responsibilities.duty: Approves applications, renewals, site changes and any voluntary surrender.
Files applications and renewals, obtains DDA approval for site changes, enforces capacity limits and maintains the licensing file.
Maintains the MA number for each site, MPRIME revalidation and SDAT good standing.
Verifies licensed capacity before every admission.

documentation: Current license for each site and renewal calendar
Renewal applications and decision letters
DDA site approvals and completed DD.ADD.1.0 with attestation
Capacity tracker and any Director approvals to exceed capacity
PT 90 DDA addendum and MA number for each site
MPRIME enrollment and revalidation confirmations and SDAT good standing records
Closure schedule and Director approval, if applicable

policies.title: Quality Assurance, Standing Committee, Data Review and Mortality Review
policies.applies_to: Governing body, Program Director, QA Lead, Standing Committee members, all staff
policies.purpose: To describe [AGENCY NAME]'s internal quality assurance system. It ensures the system focuses on individual choice, preference and satisfaction, uses data to drive improvement, and includes a standing committee that reviews incidents, restrictive behavior plans and rights restrictions. It also includes review of each death.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] maintains a DDA-approved quality assurance (QA) plan and submits the plan and any substantive changes to DDA for approval (COMAR 10.22.02.14A). The QA system focuses on individual choice, preference and satisfaction, including personal contact with individuals. It has measurable outcomes, analyzes trends, responds promptly when health or safety is at risk, and tracks restrictive techniques used under behavior plans (COMAR 10.22.02.14B). The agency sets goals and standards, keeps records, and implements changes based on the data (COMAR 10.22.02.14C). A standing committee meets the requirements of COMAR 10.22.02.14E. The agency reviews every death through the mortality review process and reports results to the standing committee. The governing body, which is legally responsible for compliance under COMAR 10.22.02.02A(2)-(3), receives QA reports and acts on them.

definitions.definition: The committee required by COMAR 10.22.02.14E, with equal numbers of agency staff and non-employees (individuals, proponents or community members).
A person who advocates for an individual, such as a family member, guardian or friend.
Any intervention in a behavior plan that limits an individual's freedom of movement or access to things; see PA-09.
A structured review of the circumstances, care and any contributing factors of each death of an individual served.
Review of data over time to find patterns in incidents, health events, complaints, restrictions and satisfaction.

procedures: The Program Director and QA Lead write the QA plan, including goals, standards, measurable outcomes, data sources, the schedule for review and who is responsible. They submit it to DDA for approval, and the governing body approves it first.
Before implementing any substantive change to the QA plan, the Program Director submits it to DDA for approval (COMAR 10.22.02.14A).

The QA Lead gathers data at least monthly: incidents, medication errors, health events and hospital visits, grievances, rights restrictions, behavior plan use, staffing, training completion and drill results.

The QA Lead or a designee makes personal contact with each individual at least [FREQUENCY] to ask about their choices, preferences and satisfaction. The responses are recorded in the individual's QA record and analyzed.

The QA Lead tracks each use of a restrictive technique under a behavior plan, recording who, which technique, date and time, whether it was an emergency use or planned use under the plan, and its effectiveness.
If data shows that health or safety is at risk, the QA Lead notifies the Program Director immediately. The Program Director responds the same day with protective action and records it.
The QA Lead prepares a quarterly trend report with measurable outcomes against goals and presents it to the Program Director, the standing committee and the governing body.

The standing committee is made up of an equal number of agency staff and non-employees (individuals, proponents or community members). The Program Director keeps the roster, and the non-employee members are not paid staff.

The standing committee meets at least [FREQUENCY] and as needed, with a majority present. It reviews the incident protocol and all incidents (PA-06), and approves every behavior plan that uses restrictive techniques (PA-08, PA-09).
The committee reviews rights restrictions not related to challenging behavior and sets time frames for each (PA-02). It also reviews the agency's policies for protection of rights.
A committee member who was involved in an incident or behavior plan does not decide on it. The member leaves the discussion, and the minutes record the recusal.
Committee members sign a confidentiality statement and the committee protects information as required by Health-General §7-1010 (PA-03).

For each death, the Program Director notifies the QA Lead within 24 hours of learning of it. The QA Lead completes the mortality review within [NUMBER] days, using the incident report, health records, the RN's findings and any external reports (HW-03).

The mortality review looks at the circumstances, health history, supports provided, response to any change of condition, and whether any process changes could reduce risk. The QA Lead reports the results to the standing committee at its next meeting.

The committee and the Program Director decide on changes, assign an owner and due date for each, and record them in the QA Action Log. The QA Lead verifies that each change is implemented and checks results in the next quarter.
The QA Lead keeps records of all QA activity, including data, reports, minutes, action logs and the changes made as a result (COMAR 10.22.02.14C).

responsibilities.duty: Approves the QA plan, reviews QA reports and ensures changes are made.
Submits the QA plan to DDA, responds to risks, and ensures committee membership and meetings.
Collects data, makes personal contacts, analyzes trends, completes mortality reviews and tracks action items.
Reviews incidents, approves restrictive behavior plans, reviews rights restrictions and policies protecting rights, and maintains confidentiality.

documentation: DDA-approved QA plan and approval letters for changes
Quarterly trend reports and QA Action Log
Individual satisfaction and choice contact records
Restrictive technique tracking log
Standing committee roster, minutes, recusal records and confidentiality statements
Mortality review reports and committee follow-up

policies.title: Medicaid Compliance, Billing and Service Documentation
policies.applies_to: Program Director, Fiscal Officer, billing staff, Residential Managers, direct support staff who document services
policies.purpose: To ensure [AGENCY NAME] bills Medicaid accurately and only for services that are authorized and delivered, and to ensure that claims, the number of people authorized and retainer days are handled correctly.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] bills only for services authorized in the individual's approved Person-Centered Plan (PCP) and Detailed Service Authorization in LTSSMaryland, using the Community Living – Group Home code W5600, billed per person per day. The agency enters the correct 'Number of People Authorized' on each claim, because the rate follows the number of people living in the home and present, or on retainer days. For example, when one resident leaves a 4-person home, the daily rate for the other three drops from $403.30 to $355.23 (standard rates effective Oct 1, 2026). Rates follow DDA's current published schedule. Retainer days are limited to 18 per person per year, and a person on retainer still counts toward home size. Room and board are excluded from the Medicaid rate (see PCS-01), and transportation is included in the daily rate. EVV is not required for Community Living – Group Home, but it is required for Personal Supports and Respite. No payment is made to relatives, legal guardians or legally responsible persons. Each licensed site bills under its own MA number (PT 90 DDA). The agency complies with the HCBS settings requirements of 42 CFR 441.301(c)(4) as a condition of billing for services delivered in its provider-owned or controlled residences. It screens staff and owners against the OIG exclusion list, and it plans for payment that may lag up to 180 days from service initiation.

definitions.definition: The LTSSMaryland billing code for Community Living – Group Home, billed per person per day.
The authorization in LTSSMaryland that specifies the services, units and dates the agency may bill.
The count of people living in the home and present, or on retainer days, that sets the residential billing rate.
A day the individual is away and the bed is held, billable up to 18 days per person per year.
Electronic Visit Verification, required for Personal Supports and Respite but not for Community Living – Group Home.
The federal list of persons and entities excluded from participating in federal health care programs.

procedures: Before the first claim for a person, the Fiscal Officer confirms that the approved PCP and Detailed Service Authorization in LTSSMaryland list W5600 for that person, the site and the dates of service, and files a copy of the authorization.
Each day, direct support staff document the individual's presence or absence in the daily record (PA-01), and the Residential Manager checks it for completeness by the next business day.

The Residential Manager reports to the Fiscal Officer by the 2nd business day of each month the number of residents in the home each day, absences, hospital stays, retainer days and any move-in or move-out.
The Fiscal Officer determines the 'Number of People Authorized' for each day from that report, counting people living in the home and present or on retainer days, and enters it on each claim.
The Fiscal Officer bills only for days of service actually delivered or covered by an allowable retainer day. The agency does not bill for room and board.

Retainer days are used only for planned or medical absences where the bed is held. The Fiscal Officer keeps a running count per person per calendar year, stops billing after 18 days and alerts the Program Director when a person reaches 15.

When a vacancy occurs, the Program Director notifies the Fiscal Officer the same day. The Fiscal Officer adjusts the 'Number of People Authorized' from the vacancy date, and the Program Director reports the revenue effect to the governing body.

The Fiscal Officer reconciles claims to daily records and authorizations monthly. Any mismatch is corrected before submission. Any overbilling found later is reported to the Program Director and repaid within the time the payer requires.
The Fiscal Officer submits claims under the MA number assigned to each licensed site and does not combine sites on a claim (see GOV-02).

The Fiscal Officer confirms that no payment of any kind is made from Medicaid funds to a relative, legal guardian or legally responsible person of an individual for services delivered to that individual.

The Fiscal Officer screens every employee, board member, owner and contractor against the OIG exclusion list before hire or appointment and at least monthly. The Fiscal Officer reports any match to the Program Director immediately. The person is removed from any role paid by or tied to Medicaid while the match is resolved.

The Program Director ensures that service documentation (daily notes, progress notes, attendance and the PCP) is complete, signed, dated and kept for the retention period in REC-01, and available to DDA, OHCQ and Medicaid auditors on request.
The Program Director ensures the agency is in compliance with the HCBS settings requirements (42 CFR 441.301(c)(4)) in each site and documents it through settings reviews (PA-02, PCS-01).
The Fiscal Officer does not use EVV for CL–GH. If the agency ever provides Personal Supports or Respite, the Program Director establishes EVV before the first billing.
The Fiscal Officer keeps a cash-flow plan that covers payment delays of up to 180 days and reports it to the governing body at least quarterly (see PA-13).
The Fiscal Officer reviews rate notices from DDA, including any budget-based rate change and its effective date, and updates the billing system only once DDA confirms the new rate.

responsibilities.duty: Ensures the agency bills only for authorized, documented services and responds to audit requests and overpayments.
Verifies authorizations, enters 'Number of People Authorized', bills, tracks retainer days, reconciles claims and performs OIG screening.
Ensures daily records are complete and sends the monthly census and absence report.
Document each day of service accurately and truthfully.
Reviews billing compliance and cash-flow reports.

documentation: Approved PCP and Detailed Service Authorization in LTSSMaryland for each person
Daily records and monthly census/absence reports
Claims, remittances and monthly reconciliation
Retainer day tracking log
OIG exclusion screening records
MA number record for each site (PT 90 DDA)
Overpayment and correction records
Settings review records

policies.title: Referral, Admission, Residency Agreement, Room and Board, and Transition In
policies.applies_to: Program Director, Admissions Coordinator, Residential Managers, direct support staff, RN Delegating Nurse
policies.purpose: To set how [AGENCY NAME] accepts referrals, admits individuals, enters into residency agreements and room and board agreements, and supports a person's transition into the home, in line with licensing capacity and the HCBS settings requirements.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] admits people to a group home only when DDA has authorized the service, the home has an open bed within licensed capacity, and the home can meet the person's needs. No home serves more than 4 residents unless DDA previously approved a different number, and each resident has a private bedroom. A resident may share a bedroom only by their own choice. The agency does not exceed licensed capacity (COMAR 10.22.02.06). Each resident has a lease or equivalent residency agreement as required by the HCBS settings rule (42 CFR 441.301(c)(4)). The agency also provides privacy, lockable doors, roommate choice, and access to food and visitors. Room and board is excluded from the Medicaid rate and is collected from the resident under a written agreement, at an affordable amount. The agency documents roommate choice and offers a trial-experience option before the person decides. The agency's sites meet the settings-rule items on the DDA site addendum (DD.ADD.1.0) and the DDA New Site Visit Checklist, which cover institutional or isolating characteristics and heightened scrutiny, including proximity to the provider's other sites.

definitions.definition: A written lease or equivalent agreement giving the resident the same protections as a tenant, including notice before any move.
A written agreement stating the amount the resident pays for housing and food, how it is paid and what it covers.
A visit, meal, day or overnight stay arranged so a person can decide about moving in.
CMS review of settings that may have the qualities of an institution or isolate residents, for example a setting near other sites of the same provider.
A family member, guardian, friend or other person who advocates for the individual.

procedures: The Admissions Coordinator logs every referral on the date received, with the referral source, the person's information and the date of the response. The agency makes no discriminatory decision on any basis protected under PA-05.

Before accepting a referral, the Admissions Coordinator confirms that the home has an open bed within licensed capacity (GOV-02), that the home would not exceed 4 residents unless DDA previously approved a different number, and that a private bedroom is available.

The Admissions Coordinator confirms DDA authorization of Community Living – Group Home in the person's approved PCP and Detailed Service Authorization in LTSSMaryland (GOV-04) before any move-in date is set.

The Admissions Coordinator gathers the person's assessments, PCP, health information, medication list, behavior plan if any, and rights restrictions if any, and asks the individual and proponent about preferences. The RN Delegating Nurse reviews the health information and identifies any nursing needs (NU-07).

The Program Director and RN decide in writing, within [NUMBER] business days of receiving the complete referral, whether the home can meet the person's needs, based on staffing, the home's accessibility (HE-01) and the compatibility of current residents. The Program Director documents the reasons for any decision not to admit and informs the referral source.
The Admissions Coordinator arranges one or more trial experiences, such as a visit, a meal or an overnight, and records the person's reaction and choices.

The person has the opportunity to meet the current residents, and the current residents are asked about their views and choices on a new housemate. The Admissions Coordinator documents roommate choice for everyone affected. Current residents are not required to accept a housemate.
The Program Director ensures that the person chooses their bedroom and that it is private. If a person chooses to share, the choice is recorded in writing and reviewed at the next PCP meeting.

Before move-in, the Program Director and the person (and proponent as applicable) sign a residency agreement. It states the address, move-in date, rights and responsibilities, rules about house guests, notice requirements before any discharge (PCS-04), and the grievance process (PA-04, DG-01). The person receives a copy in an accessible format with help understanding it.

The Admissions Coordinator completes a written room and board agreement with the person and proponent. It states the amount, what it covers, how it is paid and how changes are made. The amount is set so that it is affordable for the person and is based on the person's income. Room and board is not billed to Medicaid.
Room and board funds are handled under PA-14, and the person's funds are never used to pay for services covered by the daily rate.

The Residential Manager confirms before move-in that the bedroom has a lock and the person has a key, that the person controls access to the room, that visitors are welcome at any time unless a documented, approved restriction applies, and that food is available at any time (PA-02).

The Residential Manager ensures that the home and its location are free of institutional or isolating characteristics, and tells the Program Director if the home is close to other sites operated by the agency, so that this can be disclosed to DDA for heightened scrutiny review.
On the move-in day, the Residential Manager helps the person move in, shows them the home, the emergency plan and exits (EP-01), and arranges the medication and health supports needed (NU-01).

During the first 30 days, the Residential Manager meets with the person at least weekly to ask how things are going, and the team makes any changes the person requests. The first PCP meeting after move-in is held within the time set by DDA and PCS-02.

The Admissions Coordinator completes the admission file (REC-01) within [NUMBER] days of move-in and the Program Director reviews it. The Fiscal Officer is told of the move-in date the same day so the 'Number of People Authorized' is updated (GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Decides on admissions, ensures that capacity and settings rule requirements are met and signs residency agreements.
Logs referrals, verifies authorization and capacity, arranges trial experiences, and completes agreements and the admission file.
Reviews health needs before admission and plans nursing supports.
Prepares the home and supports the person through the transition.
Updates billing and room and board records when a person moves in.

documentation: Referral log and decision letters
DDA authorization and PCP
Needs determination and RN review
Trial experience notes and roommate choice record
Signed residency agreement and room and board agreement
Settings-rule checklist for the site (including the DDA New Site Visit Checklist and DD.ADD.1.0 attestation)
30-day transition notes and admission file

policies.title: Person-Centered Planning and the Individual Plan
policies.applies_to: All individuals receiving Community Living – Group Home services from [AGENCY NAME]; the Program Director, RN, Direct Support Professionals (DSPs), and all staff who implement the Individual Plan.
policies.purpose: To make sure each person's supports come from a person-centered plan that reflects the person's goals, preferences, health and safety needs, and rights.
