The plan must be authorized, kept in the record, carried out by staff, and documented every day, as COMAR 10.22.02.09, COMAR 10.22.02.13 and the Community Pathways Waiver require.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] delivers services only as described in the person's current Individual Plan (IP) and the person-centered plan (PCP) authorized in LTSSMaryland. The IP, as defined in COMAR 10.22.05, is kept in each person's record at the site where the person is served (COMAR 10.22.02.13 B). [AGENCY NAME] follows its DDA-approved Program Service Plan (COMAR 10.22.02.09 D) and submits any revision to DDA for approval before putting the change into effect (COMAR 10.22.02.09 B). The person, and the person's proponent or legal decision-maker where applicable, directs the planning process and decides who takes part. Any modification of a right or of a setting-rule condition under 42 CFR 441.301(c)(4) must be justified and documented in the plan before it is used (see PA-02). Where dedicated hours are shared among residents, the arrangement must be documented in each affected person's PCP. IP time frames follow COMAR 10.22.05 and DDA instructions; the Program Director confirms the current time frames in COMAR 10.22.05 and records them in the agency plan calendar.

definitions.definition: The plan for a person's services and supports as defined in COMAR 10.22.05. It must be kept in the individual's record.
The plan developed in LTSSMaryland through the person-centered process. Services are authorized in it.
The agency's DDA-approved description of each service it provides, covering rationale, scope, staffing and training, and setting and location (COMAR 10.22.02.09).
Additional authorized staff hours (billed as W1999) that DDA authorizes for a person's identified support needs. They may be shared among residents only as documented in each person's PCP.
A person who advocates for the individual and is involved in the individual's planning, such as a family member, guardian or other representative.

procedures: At admission and before each plan meeting, the Program Director asks the person how they want to be involved, who they want invited, and where and when they want to meet. The Program Director records these choices in the record.

The Program Director schedules the plan meeting so that the person's team (the person, the proponent or guardian, the DDA-funded Coordinator of Community Services, the RN, residential staff who know the person well, and others the person invites) can attend. Meetings are held at times and places that suit the person.

The Program Director confirms the current IP and PCP time frames from COMAR 10.22.05 and DDA instructions and enters each person's due dates on the agency plan calendar. The calendar is reviewed at least monthly. No due date is estimated from memory.

Before the meeting, the RN prepares a current health summary (diagnoses, allergies, medications, HRST results, risk areas such as seizures and choking, and any recent change of condition). The Program Director prepares a summary of the person's progress, preferences, community activities and incidents.

At the meeting, staff present information in the person's preferred communication method (see PA-05). Staff ask what is important to and for the person, what is working, and what should change. The person's own words are recorded where possible.

The team identifies the person's goals, the supports needed to reach them, health and safety supports (including written protocols for seizures, choking or other identified risks), and the staffing and any dedicated hours needed. The Program Director records who is responsible for each action.

If any proposed support limits a right or setting-rule condition (for example access to food, visitors, privacy or a lockable door), the team documents in the plan: the specific assessed need, positive interventions and less intrusive methods already tried, a description of the proposed condition, how data will be collected and reviewed, a review date, the person's or decision-maker's informed consent, and an assurance that the condition will cause no harm. Rights restrictions are reviewed by the standing committee (see PA-02, PA-09 and GOV-03). No restriction is applied before it is in the plan.

If dedicated hours are shared among residents, the Program Director documents in each person's PCP the arrangement, the people sharing the hours, how the hours are used, and the person's or decision-maker's agreement. The Program Director reviews the arrangement whenever a resident's needs or the household changes.

The Program Director confirms in LTSSMaryland that services and any dedicated hours the person needs are authorized in the PCP. [AGENCY NAME] does not provide or bill for a service that is not authorized (see GOV-04).

Within [NUMBER] business days after the plan is finalized (the Program Director sets this internal deadline, which must not exceed any time frame in COMAR 10.22.05), the Program Director files the signed IP in the person's record at the home and gives the person and proponent a copy in a format they understand.

The Program Director and RN convert the plan into daily support instructions: a one-page profile, health and safety protocols, and a list of goals and activities for each shift. The Program Director reviews these with every DSP who works with the person and records the staff member's signature or initials and the date.

DSPs carry out the IP and record daily documentation of the supports given, goal-related activities, community outings, choices made, and any refusals or changes, as described in PA-01. The Program Director reviews the documentation at least [FREQUENCY, e.g. weekly] and signs the review.

The RN reviews and updates the health sections of the IP after any change of condition, hospitalization, new diagnosis, HRST change or medication change, and gives updated protocols to staff the same day the change is made.

If the person's needs, preferences or circumstances change materially, the Program Director calls a team meeting sooner than the scheduled review. If the change would alter the scope of services, staffing or setting described in the Program Service Plan, the Program Director submits a revised PSP to DDA for approval before implementing the change (COMAR 10.22.02.09 B).

The governing body, through the Program Director, reviews and updates the Program Service Plan at least every 3 years, confirming that the number of individuals served, staffing and training, and setting and location still match what DDA approved (COMAR 10.22.02.09 C and E).

The Program Director checks each IP file quarterly to confirm that the current IP is present, signed, and matches LTSSMaryland. Gaps are corrected right away and reported to the standing committee under GOV-03.

responsibilities.duty: Directs the planning process, chooses participants, and agrees to or refuses the proposed plan and any modification.
Schedules and leads planning meetings, tracks IP time frames, keeps the IP in the record, and ensures LTSSMaryland authorization, PCP documentation of shared hours, and PSP compliance.
Prepares and updates health and safety sections, protocols and risk information, and trains staff on them.
Implement the IP as written and complete daily documentation.
Reviews and updates the PSP at least every 3 years and approves submission of PSP revisions to DDA.

documentation: Current signed IP and PCP in the individual's record at the site (COMAR 10.22.02.13 B)
Planning meeting notice, attendee list and notes
Plan calendar showing IP due dates from COMAR 10.22.05
Documentation of any setting-rule or rights modification, with consent and review dates
Shared dedicated-hours documentation in each PCP
Daily documentation of IP implementation and supervisor review
Staff acknowledgment of IP support instructions
LTSSMaryland authorization confirmation
DDA-approved PSP and any revision submissions and approvals

policies.title: Community Integration and Employment Choice
policies.applies_to: All individuals living in the group home, the Program Director and all staff, and the governing body for site selection and approval matters.
policies.purpose: To make sure the home and the supports [AGENCY NAME] provides are integrated into the community and are not isolating or institutional, and that each person is offered real information about, and a documented choice of, employment and day service options.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] operates each home as an ordinary residence in the community. The home is not gated, is not located so as to isolate residents, and does not carry institutional features. DDA's New Site Visit Checklist (Community Settings Rule) tests for institutional or isolating characteristics and applies heightened scrutiny to factors such as the home's proximity to the provider's other sites. [AGENCY NAME] considers these factors before it proposes or changes a site (see GOV-02). Under 42 CFR 441.301(c)(4), residents have access to the community, to visitors, and to food at any time, with limits allowed only as a documented, justified modification in the person's plan (see PA-02 and PCS-02). Each person is offered information about employment and day service options, and the person's choice is documented. All staff complete DDA-approved training on community integration within 3 months of hire (COMAR 10.22.02.11 D), and the Community Living – Group Home service standards in Appendix C of the Community Pathways Waiver apply.

definitions.definition: A person's full access to and participation in the greater community, to the same degree as people not receiving Medicaid HCBS, including community life, employment, services, shopping and relationships.
Features of a home or program that separate people from the community or from people without disabilities, such as gates, remote location, segregated or campus-like settings, or rigid schedules.
Additional CMS and DDA review of settings that may have institutional qualities, including a home's proximity to other provider sites.
Services and supports that may be available through DDA, such as employment services, community-based day activities or other options the person is eligible to use.

procedures: Before the governing body or Program Director proposes a new site or a change of site, the Program Director completes the DDA New Site Visit Checklist self-review. It covers the setting's location and appearance, institutional or isolating characteristics, and settings-rule items. The Program Director documents the proximity of the proposed home to each of [AGENCY NAME]'s other sites and the reasons the home is still integrated in the community. The results are reported to the governing body (see GOV-02).

The Program Director confirms before occupancy that the home has no gates or locked perimeter, no fencing or signage that identifies it as a program site, and no other features that would make the home look or operate like a facility, and that the home is reasonably close to community resources such as shops, faith organizations, public transportation and recreation.

At admission and at each plan review, the Program Director asks each person how they want to use the community (activities, places, groups, faith or cultural life, relationships) and records the answers in the person's plan.

Staff support each person's access to the community at any time of day, by arranging transportation, scheduling, or staff accompaniment as the person's plan requires (see HE-03). Staff do not set house-wide schedules for outings, meals or bedtime.

The Program Director posts and tells each person that they may have visitors at any time, with the person's consent, and may store and have food and drink available at any time. Staff do not lock the kitchen or limit visiting hours as a house rule. Any individual limit is handled only as a justified, documented plan modification (see PA-02).
Staff record each person's community outings, activities, and relationships in daily documentation (see PA-01), including the person's choice, who accompanied them, and any barriers.

Within [NUMBER] days of admission, and at least at each annual plan review, the Program Director gives each person (and the proponent) information about employment and day service options in a format the person understands, such as plain language, pictures or the person's preferred method (see PA-05). The Program Director may involve the DDA Coordinator of Community Services in this discussion.

The Program Director supports people who express interest in working, volunteering, training or day services by linking them to the Coordinator of Community Services and to qualified providers. Staff help with scheduling, transportation and communication, as authorized in the plan.

The Program Director documents in the plan each person's choice, including a choice not to work or attend day services, with the date, who took part, and the options offered. A person's choice is not changed to suit staffing or agency convenience.
The Program Director reviews each person's community integration and employment choice at every plan review and when the person asks, and records any change.

New staff complete DDA-approved training on community integration, supporting choice and communication skills within 3 months of hire (COMAR 10.22.02.11 D). The Program Director records the date in the staff training record (see SP-03).

The Program Director reviews monthly, with the person, whether the person is participating in the community as they want. The Program Director reports patterns of isolation, such as no outings, lost relationships or unmet requests, to the standing committee (see GOV-03) and corrects them in the plan.
If DDA or OHCQ identifies a settings-rule concern at a site visit, the Program Director corrects it and submits any plan of correction as described in REC-02 and XP-01.

responsibilities.duty: Chooses community activities, visitors, work or day service options, and when to change them.
Completes site self-review, ensures access to the community, visitors and food, provides employment and day service information, and documents each person's choice.
Support community access and activities as the person chooses, document outings, and do not impose house-wide limits.
Considers integration and proximity to the provider's other sites before approving sites and corrects settings-rule concerns.
Helps the person explore and arrange employment and day service options.

documentation: Completed New Site Visit Checklist self-review, including proximity to other [AGENCY NAME] sites
Person's community preferences in the PCP/IP
Record of information about employment and day service options given to the person and the person's documented choice
Daily community participation documentation
Documentation of any justified limit on access to the community, visitors or food, with consent and review date
Staff training records for community integration (COMAR 10.22.02.11 D)
Monthly review notes and standing committee reports on isolation patterns

policies.title: Transition, Discharge and Termination of Services
policies.applies_to: All individuals receiving services from [AGENCY NAME], their proponents, the Program Director, the Administrator, the RN and the business office.
policies.purpose: To make sure that a person's services end, or a person moves, only for good cause with the DDA Director's written approval, with required notices and hearing rights, and with a safe, orderly transition including the prompt return of funds, records and property.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] terminates services to an individual only for good cause and only with the written approval of the DDA Director (COMAR 10.22.02.02 G). [AGENCY NAME] gives the Director 90 days' written notice of the proposed termination. The person and proponent are given written notice of the right to a hearing under COMAR 10.22.16, and the regional office and the person's team are copied. Services are considered terminated after 60 consecutive days' absence unless the Director decides otherwise. When a person leaves for any reason, [AGENCY NAME] transfers the person's personal funds, records and property promptly and plans the move with the person and team. A person's move that is chosen by the person or decision-maker is a transition, not a termination. [AGENCY NAME] does not terminate services as a threat, as punishment or for convenience.

definitions.definition: A serious reason to end services, such as a situation in which the agency cannot safely meet the person's needs even with supports, or other grounds the DDA Director accepts. Good cause is not an inconvenience or a billing concern.
The agency's ending of services to a person, including a deemed termination after 60 consecutive days' absence, unless the Director decides otherwise.
The planned move of a person to another home, provider or setting, including the sharing of information and supports that make the move safe.
The DDA regional office that serves the person's area.

procedures: If the person, proponent or guardian chooses to leave or change providers, the Program Director meets with them within [NUMBER] business days, documents the request, notifies the Coordinator of Community Services, and begins transition planning. This is handled as a transition, not as a termination.

If [AGENCY NAME] believes it can no longer serve a person, the Program Director first holds a team meeting. It includes the person, the proponent, the RN, the Coordinator of Community Services and the regional office, to look for added supports, changes to staffing or behavior supports, health services, or a different home. The efforts and outcomes are recorded.

If the team cannot resolve the concern, the Program Director and Administrator prepare a written request to the DDA Director. It includes the reasons the agency believes good cause exists, a description of supports tried, relevant incident and health information, and the person's and proponent's views. Services continue unchanged while the request is pending.
The Administrator signs and sends the request, and no termination takes effect until the Director approves it in writing. The Administrator files the written approval in the person's record.
After approval, the Administrator gives the Director 90 days' written notice of the termination, with the planned end date. The same notice or a separate one goes to the individual and proponent.

The written notice to the individual and proponent states the reasons in plain language, the date services will end, the right to a hearing under COMAR 10.22.16 and how to ask for one, and who at [AGENCY NAME] and in the regional office can answer questions. Staff explain the notice in person using the person's preferred communication method (see PA-05).
The Administrator sends copies of the notice to the DDA regional office and the person's team (including the Coordinator of Community Services). Proof of delivery is kept in the record.

If the person or proponent requests a hearing, the Administrator tells the Program Director and counsel (if any) immediately, preserves all related records and takes part in the hearing as required. The Administrator confirms with the regional office how services continue while the hearing is pending.

The Program Director and RN prepare a written transition plan with the person and team. It covers the receiving home or provider, visits, belongings, communication supports, medications, health needs, daily routines, behavior supports, important relationships and any rights modifications.

At least [NUMBER] days before the move, the RN gives the receiving provider a current medication list, MAR copy, diagnoses, allergies, HRST results, protocols for seizures, choking and other risks, physician information and recent health changes. The Program Director gives the IP, behavior plan (if any) and other information the receiving provider is entitled to under privacy rules (see PA-03). Disclosures are logged.

On the move date, staff accompany the person where the person wants them to, send the person's medications as ordered and with a count signed by both staff (see NU-03 for controlled drugs), and give the person their belongings, funds and documents. A receipt is signed by the person or decision-maker and the receiving staff.

Within [NUMBER] business days after the person leaves, the business office reconciles and transfers the person's personal funds and property, gives a final accounting, and obtains a signed receipt, as set out in PA-14. Funds are never held back to settle agency charges unless the residency agreement and law allow it and the person or decision-maker has been told in writing.

The Program Director transfers records the receiving provider needs (see PA-03). [AGENCY NAME] keeps the original record at least 6 years after the person leaves, in compliance with COMAR 10.22.02.13 D (see REC-01).

The Program Director tracks the days of any absence from the home (for example hospital stays or visits away). If an absence nears 60 consecutive days, the Program Director consults the regional office and the team, and asks the Director for a decision on whether services will be considered terminated, recording the answer. Retainer days are used as DDA allows (see HW-02).

Within [NUMBER] business days after any discharge or termination, the Program Director reports the end of services in LTSSMaryland and notifies the business office to stop billing as of the correct date (see GOV-04). The Program Director also reviews the transition at the next standing committee meeting (see GOV-03).
If a person dies, HW-03 applies, not this policy.

responsibilities.duty: Requests the Director's approval, gives the 90-day written notice, ensures hearing-rights notices are given, and copies the regional office and team.
Leads team meetings and transition planning, supports the person through the move, and tracks absences.
Prepares health and medication information for the receiving provider and reviews it with the person's new team.
Returns personal funds, reconciles accounts and stops billing on the correct date.
Takes part in planning, receives written notices, and may ask for a hearing.

documentation: Team meeting notes and efforts made to continue services
Written request to the DDA Director and the Director's written approval
90-day written notice to the Director; written notice of hearing rights to the individual and proponent; proof copied to the regional office and team
Hearing request and related correspondence under COMAR 10.22.16
Transition plan and receiving-provider information log
Medication transfer and count records
Signed receipt for funds, belongings and records
Absence tracking log (60-consecutive-day rule) and any Director decision
LTSSMaryland end-of-service entry and final billing record

policies.title: Health Monitoring, Seizures and Choking Risk
policies.applies_to: All individuals served, the RN, the Program Director and all DSPs.
policies.purpose: To make sure each person's health is monitored, that risks such as seizures and choking are identified and written into the Individual Plan with clear staff protocols, and that staff are trained and certified to respond.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] identifies and monitors each person's health and safety risks, including seizure disorders and choking, and records them in the IP with a written protocol staff follow. Staff must complete DDA-approved training on seizure disorders before independent duties (COMAR 10.22.02.11 C). Staff are at least 18 and hold First Aid/CPR (American Red Cross or equivalent) with an in-person skills check (Community Pathways Waiver, Appendix C; COMAR 10.22.02.11 D). [AGENCY NAME] requires this certification before a staff member works alone and in all cases within 3 months of hire. The RN reviews each person's risk, including Health Risk Screening Tool (HRST) results, and updates plans after changes. Nursing Support Services are requested when a health change or hospital discharge makes them appropriate. [AGENCY NAME] has staff on duty with the training to carry out these protocols whenever a person is in the home.

definitions.definition: Health Risk Screening Tool, the instrument used in the DDA system to assess and rate a person's health risk.
The written, person-specific instructions for seizure types, first aid, rescue medication, timing, when to call 911, and documentation.
A person's risk of choking or aspiration identified by the physician, RN, speech-language pathologist or team, with written instructions on diet texture, positioning, supervision and response.
Additional nursing supports that may be requested through DDA after a health change or hospital discharge.

procedures: At admission, the RN completes a health review of each person (diagnoses, medications, allergies, seizure history, swallowing and choking history, physician and specialist contacts, immunizations, screenings) and confirms the HRST has been completed and is current. The RN records the findings in the record.

The RN identifies each person's health and safety risks, including any seizure disorder and choking or aspiration risk, and, with the team, writes a protocol for each. Each protocol states: signs to watch, preventive steps, what staff do, when to call 911, whom to notify, and how to document.

The seizure protocol states the seizure type(s), usual triggers and presentation, first-aid steps (safe positioning and protecting the head, nothing in the mouth, timing the seizure), any rescue medication and who may give it under MATP/delegation (see PA-07 and NU-07), emergency criteria, and the post-seizure observation and notification steps. The RN trains staff on any rescue medication before they give it.

The choking protocol states the person's diet texture and liquid consistency as ordered, feeding and positioning requirements, supervision level at meals, equipment, food that must be avoided, and emergency response (see HE-02). The RN obtains or confirms orders from the physician or other qualified clinician before a diet modification is used.
Risk protocols are placed in the IP (see PCS-02) and a quick-reference copy is kept where staff can see it quickly but in a way that protects the person's privacy (see PA-03).

Before a new DSP carries out independent duties, the Program Director verifies and documents completion of the job training and DDA-approved training on seizure disorders, medication administration, behavior change and aging, plus OSHA blood-borne pathogens (COMAR 10.22.02.11 C) (see SP-03). The RN or trainer reviews each person's specific protocols with the staff member and the staff member signs.

The Program Director verifies each DSP is 18 or older and holds a current First Aid/CPR certification (American Red Cross or equivalent) with an in-person skills check. Staff are not scheduled to work alone until it is verified. [AGENCY NAME] tracks expiration dates, schedules renewals in advance, and removes lapsed staff from solo shifts until they are recertified.

Staff observe each person's health every shift and note changes in appetite, eating, swallowing, alertness, mobility, mood, skin, bowel or bladder habits, sleep, pain, and seizure activity. They record observations in daily documentation (see PA-01).

Staff record every seizure on a seizure record with the date, start and end times, description, triggers, injuries, rescue medication given, and who was notified. Staff record every choking event or suspected aspiration on an incident report. The RN reviews these records at least [FREQUENCY, e.g. monthly] and notifies the physician of trends or changes.

Staff arrange routine and specialty health appointments (physician, neurologist, dentist, vision, hearing and others as ordered) and record the visit, orders and follow-up. The RN reviews all new orders (see NU-01) and updates plans.

The RN reviews HRST results at least annually and whenever the person's condition changes, and updates the person's IP risk protocols and staff training if the rating or recommendations change. The RN reports the changes to the team.

After a hospital discharge, ER visit, new diagnosis or significant change of condition, the RN reviews the discharge orders within [NUMBER] hours, updates protocols and staff instructions the same day, and decides with the team whether to request Nursing Support Services through the Coordinator of Community Services. The request and the response are recorded (see HW-02).

Staff follow the protocol and call 911 when a protocol or emergency criterion is met (see HW-02). After the event, staff notify the RN and guardian/proponent, complete any required incident report under PA-06, and record the event in the person's record.

The Program Director reviews each seizure and choking event and each near miss monthly. The Program Director brings trends to the standing committee (see GOV-03) and corrects training and protocol gaps.

responsibilities.duty: Assesses health risks, reviews HRST, writes and updates seizure and choking protocols, trains staff, and reviews seizure and choking records.
Ensures required staff training and First Aid/CPR certification are current, schedules coverage, and reports trends to the standing committee.
Complete required training, follow protocols, observe and document health changes, and call 911 and the RN as directed.
Takes part in health planning, informs staff of health changes, and consents to treatment and diet changes.

documentation: Admission health review and current HRST results
IP risk protocols for seizures, choking and other identified risks
Seizure records and choking incident reports
Staff training records showing seizure training, medication administration, behavior change, aging, and OSHA blood-borne pathogens before independent duties (COMAR 10.22.02.11 C)
First Aid/CPR certificates with in-person skills checks and an expiration tracking log
Staff signature sheets for person-specific protocols
RN review notes and updates after changes
Nursing Support Services requests and responses
Daily health observation notes

policies.title: Change of Condition and Emergency Medical Care
policies.applies_to: All individuals served, the RN, the Program Director and all DSPs.
policies.purpose: To make sure staff recognize a change of condition, call 911 in an emergency, notify the right people promptly, give emergency personnel the person's medical information, and document and follow up on each event.
policies.policy: Staff call 911 for any medical emergency or any time a person's protocol says to do so. After calling 911 and giving first aid, staff notify the RN, the guardian or proponent and DDA as the current DDA Policy on Reportable Incidents and Investigations (PORII) requires. Each person's medical information is kept readily accessible to emergency personnel (COMAR 10.22.02.13 C). Retainer days, up to 18 per person per year under the Community Pathways Waiver, cover the person's hospitalization or other absence as DDA allows. Staff document each event and each change of condition in the person's record and follow up until the issue is resolved. Emergency care is not delayed to reach an administrator or obtain consent.

definitions.definition: Any new, sudden or worsening change in a person's physical or behavioral health, such as new pain, fever, injury, change in eating, drinking, breathing, alertness, mobility, mood, behavior, seizures or skin.
A situation in which a person's life, health or safety is in serious and immediate danger and needs emergency medical services.
The current DDA Policy on Reportable Incidents and Investigations, which sets what incidents must be reported, to whom and when (see PA-06).
Days, up to 18 per person per year, for which DDA allows payment to hold a person's place during an absence such as a hospital stay.
A current one- or two-page summary of the person's identifying information, diagnoses, allergies, medications, physician, emergency contact and guardian, and baseline, ready to go with the person.

procedures: The RN prepares and keeps an emergency information packet for each person. It has the person's identifying information, photo, emergency contact, next of kin, guardian/proponent, physician, diagnoses, allergies, current medication list, communication needs, baseline, and code status or advance directives if any (see COMAR 10.22.02.13 B). A copy is stored in a known location in the home that all staff can reach and emergency personnel can be handed at once (COMAR 10.22.02.13 C).

The RN updates the packet whenever medications, diagnoses, allergies or contacts change, and at least [FREQUENCY, e.g. every 3 months]. The Program Director checks monthly that each packet is current.

Staff who see a possible emergency (such as trouble breathing, choking not cleared, unresponsiveness, a seizure outside the protocol, chest pain, stroke signs, serious injury, severe bleeding, suspected overdose, or other danger) call 911 right away. They then begin first aid or CPR as trained. Staff do not wait for a supervisor, RN or guardian before calling 911.

One staff member stays with the person. Another staff member (or the same caller, if alone) sends the emergency information packet and medication list with the person, unlocks and secures the home as needed, and makes sure other residents are supervised. If only one staff member is on duty, that person calls 911 and follows the on-call instructions in EP-04 to get additional coverage.

Staff go with the person to the hospital or arrange for another staff member to do so, unless the person is accompanied by a family member or guardian. Staff stay as the person's advocate, giving information to clinicians, communicating the person's communication needs and preferences, and following the person's wishes and the guardian's decisions.

As soon as it is safe, staff call the RN on-call at [PHONE]. Staff then notify the guardian or proponent, and the Program Director at [PHONE]. The Program Director or designee reports to DDA, OHCQ and others as the PORII requires and files the required report under PA-06. [AGENCY NAME] does not rely on a timeline that is not in the PORII in effect at the time of the event.

For a change of condition that is not an emergency, staff tell the RN right away by phone, record the observation (what, when, how long, vital signs if trained and ordered, pain, other signs), and follow the RN's instructions, which may be to monitor, call the physician, go to urgent care, or call 911.

The RN contacts the physician or nurse practitioner for orders, documents the call and the orders in the record, and sends updated instructions to staff the same shift. Staff follow orders as written and record what was done (see NU-01 and NU-06).

If a person refuses emergency or other medical care, staff try again to explain it in a way the person understands, contact the RN and guardian or proponent, and call 911 if the person is in danger. Staff record the refusal and the response (see PA-11 for consent).

For hospital admission, the Program Director tells the Coordinator of Community Services and the regional office as needed. Staff track each absence day and record retainer days used, up to 18 per person per year, and the Program Director informs the business office so billing is correct (see GOV-04). If an absence nears 60 consecutive days, follow PCS-04.

While the person is hospitalized, the RN or Program Director stays in contact with the hospital, brings the person's medication list, orders and communication supports, and attends discharge planning where possible. Staff visit or support the person as is appropriate.

Before discharge, the RN obtains discharge orders, new prescriptions and instructions, reviews them, and updates the MAR, protocols and IP. The RN decides whether Nursing Support Services are needed and arranges a request through the Coordinator of Community Services (see HW-01). The RN reviews changes with staff before the person arrives home.

Within the same shift, the staff member who handled the event documents it in the person's record: date, time, what was seen, actions, who was called and when, treatment and outcome. The Program Director reviews the entry the next business day and signs.

The RN follows up with the physician and staff after the event until the change of condition is resolved, and records each follow-up contact. The Program Director reviews each emergency event at the next standing committee meeting as part of incident review (see GOV-03).

responsibilities.duty: Recognize changes, call 911 for emergencies, give first aid, accompany the person, send the emergency packet, notify the RN and Program Director, and document.
Maintains emergency information packets, directs responses to changes of condition, communicates with physicians and hospitals, and updates plans after the event.
Ensures notifications and PORII reports are made, tracks retainer days, and reviews events.
Receives prompt notice, takes part in treatment decisions and advocates for the person.

documentation: Emergency information packet for each person, kept accessible (COMAR 10.22.02.13 C)
Daily documentation and event notes for each emergency or change of condition
Physician orders and RN follow-up notes
Incident report and PORII notification records (see PA-06)
Hospital records and discharge orders
Retainer day and absence tracking log
Record of refusal of care, if any
Notification log (RN, guardian/proponent, Program Director, DDA)

policies.title: Death of an Individual
policies.applies_to: All staff, the Program Director, the RN, the Administrator, and the business office.
policies.purpose: To make sure a death is reported immediately, the family or proponent is notified with care, evidence is preserved, records are kept, the death is reviewed through the mortality review process, and the person's funds and property are handled properly.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] reports the death of any person it serves immediately under the current DDA Policy on Reportable Incidents and Investigations (PORII) and notifies the family or proponent. Staff call 911 and give emergency care unless a valid directive says otherwise, and preserve the scene and medication records as authorities direct. [AGENCY NAME] keeps the person's records at least 6 years after death (COMAR 10.22.02.13 D). Each death is included in the mortality review described in GOV-03, which is part of the quality assurance system required by COMAR 10.22.02.14, and the standing committee reviews the incident. The person's personal funds and property are transferred under PA-14. [AGENCY NAME] treats the person's housemates, family and staff with dignity and support after a death.

definitions.definition: The current DDA Policy on Reportable Incidents and Investigations.
A review of each death by [AGENCY NAME], through the standing committee and QA process, to find contributing factors and system improvements (see GOV-03).
Leaving the area, equipment, medications and belongings as they are (except as needed for care or safety) until authorities release them.
A family member, guardian or other representative who advocates for the person.

procedures: A staff member who finds a person unresponsive or not breathing, or who believes a person has died, calls 911 immediately and starts CPR or first aid unless there is a valid DNR/MOLST order or the person is obviously dead. Staff follow the 911 dispatcher's instructions.

The staff member sends another staff member (or calls once help is on its way) to supervise and reassure the other residents, and moves them to another area where possible. If only one staff member is on duty, that person calls 911 and then the on-call line at [PHONE] to bring in more staff (see EP-04).

Staff preserve the scene: they do not move or clean the area, the person's belongings or equipment, except as needed to give care or protect people. They keep the medication administration record, medications, treatment records and relevant logs secured and do not alter them. They record what they saw, with times.
Staff cooperate with the police, emergency medical staff, the medical examiner and other authorities, and follow their directions on the body, the scene and records.

The staff member notifies the on-call RN and Program Director immediately. The Program Director notifies the Administrator right away and ensures the death is reported immediately to DDA, OHCQ and any other required parties under the PORII in effect at the time. The Program Director completes the required incident report under PA-06 and does not rely on any time frame not found in the PORII.

The Program Director or Administrator (not a DSP, unless no one else is available) notifies the family, guardian or proponent in person or by phone, immediately and with care. They give the facts known, say where the person is, and offer support. If the proponent cannot be reached, the Program Director keeps trying and records each attempt. The person's wishes recorded in the plan and advance directives guide who is notified and how.

The Program Director tells the Coordinator of Community Services and the regional office as required by the PORII. The Program Director tells the business office to stop billing for the person as of the date of death (see GOV-04).

The RN secures and copies the person's medication records, MAR, controlled drug counts, health records, and the person's current IP and risk protocols. The original records stay in [AGENCY NAME]'s custody unless an authority legally takes them, in which case a copy and a receipt are kept. Medications are secured, counted by two staff and handled under NU-03 and NU-02 once authorities release them.

The Program Director makes the person's records available to OHCQ, the medical examiner, law enforcement or other lawful investigators and records each disclosure (see PA-03). Records are not altered, removed or destroyed. Late entries are labeled with the date and author.

The Program Director supports housemates and staff after the death. This includes telling housemates in a way they can understand, helping them take part in memorials as they choose, arranging counseling or grief support, and offering staff a debriefing and time off as needed.

The Program Director supports the family or proponent with questions about the person's belongings, funeral and burial wishes (including documented wishes), and the return of personal items. Staff do not make funeral arrangements unless the family or proponent asks and the Administrator approves.

The Program Director and business office carry out PA-14: inventory the person's funds and property with a second staff member, produce a final accounting, and transfer funds and property to the personal representative, estate or other legally authorized person, and obtain a signed receipt.

The Program Director keeps the person's complete record, including the record of the death and investigation, for at least 6 years after the death (COMAR 10.22.02.13 D), organized for easy access and, if electronic, backed up and stored off-site (see REC-01).

Within [NUMBER] days of the death, the RN and Program Director prepare a mortality review summary: the person's health and risk history, last 30 days of care, events leading to death, any contributing factors, the response and any recommendations. The summary is given to the standing committee, which reviews the incident under COMAR 10.22.02.14 E, and is reviewed again when the final cause of death is known (see GOV-03).

The Administrator assigns corrective actions from the review, such as retraining, protocol changes or staffing changes. The Program Director tracks them to completion and reports results to the standing committee. Committee members who were involved in the person's care or the incident do not decide on that incident.

responsibilities.duty: Call 911, give emergency care, preserve the scene, notify the RN and Program Director, and document facts.
Ensures immediate PORII reporting, family or proponent notification, records preservation, housemate support and the mortality review.
Secures medication and health records, assists with the review, and counts and secures medications.
Oversees reporting, notifications, corrective actions and communication with authorities.
Stops billing at the right date and completes the personal funds accounting and transfer.
Reviews the incident and the mortality review and recommends system changes (COMAR 10.22.02.14 E).

documentation: Incident report and PORII notification records (see PA-06)
Staff statements, event timeline and 911 call information
Notification log (family/proponent, RN, Program Director, Administrator, DDA, OHCQ, others)
Copies of medication records, controlled-drug counts, and health records preserved
Records disclosure log for authorities (see PA-03)
Mortality review summary and standing committee minutes
Corrective action tracking
Final accounting and receipts for transfer of funds and property (see PA-14)
The person's complete record retained for at least 6 years after death (COMAR 10.22.02.13 D)
Support provided to housemates and staff

policies.title: Abuse, Neglect and Exploitation Prevention and Reporting
policies.applies_to: All employees, contractors, consultants, volunteers and care providers of [AGENCY NAME], at every licensed Community Living – Group Home site
policies.purpose: To protect every person supported by [AGENCY NAME] from abuse, neglect and exploitation. This policy sets out how the agency prevents these harms, how any suspicion is reported and investigated, and how people who report are protected from retaliation.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] has zero tolerance for abuse, neglect, exploitation or mistreatment of any individual. Every suspected or alleged event must be reported immediately, whether it involves staff, another resident, a family member, a visitor or anyone else. [AGENCY NAME] reports and investigates all incidents under the Maryland Developmental Disabilities Administration (DDA) incident reporting procedures (the PORII), as required by COMAR 10.22.02.10A(7). Suspected abuse is also reported to the authorities that Maryland law requires, including law enforcement and the local department of social services where applicable. These policies apply to every staff member, care provider, consultant and volunteer, who must know and implement them (COMAR 10.22.02.10C). Reporters are protected from retaliation. Before hire, [AGENCY NAME] obtains a criminal history check and will not employ or contract with anyone whose criminal history indicates behavior potentially harmful to individuals (COMAR 10.22.02.11B; Health-General §19-1902 et seq.; COMAR 12.15.03). Information gathered in a report or investigation is shared only as allowed by law, consistent with HIPAA (45 CFR 164) and PA-03.

definitions.definition: Physical, sexual, verbal or emotional harm, or mistreatment, of an individual, including any unauthorized restraint, seclusion or punishment.
Failure to provide the supervision, care, services, food, medical attention or protection an individual needs, whether intentional or not.
Use of an individual, or their money, property, benefits or labor, for the benefit of someone else without valid consent. This includes making the individual perform paid staff duties.
The DDA Policy on Reportable Incidents and Investigations, as currently in effect. It governs which incidents are reported, how, to whom, and by when.
Any adverse action, threat or harassment directed at a person because they reported or took part in a report, complaint or investigation in good faith.

procedures: Before offering employment or a contract, the Program Director confirms that the criminal history check and registry checks required by SP-02 are complete and clear. No one begins independent duties until this is done. The result is filed in the personnel record.

During orientation and at least annually, the Program Director trains every staff member, consultant and volunteer on recognizing abuse, neglect and exploitation, the duty to report, and this policy. Attendance is recorded and signed.
Staff are trained on the signs of abuse and neglect in people who communicate in non-traditional ways, and on each person's own communication supports (see PA-05).

Any person who sees, suspects or is told of possible abuse, neglect or exploitation takes immediate action to make the individual safe. This includes calling 911 if the person is in danger or needs medical care, and separating the individual from the alleged source of harm.

The person with the concern reports to the supervisor or on-call administrator immediately. If the concern involves the supervisor or administrator, the person reports directly to the next level up or to the outside authorities listed below. No one needs permission to report.

Staff may report directly and at any time to law enforcement, the local department of social services, DDA, or the OHCQ complaint line at 410-402-8100 / 877-402-8220. Internal reporting does not replace an external report.

The Program Director or designee makes the reports Maryland law requires to law enforcement and social services agencies, and the report required by the PORII. They do this within the timelines in the current PORII, and the PORII version in effect controls those timelines.

The Program Director or designee notifies the individual's guardian or proponent and the DDA regional office, and supports the individual in making any report they wish to make, as the PORII requires.

The agency then starts its own investigation, or takes part in an outside investigation, as the PORII requires. The investigator must be trained and free of conflict of interest (see PA-12). An investigator must not be someone involved in the event or reporting to someone accused.

While an investigation is open, the Program Director takes protective measures such as removing the accused staff member from contact with individuals, changing assignments or placing the staff member on leave. The agency keeps individuals safe and gets them medical care and emotional support as needed.

[AGENCY NAME] cooperates fully with OHCQ, DDA, law enforcement and social services investigators. It provides access to records, staff and the home, and preserves evidence such as schedules, logs, photographs and videos where they exist.

The Program Director completes the investigation and the PORII follow-up reports within the required timelines. Corrective actions are taken, such as retraining, discipline, termination, plan changes or referral to licensing boards, and the results are documented.

No one may retaliate against a person who reports in good faith, an individual who complains, or a witness. The Program Director investigates every allegation of retaliation, and a substantiated finding results in discipline up to termination.
Staff must never ask or allow an individual to keep an incident secret, and must never discourage a report. Doing so is itself misconduct and is handled under SP-05.

Confidential information in reports is shared only with those who have a legal need to know and in line with PA-03 and HIPAA (45 CFR 164). The identity of reporters is protected as far as the law allows.

The Program Director reviews all reports and investigations for patterns, at least quarterly, in the quality assurance review (see GOV-03). Findings lead to system changes and are used for staff training.

responsibilities.duty: Protect individuals, report immediately every suspicion or allegation, and cooperate with investigations. Never retaliate.
Receive reports at once, secure the individual's safety, notify the on-call administrator, and preserve evidence.
Ensure all required external and DDA reports and investigations are completed on time, implement protective measures and corrective action, and train staff.
Ensure the process is funded and followed, and handle any report involving the Program Director.
Review incident, investigation and retaliation data for trends, and ensure corrective actions are carried out.

documentation: Incident reports and PORII submissions, filed in the individual's record and in a central incident file
Investigation reports, evidence, interview notes and corrective action records
Notifications to guardians or proponents, DDA, law enforcement and social services, with date, time and name of person contacted
Staff training attendance records on abuse, neglect, exploitation and reporting
Criminal history and registry check results in personnel records
Quarterly incident trend review minutes

policies.title: Missing Person and Elopement
policies.applies_to: All staff and care providers at every [AGENCY NAME] group home and while supporting individuals in the community or in vehicles
policies.purpose: To make sure that a missing individual is found quickly and safely, that the right people are notified without delay, and that each person's risk of leaving unsupervised is assessed and supported through the Individual Plan (IP) without unapproved restrictions.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] treats every missing person event as an emergency. Staff begin an immediate search and notify the police, the guardian or proponent and DDA. The event is reported as an incident under the PORII, as required by COMAR 10.22.02.10A(7), using the timelines in the current PORII. Each person's elopement or wandering risk, and the supports to reduce it, are assessed and documented in the IP. This respects the person's right to go out and to community access. [AGENCY NAME] does not use locks, alarms, delayed-egress devices or other barriers on exits unless the restriction has been approved as a rights restriction under PA-02, based on a specific assessed need and documented in the IP. Exits must remain usable for fire evacuation at all times, consistent with the fire safety requirements of COMAR 10.22.02.12B and HE-01. All staff, care providers, consultants and volunteers must know and apply this policy (COMAR 10.22.02.10C).

definitions.definition: An individual whose whereabouts are unknown and who is not where the IP or schedule says they should be, and whose absence is unexplained, or who has left a supervised setting contrary to their supervision needs.
An individual leaving the home, a vehicle or an activity without staff knowledge when the IP calls for supervision.
Any limit on a person's rights or on the settings conditions that requires a documented assessed need, informed consent and approval before use (see PA-02).
A planned absence by a person who is able to be out independently under the IP, which is not elopement and does not trigger this protocol.

procedures: At admission and at each IP review, the Program Director, with the person, their team and the RN where relevant, assesses the person's elopement and wandering risk. The assessment considers history, communication, traffic and safety awareness, medical risks and the person's own wishes.

The IP records the risk level, the supports to be used (for example proximity, a check schedule, a community safety plan, identification, a photo and a description), and any approved rights restriction. Staff are trained on the IP supports before working with the person.

The agency keeps a current photo, description (height, weight, hair, clothing worn that day, distinguishing features), communication method, medical needs, medications and likely destinations for each individual, and keeps it where staff can reach it quickly and out of public view.

Staff must never use locks, alarms or barriers on exits unless the rights restriction is approved under PA-02 and documented in the IP. If a restriction is approved, it must never block emergency evacuation.

When a person is noticed missing, the staff member on duty calls out to other staff and immediately begins a search of the home, yard, garage, vehicles and nearby areas. Other individuals remain supervised so no one else is left unattended.

If the person is not found within a few minutes, or at once if the person is at high risk or in danger, the staff member calls 911 and gives the description, last seen location, time and any medical or safety concerns. Staff must not wait for a set time if the person is vulnerable.
Staff call the on-call administrator or Program Director, who directs the response, assigns additional staff or searchers, and takes over notifications.
The Program Director or designee notifies the guardian or proponent immediately, and notifies the DDA regional office. These notices follow the current PORII timelines and requirements.
Staff continue to search and check likely places, such as the person's usual destinations, workplace, family home, transit stops and local hospitals. They share updates with police as they come in.

When the person is found, staff check for injury, get medical care if needed, and give comfort. Staff call 911 or the police back to report the person found, and tell the guardian or proponent and the Program Director.

The Program Director reports the event as a reportable incident under the PORII and submits the required reports within the current timelines. If there are signs of neglect, abuse or injury, the matter is also handled under BP-01.

Within a short time after the event, the person's team reviews the cause. They look at supervision, environment, the person's wishes or unmet needs, staffing and communication. They revise the IP supports or staffing plan (see SP-01) and, if a restriction is proposed, follow PA-02 and PA-08.
Staff who were involved are debriefed, and further training is given if the protocol was not followed. Corrective actions are recorded.
A missing person drill or tabletop review is held at least annually with staff, and the protocol is included in emergency planning (see EP-01, EP-03).
The Program Director reviews all missing person events each quarter in the quality assurance review (see GOV-03) to identify patterns and system changes.

responsibilities.duty: Know each person's elopement supports, supervise as the IP directs, start the search immediately and call 911 and the on-call administrator without delay.
Direct the response, make the guardian, DDA and PORII notifications, complete the risk assessment and IP updates, and train staff.
Provide medical and medication information to responders and assist in assessing health-related risks.
Assess risk, develop supports that respect choice, and approve any restriction through the proper process.
Ensure resources and follow-up, and review all events and corrective actions.

documentation: Elopement risk assessment and supports recorded in the IP
Current photo and description sheet for each individual
Incident report and PORII submissions for each event
Log of search actions, times, and notifications to police, guardian or proponent and DDA
Post-event review, IP changes and corrective action records
Rights restriction approval documentation, where applicable
Drill and staff training records

policies.title: Residential Environment, Accessibility, Fire Safety and Water Temperature
policies.applies_to: Every [AGENCY NAME] licensed Community Living – Group Home site, its grounds and all staff responsible for the home
policies.purpose: To ensure that every home is safe, accessible, in good repair and homelike. It must comply with zoning, building and life-safety requirements, protect residents from fire and scalding, and meet the Medicaid home and community-based settings requirements for privacy and control of personal space.
policies.policy: Each [AGENCY NAME] home meets local zoning (except as provided in Health-General §7-603) and State and local building codes and life-safety requirements, is free of hazards, and is in good repair (COMAR 10.22.02.12A). Each home is free of fire hazards, has adequate smoke detectors, has working and updated fire extinguishers, and has a written fire evacuation plan (COMAR 10.22.02.12B). Hot water at taps accessible to residents does not exceed 110°F unless every resident of the home can regulate the temperature safely and this is documented in each person's IP (COMAR 10.22.02.12C). Each home houses no more than four participants unless DDA has previously approved a larger number, and each resident has a private bedroom (Community Pathways Waiver, Appendix C – Community Living – Group Home). Because the home is provider-owned or controlled, residents have a lease or equivalent agreement, privacy, bedroom doors they can lock, choice of roommates where applicable, and access to food and visitors (42 CFR 441.301(c)(4)). Any modification of these conditions, including lockable doors and control of space, requires a specific assessed need documented in the person-centered plan (42 CFR 441.301(c)(4)(vi)). The site's wheelchair accessibility is accurately reported on the DDA Addendum for Licensed Services and Sites (MDH Form DD.ADD.1.0), and [AGENCY NAME] complies with the Americans with Disabilities Act as it applies to the home and the people served. All staff must know and carry out this policy (COMAR 10.22.02.10C).

definitions.definition: State and local fire, building and occupancy rules intended to protect occupants from fire and similar hazards.
A residence owned, leased or operated by the provider, subject to the added HCBS settings conditions in 42 CFR 441.301(c)(4)(vi).
The risk of burns from water hotter than 110°F, higher for people with limited sensation, mobility or judgment.

definitions.term: DDA Addendum for Licensed Services and Sites
definitions.definition: MDH Form DD.ADD.1.0, listing each site, requested capacity, proposed occupancy date, wheelchair accessibility, and the Community Settings Rule attestation.

procedures: Before acquiring or leasing a site, the Program Director confirms with the local jurisdiction that zoning allows a community residence of the intended size, applying Health-General §7-603 where it applies, and records the result. Occupancy begins only after DDA site approval (see GOV-02).

The Program Director confirms with local and State authorities that building codes and life-safety requirements are met, and obtains any required inspections or approvals before residents move in. These are kept on file.
The Program Director limits occupancy to four residents unless DDA has previously approved a different number, and ensures each resident has a private bedroom of adequate size.

The Maintenance Lead and the Program Director install smoke detectors at levels and locations sufficient for the home, and test them at least monthly. Batteries are replaced as needed, and detectors are replaced as manufacturers require. Test results are logged.

Fire extinguishers are placed in accessible locations, are inspected and serviced at least annually (or as the fire code directs), and are replaced or recharged when out of date. Tags and the inspection log are kept up to date.
The written fire evacuation plan is posted in each home. It shows exits, routes, meeting places and each resident's evacuation support needs, and is reviewed and drilled under EP-01 and EP-02.

Staff must never block, lock or disable exits in a way that prevents emergency evacuation. Any exit alarms or similar devices require an approved rights restriction under PA-02 and must still allow safe egress.

The Maintenance Lead sets and checks water heaters so that water at taps accessible to residents does not exceed 110°F, and checks water temperatures with a thermometer at least monthly and after any plumbing or heater work. Readings are recorded.

A temperature higher than 110°F is permitted only if the IP for each resident of the home documents that every resident can safely regulate water temperature. The team revisits this at each IP review and when a resident changes or moves in.

Staff walk through the home at least weekly, and the Program Director does a documented inspection at least monthly. They check for hazards such as tripping hazards, exposed wires, poor lighting, damaged floors, broken furniture, pests, hazardous chemicals, unsafe stairs and railings, and the yard.
Repairs affecting safety are made immediately, or the area is closed off until fixed. Routine repairs are scheduled and completed promptly, and tracked on a maintenance log until completed.
Cleaning supplies, tools and other hazardous items are stored safely, in line with each resident's abilities and risks as set out in the IP and PA-15.

The home is arranged to feel like a home. Residents choose their furnishings and decorations, keep a lockable bedroom door with their own key (and staff have a key for emergencies), and control their personal space. Any limit on lockable doors or control of space may be applied only after an assessed need is documented in the person-centered plan under 42 CFR 441.301(c)(4)(vi), and under PA-02.

Residents have a lease or equivalent residency agreement (see PCS-01), choose roommates where sharing applies, and have access to food at any time (see HE-02) and visitors at times of their choosing, within any documented, approved modification.

The Program Director assesses the physical accessibility of each site for the people living there and those expected to live there, including entrances, doorways, bathrooms, bedrooms and common areas. Reasonable modifications are made as needed under the ADA and the IP.

The Program Director completes the DDA Addendum for Licensed Services and Sites for each site, accurately stating capacity, proposed occupancy date and whether the site is wheelchair accessible, and signs the Community Settings Rule attestation only after confirming the home meets it.
Any repair, renovation or change affecting capacity, accessibility or safety is reported to DDA and OHCQ as required, and the site addendum is updated (see GOV-02, REC-02).
The Program Director reviews inspection findings, maintenance records and drill results each quarter in the quality assurance review (see GOV-03).

responsibilities.duty: Report hazards at once, perform weekly walk-throughs, test detectors and keep exits clear.
Maintain the home in good repair, set and check water temperature, service extinguishers and detectors, and keep logs.
Ensure zoning, code, occupancy, accessibility and HCBS settings compliance, complete monthly inspections and the DDA site addendum.
Fund needed repairs and modifications and ensure no site is occupied without required approvals.
Document water temperature decisions and any approved modification of settings conditions in the IP.

documentation: Zoning, building, fire marshal and life-safety approvals for each site
Smoke detector test logs and fire extinguisher inspection tags and logs
Written fire evacuation plan and drill records
Water temperature logs and any IP documentation of residents' ability to regulate temperature
Weekly staff walk-through and monthly Program Director inspection records
Maintenance and repair log
DDA Addendum for Licensed Services and Sites (MDH Form DD.ADD.1.0) with wheelchair accessibility and Community Settings Rule attestation
Lease or residency agreements and documented assessed needs for any settings modification

policies.title: Food, Nutrition and Modified Diets
policies.applies_to: All staff and care providers who plan, purchase, prepare or serve food, or support residents at meals, in every [AGENCY NAME] group home
policies.purpose: To ensure each resident has nutritious food of their own choosing available at any time, that modified diets and texture requirements are ordered and followed exactly, and that staff are trained to support safe eating and respond to choking.
policies.policy: Residents of [AGENCY NAME] homes have access to food at any time, as required by the HCBS settings rule for provider-owned or controlled residences (42 CFR 441.301(c)(4)). They choose what, when and with whom they eat, and their preferences are honored and documented. Where a resident has a medical or safety need for a modified diet (for example texture-modified, thickened liquids, calorie, allergy or therapeutic diets), the diet is written in the Individual Plan (IP) and ordered by a prescriber or a dietitian, and staff follow it as written. Any limit on food access is an approved rights restriction supported by a specific assessed need in the IP (see PA-02). Staff are trained on each person's diet and on choking prevention and response before working independently, as part of DDA-approved training on characteristics and needs of individuals and staff training under COMAR 10.22.02.11. Transportation to buy food and groceries is part of the daily service rate (Community Pathways Waiver, Appendix C – Community Living – Group Home) and is not charged to residents. Room and board collected from the resident under PCS-01 pays for food, as agreed in the residency agreement.

definitions.definition: A diet changed from regular food in texture, liquid consistency, content or amount because of a health, swallowing, allergy or other medical need.
A written order from a licensed prescriber or registered dietitian stating the diet, texture, liquid consistency and any restrictions.
A swallowing difficulty that can cause choking or aspiration.
A limit on when or what a resident can eat, allowed only as an approved, documented rights restriction under PA-02.

procedures: At admission and at each IP review, the Program Director, RN and person-centered planning team ask each resident about their food preferences, cultural and religious practices, dislikes, allergies, favorite meals, and how they want to be supported at meals. The answers are recorded in the IP.

The RN or Health Care Coordinator reviews each resident's health information for conditions affecting eating, such as swallowing difficulty, diabetes, allergies, weight changes, dental problems and medication effects, and refers for a prescriber or dietitian evaluation where needed.

Any modified diet, texture or liquid consistency is obtained as a written order from a prescriber or dietitian (see NU-01). The order is entered into the IP, the health record and the kitchen diet list, with the person's name, diet, start date and any review date.

The Program Director posts, in a place that respects privacy but is accessible to staff, a current diet list and any allergy information. It is updated the same day a diet order changes, and staff on every shift are told of changes at handoff.

The RN or trained staff teaches all staff the person's diet, how to prepare it (for example, food cut or pureed to the ordered texture, liquids thickened to the ordered level), the right positioning and pacing at meals, and the level of supervision needed at meals.

Staff keep food available at all times. Residents may get snacks, drinks and meals when they wish, and have access to the kitchen and food storage, within any approved and documented restriction based on an assessed need.

Residents shop for food, plan menus and help prepare meals to the extent they want and are able. Menus reflect the residents' choices and are varied and nutritious. Staff offer healthy choices without overriding a resident's right to choose, and document concerns in the IP process (see PA-02, PA-11).

If a resident chooses a food that conflicts with an ordered diet and creates risk, staff explain the risk in a way the person can understand, offer safer alternatives, notify the RN, and document the choice. The team reviews the issue and revises the plan or the supports, including supported decision-making and informed consent (see PA-11).

Food is stored, prepared and served safely, with handwashing, clean surfaces, correct refrigerator and freezer temperatures, labeling and dating of leftovers, and separation of allergens, consistent with PA-15.

Staff are trained on choking prevention and response before working independently, including recognition of choking, abdominal thrusts and calling 911, along with First Aid/CPR. See HW-01 for choking risk assessment and monitoring.

If a resident chokes, staff give first aid immediately and call 911 if the airway is not cleared, or if there is any doubt. They notify the RN and the on-call administrator, and complete an incident report under PA-06. The event is reviewed to determine whether the diet, supervision or plan must change.

Staff record meals and any problems with eating or drinking, refusals, weight concerns or coughing at meals in the daily documentation (see PA-01), and report concerns to the RN under NU-06 without delay.
The RN reviews weights, intake concerns and diet orders at least at each health review and when there is a change of condition, and arranges prescriber or dietitian follow-up.

Any proposed limit on food access (for example, a locked pantry for a person with a medical condition) goes through the rights restriction process under PA-02, requires an assessed need and informed consent, and is documented in the IP and reviewed on schedule. Staff may not limit food as a consequence or for convenience.
The Program Director monitors compliance through meal observation and record review each month, and reports findings to the quality assurance review (see GOV-03).

responsibilities.duty: Offer food choices, follow diet orders exactly, supervise meals as directed, respond to choking, and document intake concerns.
Assess nutrition and swallowing risks, obtain and review diet orders, train staff and follow up on concerns.
Evaluate and order modified diets and review them as needed.
Ensure food is available at all times, diet lists are current, staff are trained and any restriction is properly approved.
Share preferences, take part in decisions on diet and approve any changes under the plan.

documentation: Food preferences and choices recorded in the IP
Prescriber or dietitian diet orders and the current diet list
Staff training records on diets, choking prevention and response, First Aid/CPR
Meal and intake concerns recorded in daily documentation
Incident reports for choking events
Rights restriction documentation for any limit on food access
Monthly meal observation and record review

policies.title: Transportation and Vehicle Safety
policies.applies_to: All staff who drive or arrange transportation, and all vehicles used to transport individuals, at [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To make sure residents can get to the places they choose and need to go safely, that vehicles and drivers meet legal and safety requirements, and that transportation is provided within the daily service rate and without charge to residents.
policies.policy: Transportation is included in the daily rate for Community Living – Group Home (Community Pathways Waiver, Appendix C – Community Living – Group Home). [AGENCY NAME] therefore provides or arranges transportation for residents to medical appointments, work, day activities, community events and other places in their IP, and does not charge residents separately for it. The agency uses the most cost-effective mode of transportation that meets the person's needs and preferences, which may include public transit, rides from family or friends, agency vehicles or accessible paratransit. All agency-owned and agency-used vehicles are insured. Every driver holds a valid driver's license, and staff are at least 18 years old and hold current First Aid/CPR certification. Vehicle evacuation is part of emergency planning (see EP-01). Transportation supports are matched to each person's IP and respect the person's right to community access and independent travel where they are able.

definitions.definition: A vehicle owned, leased or regularly used by [AGENCY NAME] to transport individuals.
The least costly transportation option that safely meets the person's needs, schedule and preferences, such as public transit or paratransit, without limiting community access.
A vehicle equipped with a lift, ramp or tie-downs for people who use wheelchairs or other mobility devices.
A current, unrestricted (or appropriately restricted and complied with) license for the class of vehicle driven.

procedures: At admission and at each IP review, the team documents each person's transportation needs and preferences, including mobility equipment, seating and positioning, behavioral and medical supports, travel training goals and ability to use public transit independently.

The Program Director schedules transportation for appointments, work, activities and other outings in the IP, choosing the most cost-effective mode that meets the person's needs. A cheaper option is not chosen if it would be unsafe or would limit the person's choices or participation.

Before a staff member drives, the Program Director checks and copies a valid driver's license and confirms the staff member is at least 18, holds current First Aid/CPR, and has completed required orientation. A driving record check is completed before driving duties under agency policy, and the record is kept in the personnel file (see SP-04).
A driver must report to the Program Director immediately any suspension, revocation, restriction or loss of license, and may not drive individuals until it is resolved.

The Program Director ensures all vehicles are registered and insured with liability coverage in amounts consistent with [AGENCY NAME]'s insurance policy and legal requirements, and keeps current proof of insurance in the vehicle and in the administrative file.

Each vehicle is inspected and maintained under the manufacturer's schedule and State inspection requirements. Drivers do a quick safety check (tires, lights, brakes, fluid levels, seat belts, lift or ramp) before use, and a maintenance log is kept.

Each vehicle carries a first aid kit, a fire extinguisher, emergency contact numbers, a flashlight, an emergency contact and medical information sheet for each rider, and a current copy of the vehicle evacuation instructions.

All riders use seat belts, and wheelchairs and other mobility devices are secured with tie-downs and appropriate occupant restraints at all times in a moving vehicle. Staff trained on securement operate lifts and ramps.

Drivers do not use handheld phones, text, or drive while impaired, drowsy or distracted. Medications that may impair driving are reported to the supervisor, and the driver does not drive when impaired. Smoking is not permitted in vehicles while individuals are aboard.

Staffing during transportation follows the supervision level in the IP. When a person needs support in the vehicle, a second staff member rides along as needed so the driver is not distracted by the person's needs.

Staff must not use physical restraint in vehicles. Behavior in a vehicle is handled with the positive supports in the person's behavior plan (see PA-08, PA-09). If a rider's behavior makes driving unsafe, the driver pulls over safely and calls the on-call administrator.

In an accident, breakdown or medical emergency, staff move riders to safety, call 911 if anyone is hurt or at risk, provide first aid, and notify the on-call administrator. The administrator notifies guardians or proponents and DDA as the PORII requires, and an incident report is completed (see PA-06).

Vehicle evacuation procedures are included in emergency planning, covering how riders are safely taken out of the vehicle, secured and sheltered if the vehicle is disabled or a disaster occurs (see EP-01, EP-02). Staff practice these procedures at least annually.
